items.summary: We present and validate an Implicit Monte Carlo (IMC) radiation-transport solver in the open-source, mesh-agnostic storm library, coupled to the moving-mesh hydrodynamics code rich in three-dimensional Voronoi tessellations. The solver is multigroup, or continuous in frequency, throughout; it transforms photon packets exactly between the comoving and laboratory frames, books every exchange with the material as a laboratory four-momentum so that the IMC path conserves energy to roundoff, formulates the Fleck factor in the fluid's proper time, and accelerates optically thick cells with multigroup Discrete Diffusion Monte Carlo (DDMC) behind an emissivity-preserving interface. We tested the solver on a broad suite of benchmark problems, and it performed well on all of them. The solver is built on the MPI-parallel Monte Carlo framework of storm, which scales to 13,440 cores.

items.title: Superradiant temporal transition radiation of a relativistic electron beam
items.summary: A charge in uniform motion carries a bound field that does not radiate. Transition radiation releases part of it at a boundary in space. We propose and analyze the case of radiation emission due to a boundary in time: a relativistic electron bunch passes through an aperture in a semiconductor (silicon) wafer, and while its bound field occupies the wafer, a femtosecond laser switches the semiconductor into an electron-hole plasma. The field is a valid solution of the old medium and not of the new one, so it is handed to the plasma as an initial condition for radiation emission at the plasma frequency. Because in temporal transition radiation (t-TR) the wavevector is conserved, and the frequency is not, the emission can appear in a spectral band that the bunch's own field does not populate. Every electron contributes in phase to the initial condition at the switching moment, so the emitted energy scales as $N^2$. We derive the field energy conversion at the temporal boundary and the resultant measurable amplitude and frequency line-shape of the radiation taking into consideration plasma carriers collisional loss. The simplified analytical model of the process and its scaling laws are confirmed by use of FDTD numerical computations for a reference case based on the parameters of an existing 6.5 MeV photoinjector accelerator. For this case we predict wideband t-TR radiation emission at THz frequencies, where the emission center frequency, near the plasma frequency, is selectable across an octave, set by the laser fluence, and the intensity is governed by the beam charge. The predicted radiative energy is detectable in a single shot. The experimental considerations for observing it are given in a Supplement.

items.title: Photon production at Kepler escape threshold
items.summary: We obtain an exact closed-form total photon count for a prescribed Newtonian Kepler parabola, with a fully relativistic treatment of its radiation. We also obtain closed expressions for the angularly resolved photon spectrum and elementary expressions for the total radiated energy and momenta. The count is finite, scale-independent, and analytic in subluminal speed at closest approach. At large maximum rapidity $η$, $N\sim(7α/\sqrt6)η$, while $E\propto e^{3η}$ at fixed passage timescale: the radiation chiefly hardens. For slow motion at fixed coupling and closest distance, a nearby ellipse emits fewer photons but more energy and angular momentum per orbit. The hyperbolic photon count remains IR divergent arbitrarily close to threshold, while the count at the exact parabolic threshold is finite.

items.title: Neptuna: A Comprehensive Machine Learning Framework for Benchmarking Complex Multiphase Flows
items.summary: Compressible multiphase flows involving shocks and material interfaces arise in applications such as bubble collapse and droplet breakup, where strong nonlinear interactions produce complex interface deformation, mixing, and multiscale dynamics. Developing reliable machine learning surrogates for these flows remains challenging due to the simultaneous presence of compressibility, sharp discontinuities, and multiphase effects. In this work, we introduce the first large-scale benchmark specifically designed for shock-driven compressible multiphase flows, comprising 3 TB of high-fidelity 2D and 3D datasets featuring shock-induced bubble collapse and droplet breakup. We evaluate diverse surrogate model families on our benchmarking framework: Neptuna, including convolutional, spectral, transformer-based, and pre-trained PDE foundation models. Beyond standard MSE training, we investigate composite losses that combine MSE with Sobolev, interface-aware, and structure-aware terms, along with adaptive loss balancing using SoftAdapt and GradNorm. Evaluation includes pointwise, spectral, feature-focused, structural, and physics-informed metrics. Results show that no single model performs best across all datasets and metrics, while composite losses significantly improve interface preservation and spectral fidelity. Among adaptive weighting strategies, SoftAdapt provides the most consistent improvements with almost no overhead compared to MSE-only training. The benchmarking repository and the dataset are made available at \url{https://tumaer.github.io/Neptuna/}

items.title: Self-organizing reinforcement learning: a swarm approaches the explore-exploit optimum
items.summary: The explore/exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). We show that a minimal foraging swarm approaches its optimum - the ideal-free / Nash allocation of a multi-agent resource-sharing game (an equilibrium, not a return maximum) - with no learner and no reward signal. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; this cascade cycle balances exploration and exploitation and drives foragers toward the ideal free distribution. The swarm attains the shape of this optimum (committed foragers track richness with slope 0.94) but not its exact equilibrium - it stays measurably exploitable - reaching it dynamically (~150 steps) through the coupling of recruitment to movement: remove the coupling and matching collapses (0.94 -> 0.08). The RL sits at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule: no step evaluates payoff (reward-free by construction, though the crowd signal is informationally tied to payoff), and the swarm reaches the allocation without learning it (quality plateaus and re-settles after resources move, no cumulative gain). Against a trained baseline the comparison is two-sided: in an easier, disembodied game a learner is more precise, while in the same embodied environment the reward-free swarm reaches ~65% of a validated oracle ceiling at zero training and leads until trained PPO and centralised-critic (CTDE) learners overtake it (~74-75%, 16 seeds, all above the swarm mean) after ~4,000 of 15,000 training steps - its advantage is in budget, not asymptote. In this one setting we read it not as beating RL but as a strong zero-shot, reward-free operating point: a demonstration that the self-organizing physics of a minimal swarm can carry a collective close to the optimum RL seeks, with none of RL's machinery.

items.title: Generative marginal learning for finite-size molecular simulation with application to stress calculation
items.summary: We propose generative marginal learning (GML), a framework for equilibrium sampling and local observable estimation in molecular simulations. By training a conditional diffusion model on large-system simulations, GML learns the marginal distribution of a retained region, enabling configuration generation without explicitly simulating the surrounding environment or imposing periodic boundary conditions on the retained region. We derive a marginal effective potential and the associated conditional mean-force identity, which provide the basis for both denoising and force-alignment training. As an application, we estimate the spatially averaged Irving--Kirkwood stress near a vacancy defect. Numerical results demonstrate that GML substantially improves pair structure and local stress accuracy compared with small periodic molecular dynamics simulations, mitigating finite-size effects in calculating local molecular observables.

items.title: Operator-Level Description of Transient Thermal Grating Dynamics Across Transport Regimes
items.summary: Transient thermal grating (TTG) experiments provide a powerful means of probing material properties and heat-transport dynamics at small spatiotemporal scales through the temporal response to a spatially periodic excitation. However, quantitative interpretation of the measured transient requires a forward model that consistently connects energy deposition, subsequent heat transport, and the detected TTG observable over the experimental timescale. A unified formulation linking these stages remains insufficiently developed in the TTG context. Here, we formulate a continuum, operator-based TTG forward model that describes the sequence from energy deposition through thermal transport to the temporal evolution of the selected spatial temperature mode within a unified transfer-function framework, while leaving the instrument-specific detection process outside the scope of the present formulation. Heat-transport dynamics are represented by a temporal memory kernel, allowing unresolved relaxation processes to be incorporated into the macroscopic response. The framework provides a basis for assessing the identifiability of thermal diffusivity, heat-propagation speed, and heat-flux relaxation time when flux-memory effects are resolved on the experimental timescale. These macroscopic parameters can, in turn, inform the microscopic interpretation of the measured dynamics. Analysis of the resulting model further demonstrates that the observability of heat-flux memory is not equivalent to the presence of oscillations in the measured response. Oscillations can provide a clear signature of finite flux-relaxation dynamics, but their absence does not establish the validity of Fourier heat conduction: finite flux relaxation dynamics need not produce experimentally observable oscillations under all conditions.

items.title: Dynamic Hotspot Migration and Self-Induced Resonances in Ultrafast Laser-Irradiated Silicon Thin Films
items.summary: The spatial distribution of energy in silicon thin films under femtosecond laser irradiation is demonstrated to be influenced by the interaction between carrier-induced refractive index modulation and self-induced Fabry-Pérot resonances. We resolve three characteristic excitation regions such as interface-localized, binodal and multi-nodal regimes considering the analysis of silicon-on-insulator (SOI) configurations across thicknesses of 100, 230, and 350 nm. We report a nonlinear hotspot migration effect where the transient reduction of the refractive index stretches the internal standing wave, translating intensity antinodes toward the film volume during the pulse. Numerical results demonstrate that at higher fluences, plasma-induced extinction suppresses internal reflections, triggering a transition from resonance-mediated absorption to plasma shielding. These findings establish a physical basis for depth-resolved modification in laser nanomanufacturing, providing a dual-capacity for simultaneous surface patterning and depth-resolved subsurface modification with direct applications in laser-assisted interfacial separation and 3D integrated photonic fabrication.

items.title: Spontaneous brain-wide rotational dynamics constrain cue-evoked behavior
items.summary: Uncovering low-dimensional representations of brain-wide neural dynamics and their relationship to behavior remains a central challenge. Here, we show that spontaneous brain-wide rotational dynamics constrain cue-evoked behavior and learning. To systematically establish these findings, we developed a dimensionality-reduction technique called Rotational Component Analysis (RCA) that optimizes the detection of low-variance rotational modes even within individual trials. We applied RCA to motor-cortical spike-train data from monkeys and humans, mouse cortex-wide calcium imaging, and human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). In mice, a rotational mode identified from activity recorded at rest predicts cue-evoked behavior: the phase of rotation when a randomly timed cue arrives predicts whether the animal subsequently pulls the lever. We explain this surprisingly strong correlation using both a recurrent neural network (RNN) and a minimal two-dimensional model of response learning, in which the intrinsic rotational mode serves as a dynamical constraint on response and learning. We further identify double-rotation modes containing two centers of rotation that separate preparatory from task dynamics in both mouse and human data. Remarkably, corresponding modes also organize neural dynamics during a non-motor human task, and rotational irreversibility captures early psychosis even when principal component analysis shows no group difference. Our work establishes rotational dynamics as low-dimensional coordinates that constrain how ongoing brain states are converted into behavior. More broadly, RCA provides a versatile tool for detecting hidden nonreciprocal dynamics in biological and physical datasets.

items.title: SynradG4: A Geant4-Based Extension for Synchrotron Radiation Background Studies in the ePIC Detector at the Electron-Ion Collider
items.summary: The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) will operate at high luminosity with multi-GeV, high-current electron beams, resulting in substantial synchrotron radiation (SR) emission in the electron storage ring (ESR). A detailed understanding of SR photon transport in the complex three-dimensional interaction region (IR) geometry is critical for estimating backgrounds in the ePIC detector and for developing effective shielding and masking strategies. This paper presents SynradG4, an EIC-specific extension of Geant4 for fast photon tracking in vacuum based on established models of SR reflection and rough-surface scattering. SynradG4 integrates the specular and diffuse photon reflection models of Synrad+ into the Geant4 geometry and field framework, while disabling all bulk matter interactions to achieve high-statistics transport through the 50-m-long IR vacuum system. The absorbed photons are then passed to a second-stage DD4hep simulation, in which electromagnetic processes such as photoabsorption, Compton scattering, Rayleigh scattering, and fluorescence are enabled for their propagation through the beam pipe and detector materials. SynradG4 is not intended to replace general SR simulation codes; rather, it complements them by providing the workflow and geometry integration capabilities needed for EIC-specific background studies. Benchmark tests show that SynradG4 reproduces Synrad+ to within about 1% for both specular and diffuse reflection, and that it agrees well with Synrad3D and with the native Geant4 X-ray reflection model for smooth surfaces. Using the full IR geometry and machine lattice, we present the first SR background estimates for the ePIC detector and evaluate the impact of potential SR masks.

items.title: Refined Gradient-Based Temperature Optimization for the Replica-Exchange Monte-Carlo Method
items.summary: The replica-exchange Monte-Carlo (RXMC) method is a powerful Markov-chain Monte-Carlo algorithm for sampling from multi-modal distributions, which are challenging for conventional methods. The sampling efficiency of the RXMC method depends highly on the selection of the temperatures, and finding optimal temperatures remains a challenge. In this study, we propose a refined online temperature selection method by extending the gradient-based optimization framework proposed previously. Building upon the existing temperature update approach, we introduce a reparameterization technique to strictly enforce physical constraints, such as the monotonic ordering of inverse temperatures, which were not explicitly addressed in the original formulation. The proposed method defines the variance of acceptance rates between adjacent replicas as a loss function, estimates its gradient using differential information from the sampling process, and optimizes the temperatures via gradient descent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments on benchmark spin systems, including the two-dimensional ferromagnetic Ising model, the two-dimensional ferromagnetic XY model, and the three-dimensional Edwards-Anderson model. Our results show that the method successfully achieves uniform acceptance rates and reduces round-trip times across the temperature space. Furthermore, our proposed method offers a significant advantage over recently proposed policy gradient method that require careful hyperparameter tuning, while simultaneously preventing the constraint violations that destabilize optimization.

items.title: A Level Set Method on Particle Flow Maps
items.summary: Accurate interface tracking is central to numerical simulations involving moving boundaries, including multiphase flows, free-surface dynamics, phase-change problems, and other interface-driven processes in computational mechanics. Although level set methods provide a flexible implicit representation of evolving interfaces, their grid-based advection and reinitialization procedures often introduce numerical diffusion, volume loss, and degradation of thin or highly curved structures. This paper introduces a Particle Flow Map Level Set (PFM-LS) method that addresses these limitations by transporting interface geometry through particle-carried bidirectional flow maps. In contrast to particle level set methods that use particles mainly as corrective markers, PFM-LS uses particles as primary carriers of level-set values, gradients, and Hessians within a narrow band around the interface. The method combines long-range flow-map transport, high-order particle-grid reconstruction, adaptive particle control, and a hybrid particle-grid redistancing scheme to preserve both signed-distance consistency and sub-grid geometric features. Numerical benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including topology-change tests, chamfer and Hausdorff shape-error metrics, and coupling to an incompressible free-surface flow solver, show that PFM-LS achieves strong volume preservation, high shape fidelity, and near fourth-order convergence, outperforming a broad range of existing level set and reference-map-based methods.

items.title: Fast and High-Fidelity Motional-State-Preserving Transport in Optical Tweezers
items.summary: Reconfigurable neutral-atom processors require rapid, high-fidelity transport of atoms between optical-tweezer sites. In finite-depth Gaussian traps, fast motion can leave residual motional excitation even when the atom reaches its destination. We develop a basis-parameterized gradient-ascent pulse-engineering (GRAPE) framework for one-dimensional transport of a single $^{87}$Rb atom. A shortcut-to-adiabaticity reference is refined using 17 trajectory parameters, with ten additional parameters providing bounded trap-depth modulation; depth affects both confinement and the inverse construction of the physical trap center. For a $12.6\,μ$m transfer completed in only $30.5\,μ$s, corresponding to approximately $2.75$ periods of the reference trap, the selected joint protocol achieves a ground-state infidelity of $2.41\times10^{-7}$. Because preparing an exactly pure motional ground state is experimentally challenging, we also optimize population-weighted transport for initial distributions with mean vibrational occupations $\nbar\simeq0.16$ and $1.87$, reaching same-state probabilities of about $0.99993$ and $0.9934$. Trap-depth fluctuations can further degrade transport fidelity. Robust optimization under a measurement-informed depth-noise model improves the mean error, worst sampled error, and fidelity dispersion for the specified noise realizations. Coordinated control of tweezer position and confinement thus offers a route to rapid transport with low residual excitation for flexible atom rearrangement and dynamic connectivity in neutral-atom processors.

items.title: A New Theory of the Dark Photon and Its Preliminary Experimental Verification
items.summary: The dark photon defined in this paper is fundamentally different from the dark photon in the traditional kinetic mixing framework. According to the principle of energy conservation, a complete moving photon is defined in this work as a binary composite entity consisting of a dark photon and a light-wave component. The dark photon embodies the particle nature of light, while the light-wave embodies the wave nature of light. When the light source is turned off or the light-wave component is absorbed by matter, the complete photon loses its light-wave component and transforms into a pure dark photon state. In conventional high-energy physics, dark photons from kinetic mixing scenarios exhibit no direct electromagnetic coupling and cannot be detected through experiments. In distinct contrast, the dark photon proposed in this work possesses intrinsic particle properties of light, enables direct electromagnetic interaction, and can induce the photoelectric effect upon incidence on a metal surface. Based on this self-consistent definition, a systematic theory of dark photons is established, which provides reasonable physical interpretations for several currently controversial optical phenomena. The experimental scheme in this paper is designed strictly based on the above theoretical premise. Preliminary tabletop experimental results verify the rationality and feasibility of the proposed dark photon theory.

items.title: Large Language Model Steering of Acousto-Optic Tweezer Arrays
items.summary: Controlling quantum hardware requires choosing and revising experimental strategies as nonlinear response, coupling, and drift limit calibration. We experimentally investigate a general-purpose large language model (LLM) as a human-in-the-loop strategy layer for a neutral-atom tweezer platform. Through step-by-step interaction with experimental feedback, the LLM guides a transition from multiplicative row--column correction to a drift-corrected local response-matrix method when separable feedback stalls. Deterministic software performs image analysis and numerical updates, while an experimentalist verifies and authorizes each waveform. For a $10\times10$ crossed-acousto-optic-deflector array, this workflow reduces the Gaussian-peak coefficient of variation from $20.30\%$ to $1.57\%$ in 30 candidate-update rounds. The experiment demonstrates feedback-informed strategy selection on a physical quantum-control subsystem, rather than direct generation of control parameters alone. These results highlight the potential of LLMs to guide control optimization across diverse quantum platforms by adaptively formulating and refining experimental strategies.

items.title: HEXRD and HEXRDGUI: a flexible toolkit for X-ray diffraction analysis in dynamic compression experiments
items.summary: This article describes the application of HEXRD, an open-source Python library for X-ray diffraction analysis, and HEXRDGUI, its companion graphical application, to dynamic compression experiments. Built on a generic multi-detector geometric model, the toolkit supports arbitrary instrument configurations with independently positioned planar or cylindrical detector panels, arbitrary beam directions, and multiple X-ray sources. It calibrates instruments from powder rings, Laue spots or the rings of an unknown phase, fits whole patterns by Le Bail or Rietveld refinement, and imports data from the TARDIS, FIDDLE and PXRDIP platforms at the National Ignition Facility (NIF) and OMEGA EP. Although originally developed for high-energy diffraction microscopy at synchrotron sources, HEXRD has been adopted as an analysis tool for dynamic compression X-ray diffraction experiments at facilities including the NIF, the Matter in Extreme Conditions end-station at the Linac Coherent Light Source, the Dynamic Compression Sector (DCS) at the Advanced Photon Source, OMEGA EP at the Laboratory for Laser Energetics, and the High Energy Density (HED) instrument at the European XFEL. Calibrated from the same ring positions on a single planar detector, HEXRD and the independent code pyFAI predict the same scattering angle 2$θ$ to numerical precision. On a dual-source dataset from the NIF, calibrating the detectors against both X-ray sources at once fits the rings of both to an RMS of 0.18° in 2$θ$, about one image-plate pixel, whereas a fit to either source alone, with the plate tilts held at their nominal values, fits its own rings nearly as well but mispredicts the other's by about 0.6°. The software is freely available under a BSD license.

items.title: Strong Thermal Conductivity Suppression in Isotope Purified Single Crystal Diamond with Phonon Scatterings of Color Centers
items.summary: The thermal conductivity of natural diamond can be further improved by ~50% by eliminating isotope impurity to obtain pure 12C diamond. However, unlike isolated point defects, how color centers scatter phonons and correspondingly limit the thermal conductivity remain poorly understood. Here, we report the thermal conductivities of two isotope-purified diamond with different Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) color center concentrations, confirmed by photoluminescence (PL) and secondary-ion mass spectrometry (SIMS). Results show ~ 3200 W m-1 K-1 and ~ 2100 W m-1 K-1 for two samples of low and high NV concentrations, respectively. Modified Callaway model analyses show that first-principles-derived scattering parameters can reproduce room-temperature thermal conductivity of the high NV concentration sample under a vacancy concentration assumption (~30% of the total Nitrogen concentration), but fail to reproduce its temperature dependence. Compared to PL and SIMS results, which show ~7.1-fold NV concentration and ~92-fold difference in total Nitrogen concentration between two samples, suggesting the assumed 30% vacancy fraction may be greatly overestimated. Taken together, these results suggest that NV-color-center defects may scatter phonons more strongly than models treating Nitrogen and vacancy as independent point defects, providing new insights into color-center-induced phonon-scattering mechanisms.

items.title: Active rheology shapes collective flows in uniaxially compressed 3D spheroids
items.summary: How compression changes both the magnitude and organization of cell motion remains unclear. Using a three-dimensional active vertex model, we examine how tissue state and active dynamics shape the response of confined spheroids to uniaxial compression. With polarity alignment switched off, compression enhances transverse motion in solid-like spheroids throughout the tested activity range, whereas the fluid-like response reverses from acceleration at low activity to slowing at high activity. Changes in contact persistence organize these responses along a common empirical trend. Passive five-cell calculations reveal how compression reshapes local rearrangement barriers: the response depends on geometry and loading direction, and a high-strain increase in the fluid-like mean coexists with many low-barrier paths. In a separate high-alignment regime, strong compression induces coherent rotation in solid-like spheroids, while fluid-like spheroids show no comparable collective rotation. The rotating solids have a higher contact-persistence index than the fluids and exhibit tangential peripheral cell organization. Controlled perturbations reveal compression-induced softening of a differential-twist mode and slower relaxation with activity. Together, these results identify an activity-dependent reversal of the motility response and compression-induced coherent rotation as two distinct outcomes of loading, linking them to contact persistence, local rearrangement costs, and active coordination.

items.title: On the bottom-up construction of many-electron relativistic QED Hamiltonian
items.summary: It was shown more than a decade ago [J. Chem. Phys. 139, 014108 (2013)] that a many-electron relativistic quantum electrodynamics (QED) Hamiltonian for high-precision electronic structure calculations can be constructed in a bottom-up fashion, by virtue of charge-conjugated contraction (CCC) of fermion operators when normal-ordering the starting unbounded relativistic Hamiltonian (second-quantized in terms of the electronic Dirac field) with respect to the filled negative-energy Dirac sea of electrons. It is shown here that the same relativistic QED Hamiltonian can also be obtained by equal average of the two relativistic Hamiltonians resulting from the normal-ordering of the starting unbounded relativistic Hamiltonians (second-quantized in terms of the electronic and positronic Dirac fields, respectively) with respect to the filled negative-energy Dirac seas of electrons and positrons, respectively, via the standard contraction of fermion operators. In essence, both procedures incorporate properly the fundamental charge-conjugation symmetry of relativistic quantum mechanics to ensure the symmetric treatment of the electronic and positronic degrees of freedom.

items.title: PASPT2: a size-extensive and size-consistent partial-active-space multi-state multi-reference second-order perturbation theory for strongly correlated electrons
items.summary: A partial-active-space (PAS) multi-state (MS) multi-reference second-order perturbation theory (MRPT2) for the electronic structure of strongly correlated systems of electrons, dubbed PASPT2, is formulated by linearizing the intermediate normalization-based general-model-space state-universal coupled-cluster theory with singles and doubles [IN-GMS-SU-CCSD; J. Chem. Phys. 119, 5320 (2003)]. At variance with the existence of disconnected terms in the IN-GMS-SU-CCSD amplitude equations, the disconnected terms in the PASPT2 amplitude equations can be avoided completely by choosing a special reference-specific zeroth-order Hamiltonian. The corresponding effective/intermediate Hamiltonian can also be made connected and closed, so as to render the energies obtained by diagonalization fully connected. As such, PASPT2 is strictly size-extensive, in sharp contrast with the parent IN-GMS-SU-CCSD. It is also size-consistent when the PAS of a supermolecule is chosen to be the direct product of those of the physically separated, non-interacting fragments. Prototypical systems are taken as showcases to reveal the efficacy of PASPT2.

items.title: Undulatory Swimming in Sand: Subsurface Locomotion of the Sandfish Lizard
items.summary: The desert-dwelling sandfish (Scincus scincus) moves within dry sand, a material that displays solid and fluidlike behavior. High-speed x-ray imaging shows that below the surface, the lizard no longer uses limbs for propulsion but generates thrust to overcome drag by propagating an undulatory traveling wave down the body. Although viscous hydrodynamics can predict swimming speed in fluids such as water, an equivalent theory for granular drag is not available. To predict sandfish swimming speed, we developed an empirical model by measuring granular drag force on a small cylinder oriented at different angles relative to the displacement direction and summing these forces over the animal movement profile. The agreement between model and experiment implies that the noninertial swimming occurs in a frictional fluid.

items.title: Sensitive dependence of the motion of a legged robot on granular media
items.summary: Legged locomotion on flowing ground ({\em e.g.} granular media) is unlike locomotion on hard ground because feet experience both solid- and fluid-like forces during surface penetration. Recent bio-inspired legged robots display speed relative to body size on hard ground comparable to high performing organisms like cockroaches but suffer significant performance loss on flowing materials like sand. In laboratory experiments we study the performance (speed) of a small (2.3 kg) six-legged robot, SandBot, as it runs on a bed of granular media (1 mm poppy seeds). For an alternating tripod gait on the granular bed, standard gait control parameters achieve speeds at best two orders of magnitude smaller than the 2 body lengths/s ($\approx 60$ cm/s) for motion on hard ground. However, empirical adjustment of these control parameters away from the hard ground settings, restores good performance, yielding top speeds of 30 cm/s. Robot speed depends sensitively on the packing fraction $φ$ and the limb frequency $ω$, and a dramatic transition from rotary walking to slow swimming occurs when $φ$ becomes small enough and/or $ω$ large enough. We propose a kinematic model of the rotary walking mode based on generic features of penetration and slip of a curved limb in granular media. The model captures the dependence of robot speed on limb frequency and the transition between walking and swimming modes but highlights the need for a deeper understanding of the physics of granular media.

items.title: Second-Order Correction for Statistical Bias in Monte Carlo Depletion Calculations
items.summary: Depletion analyses are often driven by Monte Carlo neutron transport methods that introduce uncertainty into the transmutation matrix used to evolve a material composition. The nonlinearity of the matrix exponential applied to this transmutation matrix causes the uncertainty to introduce a systematic bias in the computed isotope vectors. This work derives a second-order correction for this bias that can be computed with quantities obtainable from typical Monte Carlo transport routines. An augmented Bateman system is formulated to evaluate these quantities and an adapted Chebyshev rational approximation method uses transmutation matrix factorizations for efficient evaluation of the second-order correction. Then, the correction is demonstrated using a ten-nuclide verification problem, an ITER port-plug activation problem, and a 9-pin boiling water reactor lattice containing self-shielded gadolinium-bearing fuel.

items.title: Frustration and topology in the phase behavior of solute-frustrated $q$-clock models
items.summary: Frustration can enhance fluctuations and create new and interesting phase behavior. When combined with the ability to host topological defects, frustration can increase the complexity of a system's phase diagram through topological and frustrated topological transitions. To understand the interplay of frustration and topology on phase behavior, we introduce and study solute-frustrated $q$-clock (SF$q$C) models, in which solute sites are added to the $q$-clock model, a lattice model where each spin can take one of $q$ orientations. The $q$-clock model can exhibit spontaneous symmetry breaking and topological transitions, and the interaction between the spins and a solute frustrates the system, in essence by creating a fixed lower bound on the concentration of positive topological defects or vortices. We perform Monte Carlo simulations and develop theoretical descriptions of SF$q$C models with $q=4$ and $q=6$ to understand their phase behavior. We find that these systems exhibit rich phase diagrams that depend on the choice of parameters. In particular, SF$q$C models have a wide range of interesting low-temperature phases, including the presence of strongly frustrated domains and the absence of long-range order. We also find topological effects even at low temperatures; for instance, we find that topological defects can drive crystallization. We anticipate these results to guide the development of materials that take advantage of frustration and topology to tune phase behavior and fluctuations.

items.title: A robust and modular cesium magneto-optical trap using divergent laser beams
items.summary: Magneto-optical traps (MOTs) are a workhorse technology for neutral-atom quantum sensing, simulation, and computing. Here, we demonstrate a MOT optimized for inertial quantum sensing and precision metrology applications. Our MOT traps $4\times10^8$ cesium (Cs) atoms in a robust, modular system that achieves stable operation through two design features: (1) we use divergent cooling laser beams to reduce unwanted reflections and (2) optical elements are mounted in a fiber-coupled, compact, and modular cage rigidly attached to the vacuum chamber. Following polarization-gradient cooling (PGC), the system produces atom samples with temperatures below 10 $μ$K, similar to those achieved in conventional MOTs that use collimated laser beams. In addition, we observe trapping of $2\times10^7$ Cs atoms in a non-conventional MOT geometry, where the cooling laser beams are diagonal to the principal axis of the quadrupole magnetic field.

items.title: Distorted-Wave calculations of atomic ionization by bare ions and antiprotons
items.summary: We present \textit{ab initio} calculations of atomic ionization by bare ions and antiprotons within the continuum distorted-wave eikonal initial-state (CDW-EIS) model. The dataset covers atomic targets from H to Kr, impacted by bare ions over a broad range of projectile charges and by antiprotons. Particular attention is given to elements in periods 3 and 4 of the periodic table, which are relevant to pigment analysis and technologically important materials. The resulting subshell-resolved total ionization cross sections are made openly available through an online repository covering a broad range of projectile--target systems, occupied initial subshells, and projectile velocities. We analyze systematic trends in the cross sections, including their dependence on projectile charge and velocity, binding-energy scaling, and charge-sign effects in proton and antiproton impact. To extend the practical coverage of the database, we also develop a neural-network surrogate, CDWEIS-NN, trained on the subset of the database with projectile charge $|Z_\mathrm{P}|\leq 8$. The network interpolates the CDW-EIS results to additional projectile--target systems and impact energies, reproducing both held-out CDW-EIS calculations and the experimental benchmarks considered in this work with satisfactory accuracy.

items.title: Hidden Perturbative Structure in Attosecond Streaking
items.summary: Attosecond streaking is inherently multiphoton, yet we uncover a hidden perturbative structure revealing the underlying continuum--continuum angular-momentum propensity. By filtering the inversion-odd response in helium streaking data at the IR fundamental, we isolate an angular distribution dominated by the $P_1$ and $P_3$ Legendre components, whose complex coefficients yield an effective $s/d$ two-photon amplitude ratio. Multichannel, two-electron time-dependent Schrödinger equation calculations demonstrate that the characteristic Fano propensity survives electron correlation. Incorporating the experimental XUV attochirp reproduces the measured emission-edge trend, while near-threshold calculations predict resonant amplitude and phase signatures associated with the bound He $np$ Rydberg series. This symmetry- and frequency-filtering approach offers a general spectroscopic framework with potential applications to atomic, molecular, and solid-state systems where attosecond streaking is established.

items.title: Scaling laws for contamination traversal times during vacuum breaks in superconducting accelerators
items.summary: A sudden loss of vacuum in a superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) accelerator drives warm gas into the evacuated beamline, where it propagates through interconnected SRF cavities cooled by liquid helium, causing surface contamination, intense heat deposition, and dangerous pressure buildup. Yet predicting how such a failure propagates through realistic multicell cavities has remained difficult because compressible gas dynamics, condensation and cryogenic heat transfer are strongly coupled. Here we develop and experimentally validate a multidimensional computational framework that resolves these processes, and apply it to a full-scale nine-cell SRF cavity. We find that the repeated cell geometry produces staircase-like gas-front propagation, as impingement, recirculation and localized cryopumping strongly retard the bulk flow within each cell. Across a broad range of breach sizes, the cavity traversal time follows a robust power-law scaling with leakage area, providing quantitative guidance for the response time of beamline isolation and protection systems. The simulations also reveal a geometry-confined Mach disk whose position and size track the advancing gas front, suggesting that its acoustic emission could potentially enable rapid, non-invasive detection and localization of vacuum failures. These findings pave the way for a new generation of predictive diagnostics and protection strategies to safeguard large-scale superconducting accelerators.

items.title: A general mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy
items.summary: Foraging recruitment is a contagion: an agent finding a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade -- the model for rumour and adoption spread on social networks -- embedded in space. Because activation is degree-normalized, the same rule that spreads the cascade also stifles it as neighbourhoods crowd (density-dependent blocking), so the swarm aggregates on a resource, then releases to explore again. The cascade runs on the communication network, but acting on it moves agents in physical space, and that motion rewires the network: network and physical space are one coupled system, and this feedback -- not tuning -- makes the coordination self-limiting. Because recruitment chains along the graph rather than near neighbours alone, whether a discovery stays local or spans the swarm is a matter of percolation, and past a critical connectivity the swarm holds itself in a cascade window -- locally near-critical though globally subcritical, a self-organized, sandpile-like drive-avalanche cycle. Nothing is tuned, yet behaviours foraging biology documents separately emerge together -- recruitment, marginal-value patch-leaving, and Levy search with a switch to local exploitation. These are not coincidences but one least-committal principle: the resource field and the search both follow from maximum entropy -- Levy search matched to the field's sparsity, recruitment to its clustering, so active-matter order and optimal foraging are one system in two domains. The gains are real but conditional: up to 7.6x the harvest of solitary search when resources are sparse and clustered, shrinking to nothing when search is already easy. Percolating cascades yield a large return on minimal communication. And that sparse, clustered field is the generic one -- resources almost inevitably aggregate, and maximum entropy makes it the least-committal one once they do -- so one untuned rule should recur widely.

items.title: A 4-20 GHz Superconducting 90deg Hybrid Using Capacitively Loaded Coupled Lines for 2SB Heterodyne Receivers
items.summary: We report the design and cryogenic characterisation of a broadband superconducting 90deg intermediate-frequency (IF) hybrid covering 4 to 20 GHz for sideband-separating (2SB) heterodyne receivers. The hybrid is implemented in thin-film niobium using capacitively loaded edge coupled transmission lines, avoiding the air-bridge interconnections required in Lange-coupler layouts while retaining a compact superconducting implementation with low loss and good quadrature balance. Cryogenic measurements using Vector Network Analyser (VNA) show amplitude and phase imbalance better than 0.6 dB and 6deg, respectively, across the full band. When used in a 2SB receiver, this level of IF balance is consistent with the observed image-rejection performance in the 10-20 dB range, for the full receiver. The design supports the development of wide-instantaneous-bandwidth 2SB receivers for millimeter and submillimeter observatories, improving spectral grasp for broadband line surveys and high-redshift line searches.

items.title: Only skin deep? Depth-resolved photo-oxidation of 3D printed polymers PLA, ABS, PETG, HIPS and PC after 322 days of continuous UV exposure
items.summary: This study investigates the effect of long-term UV radiation exposure on the mechanical and structural properties of selected polymeric materials - PLA, ABS, ABST, PETG, HIPS and PC - fabricated using 3D-print based Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) method. Existing research in the field of polymers weathering has predominantly examined combined degradation factors (UV irradiation, humidity and thermal cycling) over the timescales rarely exceeding a few months, which prevents attribution of property changes to individual agents. To isolate the contribution of UV radiation specifically, samples were exposed up to 7744 consecutive hours (i.e. 322 days) of UV irradiation in an environmental cell with controlled humidity and temperature. The mechanical properties were characterized using nanoindentation, which allows for spatially resolved measurements of hardness and elastic modulus in the near-surface region, thereby enabling the detection of degradation gradients on the order of tens of micrometers. The lack of methodological consistency in the current literature hinders the cross-material comparison; this study addresses the gap by applying nanoindentation uniformly across wide range of selected materials prepared and tested under identical conditions, while studying these properties after a very long exposure to UV radiation.

items.title: $f$-2$f$ self-referencing for silicon nitride photonics via a heterogeneously integrated lithium niobate layer
items.summary: Heterogeneous integration combines complementary material properties in a single photonic platform. Here, we demonstrate on-chip $f$-2$f$ self-referencing in a heterogeneously integrated Si$_3$N$_4$/LiNbO$_3$ platform, in which supercontinuum generation in a Si$_3$N$_4$ waveguide and second-harmonic generation in a LiNbO$_3$ layer are spatially separated and linked by adiabatic escalator couplers. Pumped by a 1560 nm mode-locked laser with 75 pJ on-chip pulse energy, we detect the carrier-envelope offset frequency with 30 dB signal-to-noise ratio in 300 kHz resolution bandwidth. A comparative measurement confirms that the second harmonic originates in the LiNbO$_3$ layer and indicates opportunity for further improvements through periodic poling. These results establish heterogeneous Si$_3$N$_4$/LiNbO$_3$ integration as a viable building block for self-referenced ultrafast pulse sources in low-loss Si$_3$N$_4$ photonics.

items.title: When Does Cheap Physics Help? Gated Multi-Fidelity Physics-Informed Networks with Provable Sample Savings and Conformal Guarantees
items.summary: High-fidelity (HF) simulations of parametric partial differential equations are expensive, whereas low-fidelity (LF) models such as coarse grids or simplified physics are cheap but biased. Multi-fidelity physics-informed neural networks combine the two, yet it remains unclear when cheap physics actually reduces the number of HF solves, and existing methods silently fail when the LF model is misleading and offer no guaranteed uncertainty. We answer the first question with a sharp sample-complexity bound: learning the HF field through its discrepancy from the LF model reduces the number of HF samples needed for accuracy $\varepsilon$ by the factor $κ^{2γ}$, where $κ$ is the ratio of the complexity of the discrepancy to that of the HF field and $γ$ is the effective-dimension exponent, and we confirm the predicted scaling with exact risk computations in a kernel model. Guided by the analysis, we propose GaMF-PINN, a gated multi-fidelity PINN that learns where to trust the LF model and falls back to physics-only learning where it does not, together with a function-level conformal procedure that returns uncertainty bands containing the entire HF solution with probability at least $1-α$ in finite samples. We release MFPDE-Bench, an open benchmark of paired LF/HF solvers for four parametric PDEs with coarse-grid and simplified-physics LF models. Across MFPDE-Bench, GaMF-PINN reaches the accuracy of a standard HF-PINN with up to 8x fewer HF solves, remains robust when the LF model is deliberately corrupted, and attains the nominal coverage where Bayesian PINNs and deep ensembles under-cover.

items.title: Low-Field J-Coupling Spectroscopy Measured with a Diamond Nitrogen Vacancy Spectrometer
items.summary: Nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond (NVs) are point defects well suited to quantum sensing of magnetic fields. NV spin states can be initialized and read out optically with high spatial resolution, enabling detection of pL-scale volumes of nuclear spins. Using Coherently Averaged Synchronized Readout (CASR), standard NMR spectroscopy techniques such as free decay, spin echo, and PGSE have been performed with Hz-scale spectral resolution using NV-diamond sensors. However, using NV detection for conventional high-resolution NMR at multi-tesla fields is challenging due to the need to manipulate NV electronic spins at resonance frequencies 100 GHz or higher. Low-field J-coupling spectroscopy provides an alternative path to chemical resolution in a regime more easily accessible to NVs. Here, we demonstrate homonuclear and heteronuclear J-coupling spectroscopy using an NV-NMR spectrometer based on permanent magnets operating at $\sim$890 kHz proton Larmor frequency (bias magnetic field $\sim$21 mT). This field strength enables chemical characterization based on J-coupling using sequences such as Synchronized Echo (SyncE) and Spin-Echo Double Resonance (SEDOR), which do not require the strong chemical shift dispersion and pristine field homogeneity of high-field NMR. The frequency range is easily detected by NVs using standard XY dynamical decoupling sequences and is well-suited for applying Overhauser DNP, which can boost proton signal by two orders of magnitude. We acquire initial NV-NMR measurements of T$_1$, T$_2$, and Overhauser DNP in glycerol before advancing to SEDOR spectroscopy of methanol-$^{13}$C and a methanol-$^{13}$C/acetonitrile-2-$^{13}$C mixture at sample volumes $\sim$50 pL, in which we demonstrate measurement of $^1J_\text{CH}$ couplings and resolution between species. We also acquire a homonuclear J-coupling spectrum of a natural-abundance propylene carbonate sample.

items.title: BridgeCast: Bridging Ocean Wave Forecasts to Reanalysis via Flow Matching with Exogenous Variables
items.summary: Ocean wave forecasting is essential for maritime safety, offshore operations, and coastal resilience, yet remains challenging due to systematic biases in physics-based models. Physical models, while widely used, rely on approximations and parameterizations that limit their accuracy under complex ocean-atmosphere conditions. To enhance ocean wave forecasting, we propose BridgeCast, within a physics-AI hybrid framework for bias correction. BridgeCast is a probabilistic model based on conditional flow matching (CFM) that learns to transform physical model forecasts into reanalysis-like fields. It treats physical forecasts as corrupted observations and employs a continuous-time generative process to bridge their distribution toward that of reanalysis data. BridgeCast is parameterized by a Transformer-based architecture that enables spatiotemporal modeling, incorporation of exogenous atmospheric variables, and flexible inference via both ordinary and stochastic differential equation formulations. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that BridgeCast consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across regions and forecast lead times.

items.title: From Poincare Invariance to Gauge Theories: Yang-Mills and General Relativity
items.summary: This article is founded on two fundamental principles: the principle field equations introduced in Refs. \cite{S, S1, S2} and the Fock-Ivanenko covariant derivatives \cite{FI, F}. The former yields the equations of motion for free fields of arbitrary spin and helicity. In the massless case, it also dictates that Lorentz transformations for tensor fields acquire an additional term, which takes the form of a gauge transformation \cite{W, S1}. The latter principle, the Fock-Ivanenko derivative, introduces interactions based on the intrinsic and Poincare groups. This framework allows us to recover a complete Yang-Mills theory, as well as general relativity in the connection-based formulations of Palatini and Ashtekar, both of which are theories with local gauge symmetries. While the standard approach begins with the symmetries of a matter action, we will instead derive dynamics directly from Poincare invariance. This perspective reveals that for free fields, Lorentz invariance induces the gauge symmetry of massless tensors. A proper definition of these gauge transformations, in turn, requires the covariant derivatives provided by the Fock-Ivanenko approach. Considering matter fields, we derive the interacting Dirac equation in the presence of Yang-Mills and gravitational fields from its free counterpart.

items.title: Physics-informed data-driven inference of an interpretable equivariant LES model of two-dimensional incompressible fluid turbulence
items.summary: Restrictive phenomenological assumptions limit the accuracy and generality of subgrid-scale models of fluid turbulence, especially in flows where coherent structures and bidirectional energy transfer play an important dynamical role. This paper introduces a symbolic, physically-informed data-driven subgrid-scale closure for two-dimensional incompressible turbulence. The closure is inferred from filtered direct numerical simulation data using symmetry-constrained sparse regression, together with dimensional-consistency constraints on the inferred coefficients. While the model is inferred using LES-style spatial coarse-graining, its structure is found to be more similar to RANS models, as it employs an additional field to describe the dynamics of unresolved scales. For the range of two-dimensional benchmark flows considered here, the inferred model substantially improves upon widely used LES models, yielding accurate predictions of subgrid-scale stresses, local and global fluxes between different scales, and other key quantities in both a priori and a posteriori benchmarks.

items.title: Modeling the Coevolution of Human Skills and AI Adoption
items.summary: The value of relying on generative AI depends on two quantities that evolve with its use: users' unaided skill, which may decline without practice, and the originality of AI-assisted work, which may decline as more people rely on similar tools. We model this process as a coevolutionary game in which individuals choose between autonomous and AI-assisted work, with autonomous practice strengthening their skills while reliance on AI gradually erodes them. When the reinforcing effect of skill erosion outweighs the crowding cost of lost originality, the population exhibits two alternative stable states: low AI adoption with high average skill, and high AI adoption with low average skill. Because skill is individual, autonomous workers remain more skilled than AI users, making autonomous work less vulnerable to population-wide skill decline. The strength of this effect is governed by a timescale ratio: the rate at which skills adapt relative to the rate at which individuals change strategy. The same ratio determines the full distribution of skills, which we derive analytically. Populations with identical AI adoption and average skill can differ sharply: when strategies change frequently, skills remain homogeneous and collective lock-in to high AI adoption is stronger; when strategies persist, lock-in weakens but the population can polarize into highly skilled autonomous workers and AI-dependent individuals. Modeling output overlap further shows that more diverse AI outputs can make widespread adoption harder to reverse. Together, these results expose tradeoffs between the benefits of widespread AI adoption and its long-run risks, making collective lock-in and skill polarization distinct intervention targets.

items.title: Strategic Origins of Network Structure
items.summary: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.

items.title: Bi-stable Nonlinear Energy Sinks (BNESs) for Response Mitigation and Drag Reduction of Subsea Cables Undergoing Vortex-induced Vibrations
items.summary: A methodology for passive mitigation of vortex-induced vibrations (VIVs) in subsea dynamic power cables is developed using optimized, strongly nonlinear bi-stable mass-spring-damper attachments, termed bi-stable nonlinear energy sinks (BNESs), within the open-source MoorDyn library. A fully three-dimensional time-domain framework captures cable dynamics, Morison-type hydrodynamic forcing, nonlinear vibration-mitigation mechanisms, and spatially and temporally varying currents. The BNESs are consistently integrated into the cable model, allowing treatment of highly non-stationary VIVs. A data-driven optimization study samples the BNES design space across multiple current profiles and shows that properly tuned configurations substantially reduce peak-to-peak cable vibration amplitudes. The BNESs also produce significant and robust reductions in cumulative VIV-induced energy intake from the surrounding flow and in drag energy. To the authors' knowledge, passive nonlinear attachments are shown for the first time to reduce both energy intake and drag amplification in a subsea cable, with potential benefits for short- and long-term fatigue. Time-frequency wavelet analysis reveals targeted nonlinear energy transfers and scattering from dominant high-amplitude, low-frequency cable modes to lower-amplitude, higher-frequency modes. This modal redistribution promotes rapid dissipation through hydrodynamic damping and internal structural losses, explaining the simultaneous reductions in vibration amplitude and cumulative energy intake. The results demonstrate that BNESs can provide effective and robust VIV mitigation for subsea power cables under realistic unsteady operating conditions and motivate future studies involving combined current-wave loading, platform-induced motion, and fatigue-life assessment.

items.title: Epitaxial Displacement-etched GaAsSb Quantum Dots Emitting at Telecom Wavelengths
items.summary: Semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are essential components for integrated photonic and quantum information systems, yet current epitaxial growth techniques face significant limitations in complexity of growth, material selection, and density tunability. Here we report a displacement etch technique that enables controlled formation of GaAsSb QDs with emission at telecommunications wavelengths. Our approach uses arsenic molecular flux (As$_2$) to react with antimonide surfaces through thermodynamically favorable displacement reactions, creating three-dimensional quantum confined nanostructures without requiring strain-driven growth or complex droplet-based processes. Density functional theory shows the two competing As-for-Sb exchange pathways to be nearly equivalent in both reaction energy and activation barrier, which places morphological control in the subsequent adatom kinetics rather than in the surface reaction itself. A single process parameter, the As$_2$ exposure, sets the QD areal density across three orders of magnitude, from 10$^2$ to 10$^5$ $μm^{-2}$, covering both isolated emitters and dense gain media. Structural analysis reveals well-defined GaAsSb QDs with a mixed GaAs/GaSb composition and no extended defects. Temperature-dependent photoluminescence measurements confirm emission at 1550 nm (0.8 eV) within the telecommunications C-band, with characteristic QD-like temperature dependence. Because the QDs form on a lattice-matched GaSb surface in a single growth step, the technique offers a practical route to C-band emitters built into the GaSb/AlGaSb device family already used for mid-infrared sources and detectors.

items.title: Analysis of collisional and facility effects in a magnetic nozzle plasma expansion
items.summary: An axisymmetric, quasineutral three-fluid model is proposed to study the plasma expansion in a magnetic nozzle under the presence of neutrals coming either from the plasma source or as an homogeneous background. As a difference with other models, electron cooling in the plume is achieved by treating the electron energy flux as mainly convective and without the need to postulate any anomalous resistivity. Solutions are presented for the electron high-magnetization limit, in which the electron main magnitudes can be integrated along magnetic lines. Ionization, elastic and charge-exchange collisions with neutrals do not change the main qualitative features of the plasma expansion, known from previous collisionless models. Ionization enhances the plasma flow in the nozzle, and leads to additional electron cooling, which decreases the electric potential fall along the nozzle. The efficiency of the nozzle is quantified in terms of the gain of magnetic thrust and the plume divergence angle. Two types of boundary conditions are discussed for the electron flow: local current ambipolarity conditions at the nozzle throat and global current-free conditions at the outer boundary (i.e., metallic vacuum chamber walls). These last ones are shown to be physically more reliable: they introduce the influence of the chamber walls on the plasma expansion by shaping the ambipolar electric field; they permit the extrapolation to undisturbed free space conditions; and they approximate better experimental trends with the background pressure.

items.title: Vertical ionization energies from inverse generalized Kohn-Sham calculations at fixed electron density
items.summary: The exact Kohn--Sham (KS) system must have its highest occupied orbital energy equal to the negative of the lowest vertical ionization energy (VIE). No comparable theorem connects the deeper occupied levels $\varepsilon_k$ to the higher VIEs $I_k$. Chong, Gritsenko and Baerends (CGB) established empirically that $I_k + \varepsilon_k\propto\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HOMO}}-\varepsilon_k}$. We ask whether a similar relation holds for the exact generalized Kohn-Sham (GKS) system, which incorporates a fraction $α$ of Hartree-Fock exchange. We invert near-exact CCSD/aug-cc-pVQZ ground-state densities of LiH, LiF, H$_2$O, HF, CO, N$_2$ and F$_2$ at $α= 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0$ and obtain the exact GKS systems at each admixture. As the density is held fixed and only the operator is varied, the resulting occupied spectra separate the effect of exact-exchange admixture on orbital energies from its effect on the density, two contributions inseparable in a self-consistent hybrid calculation. The CGB relation holds broadly across the family, with a proportionality coefficient linear in $α$, $c(α)=c(0)-sα$, where $c(0)=1.185\pm0.017$ eV$^{1/2}$ and $s=1.987\pm0.041$ eV$^{1/2}$, with $R^{2}\ge0.9996$ for H$_2$O, CO, HF and N$_2$. Using the response-potential matrix elements tabulated by Gritsenko, Braïda and Baerends, we decompose the CGB coefficient into response and spectroscopic parts, and find $s$ to agree with the homogeneous-electron-gas step-height coefficient $K_g = 1.9932$ eV$^{1/2}$, which we conjecture is its origin. The coefficient vanishes at $α^{*}=0.597\pm0.008$. At $α^{*}$ the HOMO-referenced GKS occupied levels satisfy $\varepsilon_k\approx-I_k$ across the whole occupied range. The zero crossing is fixed by the core orbitals; in the outer valence the CGB coefficient is already indistinguishable from zero at $α=0$.

items.title: Prospects for Astrobiology and Technosignature Searches with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time
items.summary: he Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will repeatedly measure the brightness of billions of astrophysical sources using six colour filters. We test a simple idea: real physical signals tend to appear as coordinated patterns across several measurements, whereas noise does not; we call this behaviour ``coherence''. We illustrate the approach with three LSST-like simulations: (i) five Kuiper Belt Object (KBO) surface/activity states, (ii) 648 exoplanet spectra with an injected vegetation-red-edge-like spectral feature, and (iii) 500 multiband light curves. In idealised simulations, a weakly active KBO is strongly separated from its inactive counterpart when all five colours are combined. The injected red-edge-like feature becomes detectable at effective visible-disc coverage of about 13\%, and stacking about 150 detections could reach 5$σ$. Coherent, natural, and noise-like variability occupy distinct regions. A small Gaia DR3 stellar sample illustrates how colour and stability may help prioritise Galactic search regions.

items.title: Boosting fluorescence and polarization with nanophotonics for single-molecule chiral sensing
items.summary: Detecting chirality is essential in chemistry and biomedicine. Circular dichroism identifies chiral molecules through their differential absorption of circularly polarized light. However, its sensitivity is limited by vanishing absorption at low concentrations. Fluorescence-based methods have already enabled other optical techniques to reach the single-molecule limit and could, in principle, also extend chiral detection to reach this sensitivity regime. They are marred, however, by the combination of weak fluorescence signals and low polarization contrast. To overcome these limitations, we leverage high-index dielectric nanophotonics to simultaneously enhance both fluorescence and polarization for chiral sensing. We propose a reciprocity-based analytical framework for a chiral dipolar emitter coupled to a nanoantenna and reveal the different contributions and trade-offs governing the enhancement of circularly polarized fluorescence. Guided by this insight, we tailor achiral dielectric nanostructures to reach a 1000-fold enhancement of fluorescence intensity together with a 10-fold increase in polarization. Crucially, we show that accounting for extrinsic polarization effects in the angular emission patterns of nanophotonic structures is indispensable for reliable enantiomer discrimination. Our approach opens a realistic path for single-molecule chiral sensing.

items.title: A Targeted Quadrature Framework for Simulating Large-Scale 3D Anisotropic Electromagnetic Measurements
items.summary: A new efficient and accurate method is presented for simulating frequency-domain borehole electromagnetic (EM) measurements acquired in the presence of three-dimensional (3D) variations of anisotropic subsurface conductivity. The method is based on solving the quasi-static Maxwell equations with a finite-volume discretization via goal-oriented block-quadrature reduced-order modeling. Discretization is performed with a Lebedev grid that enables accurate and conservative solutions in the presence of any form of anisotropic electrical conductivity. Likewise, the method makes use of a new effective-medium approximation to locally account for non-conformal boundaries and large contrasts in electrical conductivity, especially in the vicinity of EM sources and receivers. The finite-volume discretization yields a large symmetric linear system of equations, which is reduced to a set of smaller structured problems via block Lanczos recursion. The formulation also enables the efficient calculation of the adjoint solution, which is necessary for gradient-based inversion of the measurements to estimate the associated spatial distribution of electrical conductivity, i.e., to solve the inverse problem. The method is applied and verified for borehole ultra-deep azimuthal resistivity (UDAR) measurements commonly used in subsurface geosteering and well navigation. Efficiency, robustness, and scalability are demonstrated using synthetic UDAR data generated in a three-dimensional formation inspired by North Sea geology. The numerical results confirm suitability for integration into real-time UDAR processing frameworks.

items.title: First-Principles Effective Mass in the Three-Dimensional Uniform Electron Gas
items.summary: The quasiparticle effective mass $m^*$ of the three-dimensional uniform electron gas (UEG) is a fundamental Fermi-liquid parameter whose value and density dependence have remained controversial for decades. Using renormalized perturbation theory with explicit counterterms, we determine $m^*$ in the metallic regime ($r_s \le 6$) from first principles by two complementary routes -- the self-energy and the forward-scattering four-point vertex via the $p$-wave spin-symmetric Landau parameter $F_1^s$ -- that agree within uncertainties at each density through sixth renormalized order. The resulting $m^*/m$ remains close to unity throughout the metallic regime, with a shallow non-monotonic density dependence -- a minimum near $r_s\approx 1$ followed by a gentle upturn -- reflecting the interplay of exchange and dynamical screening in the self-energy, and disfavoring strong monotonic suppression. This finding supports a physical picture for the metallic UEG in which dominant charge correlations are concentrated in nearly forward scattering and generate only a weak $F_1^s$ component.

items.title: Solar photocatalytic disinfection of well water using immobilized TiO$_2$: A comparative field study with SODIS in Antananarivo
items.summary: Access to safe drinking water remains a major challenge in rural areas of developing countries. This study investigates the feasibility of a simple, low-cost solar photocatalytic reactor coated with a commercial titanium dioxide (TiO$_2$) pigment for the disinfection of well water contaminated with fecal coliforms. A TiO$_2$ film was deposited on a glass plate using a straightforward acetone slurry method and exposed to natural sunlight in Antananarivo, Madagascar. The efficiency was compared with the conventional SODIS method (solar disinfection without catalyst). Water samples from ten different wells were characterized for physicochemical and bacteriological quality. After 10 minutes of solar exposure, the photocatalytic reactor reduced presumptive fecal coliform counts below the method detection limit ($<$1~CFU/100~mL) in all ten samples tested, whereas the SODIS control reduced the initial count by approximately 51\% in a representative sample. While disinfection kinetics varied slightly with water turbidity and pH, inactivation below the detection limit was consistently achieved. Pearson correlation analysis showed no statistically significant linear correlation between the inactivation rate constant and any measured water-quality parameter (all $p > 0.4$). The results demonstrate that even a non-uniform, low-purity TiO$_2$ coating significantly accelerates bacterial inactivation under solar radiation, offering a promising and affordable household-scale treatment technology for low-resource settings. However, longer-term validation, catalyst stability, dark-control assessment, and leaching studies are still required before widespread implementation can be recommended.

items.title: Realization of valley-controlled orbital angular momentum via inter-orbital coupling
items.summary: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) represents a fundamental degree of freedom (DoF) for understanding novel phenomena in solids and synthetic lattices. However, the generation and control of OAM in lattice systems remain challenging. Here, we experimentally observe valley-controlled OAM states in inversion-symmetry-broken photonic honeycomb lattices consisting of s- and higher-orbital sublattices. These OAM states manifest as chiral vortex arrays in real space. By selectively exciting s-orbital modes carrying no initial OAM at either the K or K' valley, we observe higher-orbital OAM modes generated via inter-orbital coupling in neighboring sites. Specifically, s-p orbital coupling generates OAM states with topological charge l=+1 or l=-1, while s-d orbital coupling yields higher-charge OAM states with l=+2 or l=-2. The sign of the topological charge is determined by the valley DoF, enabling deterministic control of vortex chirality across the entire array. Our theory further reveals that a local vortex-chirality symmetry enforces the valley-dependent selection of vortex chirality at the K and K' valleys, establishing a direct connection between the valley DoF and real-space vortex chirality. These results establish a versatile platform for engineering chiral vortex arrays via orbital physics and exploring orbital- and topology-mediated phenomena in photonic systems and beyond.

items.title: Charge-Selective Displacement of Spatiotemporal Optical Vortices at a Spatially Uniform Time Boundary
items.summary: At a spatially uniform, in-plane-isotropic time boundary, the transverse displacement of a spatiotemporal optical vortex changes sign with its topological charge, despite a charge-independent conversion weight. Radial spectral filtering couples to the vortex phase while preserving identical converted spectral intensities for opposite charges. For a narrow scalar Gaussian spectrum, the displacement follows the logarithmic slope of the spectral weight and occurs with zero mean transverse momentum. In a finite pumped GaAs waveguide, unequal attenuation during extraction adds angular deflection. Independent Maxwell--Drude simulations test this extraction-induced response and give $\pm42$~mrad before detector filtering. Calculated centroid traces at multiple planes separate propagation-induced drift from position offsets.

items.title: Spherical Physics-informed Neural Operator with Multi-scale Coupling for Meteorological Downscaling
items.summary: Meteorological downscaling is crucial for high-resolution regional climate forecasting and disaster early warning. While neural operators have emerged as a promising paradigm for modeling complex spatiotemporal mappings, existing frameworks often struggle with spherical manifold geometric distortions, inherent atmospheric multi-scale coupling mismatches, and lack of explicit atmospheric laws. We propose the Spherical Physics-informed Neural Operator, which utilizes a Spherical Laplacian Decomposition to partition atmospheric fields into hierarchical frequency components, maintaining exact point-wise correspondence across scales. To evaluate these representations at arbitrary locations, we introduce a localized spherical integral operator that approximates continuous kernel transforms via geometry-aware attention. Dynamical consistency is further enforced by embedding differentiable constraints into the learning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework attains superior accuracy and zero-shot generalization across various meteorological variables and unseen queries, representing a robust and interpretable solution for global-to-regional meteorological downscaling.

items.title: Transient growth and Counter-propagating Rossby Waves in a sloped Eady problem
items.summary: A mechanistic interpretation for baroclinic normal mode instability with exponential growth is the interaction arising from Counter-propagating Rossby Waves (CRWs), where pairs of CRWs phase-lock and interfere constructively. On the other hand, an arbitrary initial condition can lead to finite transient growth as long as there is constructive interference. The present work investigates the characteristics of finite time transient instabilities and its description in terms of CRWs in a baroclinic system with asymmetric interaction, in contrast to usual settings where there is an inherent symmetry that leads to equal and opposite CRWs. A sloped Eady problem on a $f$-plane is considered here, which has the benefit that there are only two CRWs in the system, and the presence of a bottom topographic slope can be formulated in a such a way that only one of the CRW is affected and controlled by a single parameter representing the asymmetry, via modifying the bottom background potential vorticity gradient. We derive conditions where the instantaneous growths have key CRW properties that are independent of the asymmetry parameter for a reasonably general family of norms, and that the instability characteristic in the total energy norm is entirely independent of the asymmetry parameter. For finite time transient growth, the optimal initial condition is in some sense counter to that of the exponential growing normal mode: where the bottom slope is such that it is strengthening the bottom CRW, the normal mode has a larger bottom CRW, but the finite time optimal initial condition wants the bottom CRW to be weak instead, and vice-versa. While the results presented here are for the sloped Eady problem, the same results were also found for an analogous Phillips problem, and we speculate the instability characteristics may have origins in the underlying symmetries that are common to those two problems.

items.title: Translation dynamics of evaporating sessile binary-mixture droplet populations
items.summary: The translation dynamics of two binary mixture droplets is investigated theoretically and is corroborated with experiments. The proposed model accounts for the effects of Marangoni stresses generated by evaporative cooling and concentration gradients, as well as vapour diffusion, for both components of the binary mixture. We consider thin droplets, allowing us to use the lubrication theory to derive the evolution equation for the droplet profiles. We numerically solve the evolution equations using the finite element method and examine various cases of pure and binary droplet pairs exhibiting translational behaviours like attraction, repulsion, and 'chasing'.
