In the Stokes limit, bolus formation is governed by the classical trapping mechanism and exhibits a remarkable wavelength-normalized similarity, with both bolus morphology and transport characteristics approaching common asymptotic behaviors as the wavelength increases. As fluid inertia becomes significant, this similarity progressively breaks down and wavelength-dependent trapping behavior emerges. In the short-wavelength regime, the pronounced geometric bending of the wave reorganizes the local flow structure and produces a distinct off-axis bolus associated with a curvature-induced trapping mechanism. The influence of this mechanism expands toward longer wavelengths with increasing Reynolds number and occupies an increasingly large portion of the parameter space considered in the present study. The results reveal that bolus formation cannot be described by a single universal mechanism. Instead, the observed trapping behavior arises from the competition between classical trapping and curvature-induced trapping, whose relative importance is controlled by wavelength, wave amplitude, and Reynolds number. These findings establish a unified physical framework for understanding bolus formation and transport in peristaltic-wave-driven flows.

items.title: Intercity connectivity and urban innovation
items.summary: Urban outputs, from economy to innovation, are known to grow as a power of a city's population. But, since large cities tend to be central in transportation and communication networks, the effects attributed to city size may be confounded with those of intercity connectivity. Here, we map intercity networks for the world's two largest economies (the United States and China) to explore whether a city's position in the networks of communication, human mobility, and scientific collaboration explains variance in a city's patenting activity that is unaccounted for by its population. We find evidence that models incorporating intercity connectivity outperform population-based models and exhibit stronger predictive power for patenting activity, particularly for technologies of more recent vintage (which we expect to be more complex or sophisticated). The effects of intercity connectivity are more robust in China, even after controlling for population, GDP, and education, but not in the United States once adjusted for GDP and education. This divergence suggests distinct urban network dynamics driving innovation in these regions. In China, models with social media and mobility networks explain more heterogeneity in the scaling of innovation, whereas in the United States, scientific collaboration plays a more significant role. These findings support the significance of a city's position within the intercity network in shaping its success in innovative activities.

items.title: Colour-Field Based Particle Categorization for Residual Stress Detection and Reduction in Solid SPH Simulations
items.summary: Residual stress remains in an object even in the absence of external forces or thermal pressure, which, in turn, may cause significant plastic deformations. In case the residual stress creates unwanted effects on the material and so is undesirable, an efficient solution is necessary to track and eliminate this stress. Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics has been extensively used in solid mechanics simulations and the inherent colour-field generation approach is a promising tracker for the residual stress. In this paper, we propose a way to use the colour-field approach for eliminating the residual stress and prevent the undesirable premature failure of solid objects.

items.title: PhysiCal-PET: Physics-driven neural networks for the rapid position Calibration of PET Scanners
items.summary: Depth-of-interaction (DOI) information is essential for mitigating parallax error and preserving uniform spatial resolution in high-resolution and long-axial-field-of-view positron emission tomography (PET). Conventional DOI calibration relies on mechanically scanned collimated sources or detector-specific bench measurements, which become impractical as the number of detector modules grows. We present PhysiCal-PET, a physics-driven neural-network framework for fast, label-free DOI calibration of fully assembled PET scanners. Coincidences are acquired from an uncollimated point source placed at a few known positions, and a network mapping DOI-sensitive detector signals to interaction depth is trained by minimizing the distance between the known source position and the line of response (LOR) defined by the two predicted interaction positions, so that the annihilation geometry alone provides supervision, without measured DOI labels. In realistic simulations, the DOI mean absolute error decreased in parallel with the geometric loss and converged to 0.98 mm, confirming that the loss is a faithful surrogate for the unobservable DOI error. Applied to a preclinical scanner with 144 pixelated dual-ended-readout detector modules, the method calibrated the entire system from 11 manually placed source positions in 55 min of acquisition, reducing the trimmed source-to-LOR distance by 24%, improving the radial point-source FWHM from 4.99 to 2.90 mm (42%), and raising the Derenzo peak-to-valley ratio of the 1.7 mm rods from 1.28 to 1.88 while separating the 1.2 mm rods, which remain merged without calibration. Requiring no collimation, motion stages, or reference measurements, and scaling favorably with system sensitivity, PhysiCal-PET offers a practical route toward autonomous, routine DOI calibration of fully assembled PET scanners with many detectors.

items.title: The wealth-to-salary ratio: a simple indicator of inequality
items.summary: In previous studies, using agent-based simulations of a model of a capitalist economy proposed by Ian Wright, we showed that inequality in both wealth and income distributions is largely governed by a single key parameter: the ratio between average wealth per capita and the mean salary, denoted by $R$. This parameter captures the relative importance of accumulated assets compared with labor income. In the model, larger values of $R$ are systematically associated with higher levels of inequality, as measured by the Gini coefficient. In the present work, we investigate whether this relationship is also observed in real-world economies. Using empirical data from the World Inequality Database (WID) and the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), we construct empirical estimates of $R$ and compare them with standard measures of income and wealth inequality. We find a positive relation between $R$ and inequality across several empirical settings, with the strongest relationships observed for mature and advanced economies. These results provide empirical support for the role of the wealth-to-salary ratio as a simple macroscopic indicator associated with economic inequality, while also highlighting the limitations imposed by differences in data definitions and measurement across countries and periods.

items.title: The cost of connectivity: Network tradeoffs in subway expansion and historic street preservation
items.summary: As cities become increasingly interconnected, expanding regional mobility networks can come at the cost of local social networks. This study examines such tradeoffs in the case of Miaoqianzhijie, a historic street in Guangzhou, China, which was planned to be demolished for building a new interchange subway at Line 10. We introduce a network tradeoff framework that analyzes subway lines as spatial networks and his-toric streets as social networks within a single analytic frame. Empirically, we combine a participatory GIS-based social network survey with origin-destination (OD) flow analysis of Guangzhou's subway system. Our findings show that Miaoqianzhijie functions as a dense corridor of social infrastructure that support everyday routines, social ties, mutual aid, and symbolic place attachment for residents, workers, and frequent visitors. Our OD analysis found that Line 10's mobility benefits are unevenly distributed and the station closest to the demolition area sees only modest improve-ments. These findings reveal an asymmetric network tradeoff that highlights concentrated social connectivity losses versus diffuse and limited local mobility gains. This study contributes a case study and network-based methodology for representing such tradeoffs and highlights how these representations can inform more equitable planning debates around subway expansion and historic street preservation.

items.title: Time-over-threshold versus pulse-height energy reconstruction in a PbWO$_4$ calorimeter read out by SiPMs
items.summary: The time over threshold (ToT) can be measured with a comparator and a time-to-digital converter, avoiding the waveform digitizers normally used to read out calorimeter prototypes. We assess how much the energy resolution degrades when the pulse height (PH) is replaced by the ToT, using data collected in June 2024 at the CERN PS T9 beam line with 2-6 GeV electrons on OREO, a calorimeter of two $3\times3$ matrices of PbWO$_4$ crystals read out by SiPMs and sampled at 500 MS/s, and 1-6 GeV electrons on a lead-glass calorimeter sampled at 100 MS/s. The ToT is emulated offline on the recorded waveforms and converted into an amplitude, so that the same reconstruction chain is applied to both estimators. For OREO in random orientation the PH gives $σ/μ$ = 3.6% at 2 GeV and 2.4% at 6 GeV. A single-threshold ToT worsens the resolution by 50-80%, because one threshold cannot cover the dynamic range, while a dual-threshold ToT gives 3.9% and 2.6%, i.e. 6-10% worse than the PH. Extending the waveforms beyond the 1 $μ$s acquisition window shows that the window is not the limiting factor, and an emulated shaper that reduces the decay time to 50-100 ns preserves the result with a ToT of 0.3-0.5 $μ$s instead of 1.2 $μ$s. The ToT-to-amplitude conversion can also be calibrated with a scan of the two thresholds, without any digitizer, with a resolution comparable to the one obtained with PH-based curves. For the lead glass, whose pulses are less than two samples wide at half maximum, the ToT cannot be emulated reliably. We also find that a previous analysis of the same data is consistent with a drift normalization that does not subtract the pedestals; subtracting them improves the resolution by up to 1.6 percentage points.

items.title: Probing wetting and solidification dynamics of neon thin films with a high-$T_c$ superconducting circuit
items.summary: Integrating condensed noble gases with superconducting circuits offers new opportunities for operating hybrid quantum devices. In particular, electrons on solid neon have recently emerged as exceptionally coherent charge qubits, however the growth of the underlying neon films on patterned devices remains poorly controlled. We monitor neon films near the triple point using a multimode resonator fabricated from high-$T_c$ YBCO, which remains superconducting at temperatures where the liquid phase exists and whose geometry sets a thickness-sensing window near 1 $μ$m. In the liquid state we observe rich film dynamics: uniform wetting that saturates near 20 nm, drainage of thicker films, and spontaneous thickness oscillations, reflecting the extreme sensitivity of thick films in this regime. A galvanic connection to our sensing volume enables in-situ electrostatic tuning of the liquid film thickness. Statistics of freezing the neon across various liquid levels reveal variations of the solid film thickness by approximately an order of magnitude. We also observe a two-fold increase in the quality factor of the resonators at the level of $10^3$ with added neon and rule out dielectric loss as the limiting factor. Our results demonstrate that hermetic packaging facilitates the investigation of both rich non-equilibrium fluid dynamics and the impact of condensed noble gas films on microwave loss in superconducting circuits, but may not be the best modality for growing solid neon films with precisely controlled thickness.

items.title: Pulsed Optical Injection Steering in Multistable Semiconductor Laser Arrays under Correlated Noise
items.summary: We demonstrate robust programmable state preparation in small Vertical Cavity Surface Emitting Laser (VCSEL) arrays with optical feedback using transient optical injection in the form of Gaussian pulses. In Lang-Kobayashi-type models of delay-coupled two- and three-laser arrays, multistability gives rise to coexisting synchronized and symmetry-broken equilibrium branches. We show that short injection pulses applied to one or more lasers can steer the system from free-running operation to any stable equilibrium branch in the absence of noise by appropriate choice of pulse detuning and amplitude, after which the selected state persists without continued forcing. With correlated noise, injection steering remains effective, but branches with small basins of attraction are effectively destabilized by noise. These results validate pulsed injection as a practical mechanism for attractor selection in multistable VCSEL arrays and point to a feasible route toward experimental realization of programmable collective-state control.

items.title: Boundary Element Modeling for THz-SNOM Near-Field Probes
items.summary: Terahertz scanning near-field optical microscopy (THz-SNOM) enables spatially and spectrally resolved investigation of low-energy collective and topological states in quantum materials and nano-structured devices by exploiting the strongly localized near field generated by a polarized atomic force microscopy (AFM) tip. Because the THz near-field response is highly sensitive to tip geometry, understanding how geometric parameters control field confinement and decay is essential for selecting tip designs that provide the spatial resolution required for specific experiments. In this work, we develop a boundary element method (BEM) for modeling the electrostatic near-field of a conducting AFM tip in response to an external background field. The tip is represented by a simplified closed, blunt-cone geometry with its surface discretized into panels using increased mesh density near the apex. A modified Green's function is used to calculate interactions between surface panels, while an augmented linear system simultaneously enforces the equipotential boundary condition on the conducting surface and overall charge neutrality to determine the induced surface-charge distribution. We validate the BEM by comparing the resulting near-field decay with that obtained from a three-dimensional quasi-static COMSOL Multiphysics simulation. The BEM accurately reproduces the COMSOL field-decay behavior while requiring orders of magnitude fewer mesh elements and substantially reducing computational cost. These results demonstrate that the BEM provides an accurate and computationally efficient framework for systematically investigating the dependence of THz near-field confinement on AFM tip geometry. This framework can be extended to more complex and experimentally realistic tip geometries, providing a route toward rational tip selection and design for application-specific spatial-resolution requirements.

items.title: Comprehensive Analysis of Relative Pressure Estimation in Type B Aortic Dissection Utilizing 4D-Flow MRI
items.summary: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can estimate three-dimensional (3D) time-resolved blood velocity fields using 4D-flow MRI, providing rich relative pressure field information. Clinical alternatives---catheterization and Doppler echocardiography---provide one-dimensional pressure drops. While the accuracy of one-dimensional pressure drops from 4D-flow has been explored, the accuracy of 3D relative pressure field estimates requires further evaluation. This work analyzes three state-of-the-art relative pressure estimators: virtual Work-Energy Relative Pressure (vWERP), the Pressure Poisson Estimator (PPE), and the Stokes Estimator (STE). Spatiotemporal characteristics and noise sensitivity were determined in silico via comparison with CFD-derived relative pressure fields. Estimators were then validated using a type B aortic dissection (TBAD) flow phantom with varying tear geometry and twelve catheter pressure measurements. Finally, each estimator was evaluated across eight patient cases in a clinical feasibility analysis. Estimators were cross-compared and evaluated for coherence since no reference catheter pressure measurements were available. PPE outperformed STE in the in silico relative pressure analysis, while both outperformed vWERP in plane-to-plane assessment. High velocity gradients and low spatial resolution contributed most significantly to local variations in 3D relative pressure field errors. Low temporal resolution led to systematic underestimation of highly transient peak pressure events. In the flow phantom analysis, vWERP was the most accurate method, followed by STE and then PPE. Each relative pressure estimator was strongly correlated with ground truth relative pressure values, despite the tendency to underestimate peak relative pressure. Patient case results demonstrated that each relative pressure estimator could be feasibly integrated into a clinical workflow.

items.title: Shape-Constrained Bayesian Active Learning of Self-Limiting Saturation Curves
items.summary: Saturation curves, monotone responses that rise from zero to a plateau, recur across gas adsorption, enzyme kinetics, and self-limiting growth. Learning one from a few costly, noisy measurements is a common bottleneck. We present a Bayesian active-learning platform built on a penalized monotone I-spline. Non-negative weights make every posterior draw rise from zero and never fall, a survey measurement anchors the plateau in place of a flatness prior, and the input reaching any saturation level is read from the posterior by level crossing, assuming no kinetic form. Each measurement is placed where the surrogate is least certain, which beats random designs and edges a log-spaced grid of the same budget. One fixed configuration recovers five kinetically distinct regimes from twenty measurements to a saturation error of 0.037 to 0.041, below the output noise, and averages 0.045 on 250 curves from an unseen distribution. Running unconstrained Gaussian processes (GPs) and two unpenalized monotone bases through the same loop separates each ingredient's contribution. Logarithmic resolution and the roughness penalty carry the accuracy, while monotonicity guarantees a level crossing unique on every draw. The penalty keeps the surrogate the most accurate model at every noise level, and its second-order form centers the recommended input for saturation where a first-order penalty reads late (a bias of +0.32 s with 94% coverage, against +0.44 s and 64% for the matched unconstrained GP). Because the recommended input lies where the curve is nearly flat, no method can pin it down precisely, and we report it as a cost-indexed quantile with the probability of falling short.

items.title: From Critical Transitions to Sustainability Transformations: Phenomena, Theory, and Applications Across Disciplines
items.summary: There has been a recent surge in the use of terms describing systemic change processes across science, policy, and public debate. The associated change phenomena are often assumed to be abrupt and irreversible once critical thresholds are crossed. However, the interchangeable use of terms leaves definitions and the underpinning scientific theory unclear, which can lead to misconceptions about transition processes and potential impacts. Here, we present selected empirical examples representing phenomena of tipping points, regime shifts, critical transitions, phase transitions, social and socio-technical transitions, and sustainability transformations, together with their underlying theory derived from the broadly defined domains of physics and mathematics, Earth science and ecology, social sciences, and their interdisciplinary overlaps. We bring these fields into closer conversation, creating a shared understanding of each of the conceptual roots, phenomena, mechanisms, and specific applications. This can help steward the governance of social-ecological change towards more just and sustainable futures.

items.title: Nanoparticle arrays levitated in a cavity for quantum sensing
items.summary: Levitated nanoparticles are being investigated as ultrasensitive quantum sensors of forces and accelerations, with applications ranging from fundamental physics phenomena such as dark matter or quantum gravity to real world applications. Attention is now turning to multiparticle regimes, and an important question is whether collective effects offer advantages for sensing. We investigate here the spectral characteristics of collective motion of $N $ trapped nanoparticles interacting via the optical mode of a cavity. We find the collective motion typically exhibit two generic spectral features: a broad spectral feature, the collective bright mode (CBM) which has been previously studied; but we find also a new structure of sharp peaks , the mechanical mode comb (MMC). We can describe all the detailed spectral features of the system, with a simple closed-form expression, by reducing the motion to a 1D generic collective mode which is non-Hermitian. We show that the MMC is more advantageous than the usual CBM for increased sensitivity in force sensing. We find that the mechanical comb can autonomously repair loss of `teeth' due to particle loss, a feature that may offer robustness in sensing.

items.title: Interpretability of AI weather models via intermediate decoding
items.summary: AI weather prediction models are often regarded as black boxes. Despite their impressive skill, there is little understanding of how the input data is processed during inference to produce the forecast. This limitation arises from the use of high-dimensional latent representations in which individual dimensions are no longer directly interpretable in physical terms. To gain insight into how forecasts are constructed, we propose the method of intermediate decoding for AI weather models and apply it to GraphCast, Aurora and ArchesWeather. In this approach, latent states from intermediate depths are decoded back into meteorological fields. To do this, we use the decoder that has been trained to output the forecast at the end of processing. Since latent states at different depths do not share a consistent basis, we train affine transformations that align intermediate latent states with the decoder's expected input space. Applying this framework to the three models yields the following results. First, the skill of forecasts at intermediate stages of processing improves gradually through the processor layers. Second, bypassing all processor blocks shows that the encoder-decoder pair is not an identity mapping returning the input, but instead plays a significant role in the forecast construction. Third, by examining increments of individual processor blocks across model depth, we show that all three models progressively refine the forecast from coarse to finer spatial scales. Finally, we assess the physical consistency of the intermediate decoding forecasts and find that large scales remain physically balanced throughout processing, while small scales become more balanced with each additional processor block.

items.title: Revealing Detailed Transport Mechanisms in Silicon Tunneling Diodes
items.summary: Understanding carrier transport in heavily doped semiconductor junctions is essential for developing next-generation tunneling devices for cryogenic electronics and steep-slope technologies. In this work, we investigate the transport mechanisms in a silicon tunneling diode using extensive TCAD (Technology Computer Aided Design) simulations benchmarked against electrical measurements over a wide temperature range of 4 K to 440 K. The measured device characteristics show no negative differential conductance, strong temperature dependence of forward current with a nearly constant semi-logarithmic slope, and weak temperature dependence under high reverse bias. To identify the mechanisms underlying these characteristics, we investigate the contributions of band-to-band tunneling (BTBT), trap-assisted tunneling (TAT), Shockley-Read-Hall (SRH) recombination, and avalanche generation. We also enhance the Schenk TAT model by incorporating Fermi-Dirac statistics to accurately capture the transport behavior at lower temperatures. Under forward bias, TAT in the depletion region dominates the current at low-to-moderate voltages, whereas SRH becomes increasingly significant at higher voltages and temperatures. Under reverse bias, TAT dominates at low reverse voltages, particularly near and above room temperatures, whereas BTBT becomes predominant at high reverse bias, resulting in weak temperature dependence. This work provides a comprehensive understanding of the bias- and temperature-dependent transport mechanisms in silicon tunneling junctions and an enhanced TAT model suitable over a broader range of operating conditions.

items.title: Exciton-Tunable Phase Control and Superstrong Coupling Through Multimode Polariton Engineering in Planar Waveguides
items.summary: Strong light-matter coupling in optical waveguides provides a versatile platform for engineering hybrid polaritonic modes and their dispersion. Here we investigate multimode exciton-photon coupling in visible semiconductor waveguides supporting several transverse electric modes. Using rigorous coupled-wave analysis combined with a coupled-oscillator model, we show that the photonic band structure can be engineered across a range of regimes, from conventional multimode strong coupling to the superstrong coupling regime, where the Rabi splitting becomes comparable to the spacing between adjacent photonic modes. In the latter regime, hybridization between orthogonal electromagnetic modes is enabled by restricting the active material to a subregion of the mode volume where the photonic modes exhibit strong mutual overlap. This breaking of the orthogonality leads to polaritonic branches whose composition can be tuned among several photonic modes and the exciton. We demonstrate that small shifts of the exciton resonance produce pronounced changes in the propagation constants of different polariton branches, enabling exciton-controlled phase modulation through modal interference and, in the superstrong coupling regime, direct modal switching across a continuous S-shaped dispersion. The resulting figures of merit predict $π$ phase shifts for exciton energy shifts of only a few meV over propagation lengths of tens of micrometers, while larger shifts are still required for mode switching. These results establish multimode waveguide polaritons as a versatile platform spanning multiple coupling regimes, for compact phase and intensity control in integrated photonic architectures.

items.title: QRecoupling.jl: numerical and exact computation of classical and quantum recoupling coefficients
items.summary: QRecoupling.jl is a Julia package for numerical, exact and symbolic evaluation of classical and quantum recoupling coefficients and generic finite sums of quantum factorials, with one interface across the classical limit, principal unitary levels and real or complex deformation. A compact factorial rule and its cyclotomic exponents expose factor cancellation, polynomial structure and level support. The package covers quantum Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, 3j and 6j symbols and user-defined sums. Its adaptive numerical evaluation is combined with exact decisions for sums that cancel to zero. Classical 3j and 6j symbols are evaluated at a speed comparable to that of WIGXJPF, which is based on prime factorization tables, at the smallest spins, and about 6 and 10 times faster at spin cutoff 500. Under real, root-of-unity and complex deformation, the largest relative error measured against independent high-precision references is $3.5 \times 10^{-14}$ for spins up to 400. Fusion matrices with 401 channels are computed about 100 times faster than by loops over their entries.

items.title: ModeCast: One-Shot Prediction of Linear MHD Eigenmodes and Growth Rates in Tokamaks
items.summary: Large-scale magnetohydrodynamic instabilities break plasma confinement, can trigger disruptions, and constrain fusion reactor design; modeling a single configuration against them takes hours with a reference solver such as JOREK, and a design study requires thousands of hours. ModeCast is the first learned surrogate to return the complete linear stability assessment for MHD modes. Trained on a comprehensive dataset of over 45,000 JOREK simulations across thousands of equilibria, it screens stability across toroidal mode numbers n=1-4 and predicts the full spatial structure and growth rate of unstable modes. Excluding the equilibrium solve, inference on a single GPU is over 10,000x faster than multi-core JOREK linear stability runs. The gain comes from building the linear-phase physics into the formulation, objective, and inputs, yielding up to six times more training data. ModeCast misses none of the unstable held-out cases, and its predicted fields reproduce the simulation's measured physics, from magnetic island topology to resistivity trends. On a fixed-geometry resistivity scan outside its training distribution, refitting only the 22k-parameter growth rate head of the 145M-parameter network on four simulation halves the held-out internal kink growth rate error, and fine-tuning the whole network adds little. Because it is differentiable and returns full fields, ModeCast could in the future assimilate experimental measurements, providing a bridge to real devices and accelerating progress toward commercial fusion. Project page: zenithon.ai/research/modecast.

items.title: Gap edge eigenpairs from density matrix purification using moments of the Dirac distribution
items.summary: In this work, we propose a simple method to resolve the eigenstates located at the band gap edges of an electronic eigenspectrum using only the quasi-purified one-particle density matrix as input. The theoretical framework relies on the decomposition of the occupation number variance into a particle and a hole moment. These moments, when purified using power narrowing iterations, allow us to isolate the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied single-state projectors, \colp{giving ready access} to the corresponding eigenpairs. We demonstrate that when degeneracy is encountered, power narrowing remains able to deliver relevant mixed states. From a benchmark of selected molecules, we show that the method is robust and efficient since it requires from four to sixteen matrix-matrix multiplications in the worst case. The possibility of reducing the computational cost using the Lanczos subspace approach is discussed. The algorithm simplicity of power narrowing makes it very easy to implement in electronic structure codes or libraries already featuring Fermi operator expansion or density matrix purification.

items.title: Experimental Demonstration of a Balanced Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifier
items.summary: Superconducting travelling-wave parametric amplifiers (TWPAs) provide broadband gain, low added noise, and high dynamic range, making them attractive for applications requiring wide instantaneous bandwidth. This is crucial for amplifying multiplexed narrow band signals spread over a wide frequency range, such as qubit resonator arrays, or amplifying inherently wide band signals, such as in spectrometers or radiometers. In many cases, however, the useful bandwidth of a TWPA is limited by the production of the idler tone at an image frequency. For three-wave-mixing (3WM) TWPAs, for example, an input signal at $f_s$ is indistinguishable from one at $f_p - f_s$, which can produce spectral ambiguity when the input spectrum is broadband or not known in advance. We experimentally demonstrate a balanced architecture that doubles the instantaneous image-rejected bandwidth available to a 3WM TWPA by spatially separating the amplified signal from the output pump and generated idler, which resolves the sideband degeneracy. The architecture consists of two amplifiers connected between a pair of 180$^{\circ}$ hybrid couplers, with the signal and pump injected and output through the sum and difference ports, respectively. Using two kinetic-inductance TWPAs, we demonstrate approximately 20 dB of signal gain across nearly an octave of bandwidth, together with pump rejection below --20 dB and an average image rejection of approximately --15 dB over the operating band. These results establish balanced TWPAs as a practical approach to broadband parametric amplification, enabling improved contamination free bandwidth and eliminating the need for complex filtering.

items.title: Deep Learning Reconstruction for Accelerated Radial CEST MR Fingerprinting
items.summary: Purpose: To accelerate chemical exchange saturation transfer magnetic resonance fingerprinting (CEST-MRF) using temporal deep learning reconstruction. Methods: Ten healthy volunteers underwent repeated test-retest golden-angle radial CEST-MRF acquisitions with 30 measurements and 34 spokes per measurement. The Movienet network was adapted to reconstruct accelerated radial CEST-MRF data. Separate models were trained using 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 20, and 34 spokes per measurement. Temporal and coil correlations were exploited by concatenating time and coil dimensions in the input. GRASP-based locally low-rank (GRASP-LLR) reconstruction was used for comparison. Quantitative DRONE fitting generated tissue parameter maps. Movienet-8 was evaluated with leave-one-subject-out analysis. Prospectively acquired 8-spoke datasets were compared with paired 34-spoke acquisitions, and Movienet-8 and Movienet-34 were compared with a 64-spoke acquisition. Results: In the held-out retrospective series, median Pearson correlations between Movienet and GRASP-LLR were 0.795, 0.947, 0.974, 0.977, and 0.981 for 1, 8, 16, 20, and 34 spokes, respectively. Corresponding NRMSE values were 14.7, 8.2, 5.9, 5.3, and 5.1 percent. Across 10 leave-one-subject-out volunteers, median image correlation was 0.965 and NRMSE was 7.5 percent. Reconstruction of a 30-slice series required 1.7 s with Movienet versus approximately 45 min with GRASP-LLR. Conclusion: Movienet enables whole-brain radial CEST-MRF acquisition in 3 min, with image reconstruction in less than 2 s.

items.title: Active Learning for Interatomic Potentials: A Review of Uncertainty-Driven Data Efficiency
items.summary: Developing a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) that is accurate for the specific conditions under which it will be applied, rather than simply for the predefined configurations chosen by the model developer, is a significant challenge in atomistic simulation. Active learning (AL) addresses this challenge by closing the loop between candidate generation, data selection, reference calculation, and model updating. Here, we survey more than seventy studies, with an emphasis on work from 2020 to 2026, to understand how active learning has evolved from a niche, on-the-fly training technique for query-by-committee and Gaussian process force fields into a diverse family of data-efficient strategies. he reviewed examples include on-the-fly molecular dynamics, active data selection for fine-tuning pretrained models, kernel- and representation-based acquisition using frozen pretrained models, and reaction-aware sampling for chemical systems far from equilibrium. We explore the use of active learning in elemental and alloy mechanics, hydrogen and ion diffusion, ferroelectrics and effective Hamiltonians of functional materials, reactive and photochemical dynamics, high-entropy and compositionally disordered materials, as well as generative and autonomous material discovery pipelines. Drawing on a growing body of critical, methodologically self-aware literature, we also show that this achievement carries systematic caveats. Uncertainty estimates are not interchangeable across model architectures and are frequently the least reliable exactly where they matter most. We close by discussing the outlook for standardized, uncertainty-calibrated, and observable-targeted active-learning workflows in the foundation-model era.

items.title: Localizing and quantifying cerebral arterial stenosis from sparse velocity waveforms using a conditional neural operator
items.summary: Cerebral arterial stenosis alters blood flow throughout the vascular network, complicating the estimation of its location and severity from sparse velocity observations. We developed a conditional neural operator that predicts cerebral hemodynamics for candidate stenoses and enables inverse estimation through waveform comparison. Training data were generated using a sequential 0D-1D model that simulates pressure, cross-sectional area, and velocity under varying anatomical, physiological, and stenosis conditions. The operator encodes a single stenosis within vessel tokens and uses global attention to represent its effects across the network. Severity-gated coupling connects these representations to a shared field decoder, while paired healthy simulations constrain baseline predictions. After training, model weights remain fixed, and stenosis location and severity are estimated by minimizing the mismatch between predicted and observed midpoint velocity waveforms. Network-averaged relative validation errors were 0.14% for pressure, 0.59% for area, and 2.79% for velocity. For an eight-vessel observation configuration, localization accuracy across 20 candidate vessels was 99.4% without added noise and 96.0% at the 30% noise setting. Comparisons between configurations with equal numbers of observed vessels showed that measurement placement influenced recovery. Errors and localization ambiguities were greater in selected communicating and distal arteries. These results demonstrate the feasibility of surrogate-based stenosis estimation in simulated cerebral networks and highlight the importance of observation placement. Evaluation was limited to unseen stenosis scenarios within sampled anatomical and physiological conditions. Generalization to new individuals and clinical measurements requires further investigation.

items.title: An exact finite-state representation of viscoelastic memory for accelerated sea-level modeling: SLEvolve v1.0
items.summary: Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA) models solve the gravitationally self-consistent sea-level equation for the response of the solid Earth and the oceans to changing ice loads. As these models are increasingly embedded in coupled ice-sheet simulations, glacial-cycle calculations, and large ensembles, standard pseudo-spectral 1-D solvers face a steep computational barrier: they evaluate the viscoelastic response by explicitly re-summing every past load increment, scaling quadratically with time steps as $O(N^2)$. Here we show that this computational penalty is an artifact of algorithmic formulation rather than Earth physics. By exploiting the exponential form of the viscoelastic relaxation kernel, we reformulate the viscous response as an exact recursive update of a finite set of modal states, without re-summing the load history. This exact reformulation alone reduces the cost of a run to $O(N)$, yielding a 20.6-fold speed-up relative to a standard full-history 1-D GIA solver for a case study involving a 550-step Antarctic future sea-level projection. Implemented in our open-source solver SLEvolve v1.0, this formulation---combined with fewer, table-free and multithreaded spherical-harmonic transforms, improved file handling, and physics-inspired iteration starts---achieves an end-to-end speed-up of over three orders of magnitude (up to 4,000-fold) against the same 1-D GIA solver, reducing day-long simulations to under thirty seconds on a workstation. Beyond this solid-Earth application, SLEvolve illustrates how human-derived analytical reformulations can be combined with benchmark-harnessed AI-assisted engineering to modernize scientific software. In particular, Numerical regression tests and performance profiling guided the AI agents' implementation choices and helped reject ineffective optimizations.

items.title: A Rydberg atom array coupled to a high-cooperativity optical cavity
items.summary: Integrating Rydberg-state control of atom-atom interactions with cavity control of atom-light interactions enables the combination of local entangling operations with photon-mediated long-range coupling, measurement, and communication. Such integration is challenging because electric fields generated by charges on cavity optics and by cavity-stabilizing actuators may disturb Rydberg-state coherence. Here, we couple a Rydberg tweezer array to a high-cooperativity optical cavity, suppressing the electric fields produced by cavity length actuation so that the residual field variation of about $3~\mathrm{mV/cm}$ rms does not limit Rydberg coherence. We demonstrate two capabilities that neither system provides alone. First, we use Purcell-enhanced fluorescence to read out atoms directly in the ground-Rydberg basis within $7.5~μ\mathrm{s}$, well within the Rydberg-state lifetime, with ground- and Rydberg-state detection infidelities of $3\%$ and $5\%$, respectively, and with low atom loss. Second, we use Rydberg-Rydberg interactions to control collective light-atom scattering into the cavity mode. Specifically, we drive blockaded Rabi oscillations between a state with two ground-state atoms, which scatter collectively with a superradiant or subradiant rate controlled by the atomic positions, and an entangled state with a single Rydberg excitation, which scatters like a single atom. These capabilities open routes toward networked Rydberg processors, mid-circuit measurements in analog quantum simulators, and many-body quantum optics with entangled emitters coupled collectively to light.

items.title: Analysis of Transient Microscopy Data in Reciprocal Space
items.summary: Transient microscopy has evolved to include a family of well-established techniques for studying the spatiotemporal dynamics of excited states in a variety of materials systems. In these methods, a laser pulse is focused to locally excite a material, and the subsequent evolution of the excited species is visualized to extract transport parameters such as diffusivities. Typically, transport coefficients are extracted from experimental datasets using curve-fitting methods to analyze the change in the mean squared displacement (MSD) of the spatial profiles over time. However, this approach can lead to inaccurate or misleading diffusivity values under many common experimental conditions, and is only formally accurate for the case of a single diffusing species. In this work, we introduce a new approach to the analysis of transient microscopy data based on the evolution of profile shapes in reciprocal space. We use simulated datasets to quantitatively analyze the performance of our proposed methods and compare them to current state-of-the-art analysis techniques. We demonstrate that reciprocal-space-based analysis methods have the highest overall performance in terms of accuracy and precision for normal diffusive transport over a range of realistic initial conditions and signal-to-noise ratios. Furthermore, we highlight the limitations of using MSD alone to characterize anomalous transport in materials, and we show how analysis of spatial frequencies can yield a more comprehensive understanding of complex excited-state dynamics and their underlying physical mechanisms. Our results show that reciprocal-space-based analysis methods are powerful tools for characterizing and quantifying many different types of transport behaviors.

items.title: Effects of Spanwise Curvature on Hypersonic Boundary Layer Transition in Görtler-driven Flows
items.summary: The influence of spanwise convex curvature on hypersonic boundary-layer transition over a streamwise-concave surface is investigated using direct numerical simulation and Mach 7 experiments. Smooth doubly curved geometries with fixed streamwise concavity and increasing spanwise convex curvature isolate the effects of three-dimensional wall curvature on a centrifugally unstable boundary layer. Increasing spanwise curvature delays transition while preserving a Gortler-dominated route to breakdown. As spanwise curvature increases, the boundary layer thins, reducing the effective Görtler number and weakening centrifugal amplification of streamwise vortices. Consequently, growth of the primary Görtler instability is reduced, vortical structures remain closer to the wall, and secondary instability and turbulent breakdown shift downstream. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition confirms that low-frequency vortical dynamics remain dominant in controlling transition, with sinuous secondary instability of Görtler vortices providing the principal route to breakdown. Meanwhile, boundary-layer thinning modifies acoustic instability dynamics: the second Mack mode shifts to higher frequencies and higher-frequency supersonic disturbances become increasingly prominent near breakdown as spanwise curvature increases. These acoustic disturbances remain subdominant and do not replace the Görtler-sinuous mechanism as the primary transition pathway. Numerical and experimental results exhibit consistent trends in transition location, thermal-streak organisation and disturbance evolution, supporting a common physical interpretation. These findings demonstrate that spanwise convex curvature stabilises hypersonic Görtler-dominated boundary layers, primarily by suppressing centrifugal amplification and delaying secondary instability, while leaving the transition pathway qualitatively unchanged.

items.title: Neural Operators Reveal Scale-Dependent Limits on Recovering Greenland Ice Loss from Sea Level Fingerprints
items.summary: Sea level fingerprints connect the spatial distribution of rapid ice mass change to sea surface height (SSH) change, but the spatial resolving power of this inverse problem remains poorly quantified. Here we provide the first systematic, scale-resolved quantification of Greenland Ice Sheet mass change structure recoverable from its SSH fingerprint when ice loss geometry varies. We develop a physics-informed neural operator, constrained by an accurate neural-operator emulator of the forward sea level equation, to probe the information content of this ill-conditioned inverse problem. Across synthetic ice change ensembles, broad ice loss patterns can be recovered, but distinct ice fields can produce nearly identical fingerprints, so fine-scale structure depends on the assumed a-priori ice change distribution. Inversion fidelity varies with the wavelength and amplitude of ice mass change. An empirical error law separates these effects and defines a scale-dependent accuracy ceiling. For a satellite-altimetry-derived reference field, the estimated fingerprint-only ceiling is $R^2\sim0.79$ under the present SSH observation geometry and matched-prior assumption. The leading three principal components explain 99.76% of fingerprint variance, yet higher-order components retain information needed to distinguish finer ice change structure. SSH observations near Greenland carry most information on ice loss locations. Applying the leading fingerprint principal components to the observed 1993--2019 SSH rate recovers the large-scale Greenland fingerprint, while the residual field is correlated with basin-scale bathymetry, consistent with unresolved sterodynamic variability. These results establish a quantitative empirical bound on fingerprint-only ice-loss resolving power and identify how independent observations and ice sheet constraints can improve inference.

items.title: Eulerian ion energisation in three-dimensional hybrid-Vlasov-Maxwell turbulence
items.summary: In collisionless plasma turbulence, energy is transferred from electromagnetic fluctuations to the particles. However, the relative contributions of different ion energisation mechanisms remain unclear. We investigate ion energisation in three-dimensional hybrid Vlasov--Maxwell simulations of decaying turbulence at $β_{i0}=0.25$ and $β_{i0}=4$, where $β_{i0}$ is the initial ratio of ion thermal to magnetic pressure. Using the exact ion momentum equation, we decompose the ion energisation rate $\mathbf{j}_i\mathbf{\cdot}\mathbf{E}$ into the work done on the parallel, diamagnetic, curvature, agyrotropic and polarisation ion currents. This decomposition requires neither gyrotropy nor scale separation and, therefore, remains valid where guiding-centre theory breaks down. We show that the agyrotropic term, which has no guiding-centre counterpart, accounts for $21\,\%$ of the energisation at $β_{i0}=0.25$ and $91\,\%$ at $β_{i0}=4$. We find that the dominant instantaneous energisation term changes with $β_{i0}$, from the polarisation current at low $β_{i0}$ to the diamagnetic and agyrotropic currents at high $β_{i0}$, at all resolved scales. In addition, we show that reversible exchange with the ion bulk flow dominates the instantaneous rate, so the time-integrated energy transfer is larger at $β_{i0}=4$ even though the instantaneous rate is smaller. Our results provide quantitative evidence that guiding-centre drifts alone cannot describe ion energisation in kinetic-scale turbulence and that the dominant energisation term depends on $β_i$. The results also highlight the key role of non-local thermodynamic-equilibrium effects in energy conversion in collisionless plasma turbulence.

items.title: Quantum algorithms for optimal control: large-scale finite-horizon linear-quadratic regulation
items.summary: We develop quantum algorithms for optimal control over a prescribed finite time interval (finite horizon), focusing on continuous-time linear-quadratic regulation (LQR). This foundational control problem often requires solving a nonlinear matrix Riccati equation, which can be costly for large systems and long control durations on conventional classical solvers. We instead work directly with the state-costate optimality equations, reformulating the LQR problem as a multiple-shooting linear system. Importantly, we prove a condition-number bound for the system that is independent of the horizon, under stabilizability and detectability assumptions. By incorporating the initial and final conditions into a single linear system, we can solve the subsequent linear system more efficiently with a quantum linear systems subroutine. For a given initial state, our quantum algorithms return classical estimates of the optimal cost and the optimal control inputs at a selected time, without constructing a Riccati solution operator. Given sparse-matrix block-encodings, an initial-state preparation oracle and a fixed number of control inputs, the query and gate complexities scale polylogarithmically with system size and control duration, provided that sparsity, relevant norms, and stability parameters are bounded. The dependence on the target error is inverse-linear up to logarithmic factors. We establish the required bounds uniformly in system size and duration for a family of damped mass-spring chains with two endpoint controls. Numerical experiments support the analysis.

items.title: Isolated zeros of the Riemann zeta function and zeros of linear combinations of Dirichlet $L$-functions
items.summary: Let $0<γ_1\leq γ_2\leq \cdots$ be the ordinates of the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function in the upper half-plane, counted with multiplicity, and fix $c>0$. We say that a non-trivial zero $ρ_n=β_n+iγ_n$ is $c$-isolated if $\min(γ_{n+1}-γ_n, γ_n-γ_{n-1})>2πc/\log γ_n$. Note that any isolated zero is necessarily simple and on the critical line. We prove unconditionally that more than $50.87\%$ half of the non-trivial zeros are $1/6$-isolated. Previously, it was not known unconditionally that there are infinitely many isolated zeros. By allowing $c$ to be extremely small, we can push the above proportion to $13/20$. We also show that there are positive proportions of $k$ consecutive ``moderate'' gaps (gaps larger than a constant times the average local gap) between the ordinates of the zeta zeros, for $k=3, 4, 5$. As an application we combine our work on isolated zeros with an unconditional refinement of the Bombieri--Hejhal method to show unconditionally that at least $31\%$ of the zeros of a linear combination of two distinct primitive Dirichlet $L$-functions with the same conductor and parity lie on the critical line. The previous unconditional record for this proportion was $7.38\times 10^{-9}$, which was obtained by Dousselin who refined and made explicit a result of Selberg.

items.title: Newton-Based Methods for Bilevel Optimization Beyond Lower-Level Strong Convexity
items.summary: Bilevel optimization provides a framework for machine learning tasks such as hyperparameter optimization, data reweighting, and meta-learning. Existing Newton-based bilevel methods typically rely on the classical hypergradient formula, which is generally unavailable when lower-level solutions are nonunique and the lower-level Hessian is singular. We develop two Newton-based methods beyond lower-level strong convexity by exploiting curvature shared by the lower-level and multiplier updates. Newton-based GALET handles potentially singular lower-level curvature under a positive spectral-gap condition, exploiting its range structure to avoid the squared-Hessian multiplier system used in GALET. Newton-based BAMM uses a strongly convex aggregation model when the lower-level objective is convex and the upper-level objective is strongly convex in the lower-level variable. We establish convergence guarantees and improved complexity bounds relative to GALET and sl-BAMM under the corresponding assumptions. We further introduce GNBO, a generalized Newton-based framework that captures the shared-curvature structure of the proposed methods and several existing Newton and quasi-Newton bilevel methods. Experiments on synthetic problems, data hyper-cleaning, and GPT-2 data reweighting evaluate the proposed methods across different bilevel learning tasks.

items.title: Zero-free half-planes for Hecke L-functions over number fields
items.summary: In [Liu26a], varying the length and moment parameters in the cubic-theta argument of [Ope26a] gave the zero-free half-plane $Re(s)>B_{\mathrm{new}}=0.874957019420098946\ldots$ for finite-order Hecke $L$-functions over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$ and for Dirichlet $L$-functions, and its optimality in the specified exponent comparison system. In this paper, we extend the argument to finite-order Hecke $L$-functions over cyclotomic fields containing $μ_{12}$ and, by class-field descent, to every pair $(K,η)$ whose cyclic class field has metabelian normal closure over $\mathbb Q$, including every finite-order character over every abelian number field. Then, adapting the averaged numerator estimate developed by Xu and Sang [XS26] for Hecke $L$-functions over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$ and combining it with a limiting contradiction argument, we obtain the boundary $B_\flat=0.874886647039964\ldots$, the root near $0.8749$ of $133488B^4-376596B^3+384534B^2-167541B+26231$; it is the exact infimum of the refined comparison system, unattained by finite chains starting above it. Since the analytic argument uses only $μ_{12}\subset F$, we run it over $F=K(ζ_{12})$ for an arbitrary number field $K$ and descend: every finite-order Hecke $L$-function over every number field is zero-free for $Re(s)>B_\flat$. The analytic argument uses the exceptional-theta constructions and local calculations of the preprint [Ope26b].

items.title: Limit law for Brownian cover time of the two dimensional torus
items.summary: Let $\mathcal{C}_\varepsilon$ denote the time it takes a Brownian motion to come within distance $\varepsilon$ of every point in the two dimensional torus $\mathbb{T}^2$ of unit area. We prove that for an explicit non-random centering $m_\varepsilon$, the variables $\{\sqrt{\mathcal{C}_{\varepsilon}} - m_\varepsilon \}$ converge in distribution as $\varepsilon \to 0$, to a randomly shifted Gumbel law.

items.title: Controllability of polynomial systems is undecidable and not recursively enumerable
items.summary: Sontag conjectured in 1988 that global controllability of polynomial control systems with rational coefficients is undecidable, but that the controllable systems form a recursively enumerable set. We prove the first part of the conjecture and disprove the second. For every homogeneous polynomial vector field $F$ of odd degree with rational coefficients, we construct an explicit polynomial control system $Σ_F$, with one more state than $F$, that is globally controllable if and only if the origin is \emph{not} globally asymptotically stable for $\dot x=F(x)$. By a recent result, the homogeneous polynomial vector fields with a globally asymptotically stable origin form a set that is recursively enumerable but not decidable. Consequently, global controllability of polynomial systems is undecidable, and the controllable polynomial systems are not recursively enumerable. The same conclusions hold for systems of the form $\dotξ=f(ξ)+Bu$ with a polynomial drift and a constant input matrix.

items.title: Joint Lower Bounds for Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization on Euclidean Balls
items.summary: We prove a joint stochastic zeroth-order lower bound for Goldstein stationarity on a Euclidean query ball, even when the ball is guaranteed to contain a stationary point. In dimension $d$, let $f=\mathbb{E}[F(\cdot;ξ)]$, assume $\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Lip}(F(\cdot;ξ))^2]\le L_0^2$, and bound the initial objective gap over the ball by $Δ$. For neighborhood radius $δ>0$ and residual tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, our smooth hard family requires $Ω(dL_0^2Δ/(δ\varepsilon^3))$ scalar evaluations for success probability $1/2$, against randomized adaptive algorithms that may retain and repeatedly query each sampled function. The result holds for $\varepsilon\le cL_0$, $Δ\ge Cδ\varepsilon$, and $d\ge C[1+\log(2+ΔL_0^2/(δ\varepsilon^3))]$, on a constructed ball of radius $Θ(Δ/\varepsilon)$. A sequence of localized regions forces repeated direction estimation, and an adaptive Gaussian posterior argument controls sample reuse. The result establishes a joint dimension and accuracy obstruction on solvable bounded-domain instances. The gap is local to the query ball; a matching minimax characterization at a common radius and the corresponding unrestricted global-gap lower bound remain open here.

items.title: Elastic knots: compactness, contact, and variational structure
items.summary: We study bending-minimizing sequences of closed curves in a fixed knot class and the self-contact of their limits. A positive matrix-valued measure records a possible loss of curvature energy. Ambient variations, localized on arbitrary coincidence sets, force this measure to vanish and give strong convergence in $H^2$. We then derive the elastic equation on isolated strands and overlap bundles, describe the distribution that remains at contact, and prove balance and rigidity statements under their precise additional hypotheses. Equality in the bridge bound gives constant curvature. Combining strong compactness with quantitative competitors gives an alternative proof that elastic limits in classes with equal bridge and braid indices are covered circles. An independent recovery theorem identifies the strong $H^2$ closure with the regular $H^2$ part of the $C^1$ closure and also implies strong compactness. Finally, a whole-line contact model illustrates which estimates are needed for finer shape selection.

items.title: Sharp Minimax Rates for Highly Smooth Strongly Convex Zeroth-Order Optimization
items.summary: We determine the minimax dimension dependence of noisy zeroth-order optimization for globally strongly convex functions with higher-order smoothness in multilinear operator norm. Each query returns one function value with fresh independent Gaussian noise. For dimension $d$, query budget $T$, and any fixed finite smoothness order $β>2$, the minimax expected objective error satisfies $\mathcal{E}_β(T,d)=Θ_β\left(\min\left\{1,(d^2/T)^{(β-1)/β}\right\}\right)$, with dimension-independent strong-convexity, gradient-smoothness, higher-order-smoothness, noise, and minimizer-radius bounds. Thus, for sufficiently small target error $\varepsilon$, the necessary and sufficient number of noisy values is $Θ_β(d^2\varepsilon^{-β/(β-1)})$, with no logarithmic loss. The new lower bound matches the dimension and budget dependence of the upper bound of Akhavan et al. (2024), and holds for arbitrary randomized adaptive algorithms with unrestricted query points. Its key step localizes a normalized hypercube with one radial cutoff: a query can emphasize one hidden coordinate, but the aggregate information about all coordinates remains small. A self-contained multiscale spherical estimator attains the matching upper bound by cancelling lower-order bias terms. Constants in the rates depend only on the fixed smoothness order under the stated normalization.

items.title: Muckenhoupt weights for the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator on hyperbolic spaces
items.summary: On the real hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^n$, the classical Muckenhoupt condition does not describe the weights $w$ for which the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator $M$ is bounded on $L^p(w)$. We show that, for $1<p<\infty$, $M$ is bounded on $L^p(w)$ if and only if $w$ is a local $A_p$ weight and satisfies a two-layer condition, which compares $w$ and its dual weight on two layers of the shadow of a point. We also treat the weak type case, radial weights and the range $p\le1$, and we prove a weighted Herz principle for radial convolution operators.

items.title: Next Best Action: Causal Constrained Offline RL for Business Action Targeting
items.summary: Next Best Action (NBA) systems must select among customer interventions (e.g., discounts, promotions, and lifecycle actions), maximize long-term economic value, satisfy complex operational constraints, and remain causally grounded. Existing approaches lack a rigorous framework for meeting these requirements jointly. We address this gap by formulating NBA as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). We then integrate off-policy causal correction of the estimated customer dynamics directly into the Linear Programming (LP) formulation of the CMDP. The resulting policy selects actions based on customer states to maximize long-term value while explicitly enforcing business guardrails. Furthermore, the LP formulation yields shadow prices that quantify the economic trade-offs of operational constraints (e.g., fairness and user welfare), enhancing policy interpretability. We validate our proposed offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework on an industry case study involving rideshare coupon targeting, where customer states are defined by Recency, Frequency, and Monetary (RFM) stages. We evaluate performance using model-based off-policy evaluation, with causal dynamics estimated from a temporal holdout. Under the observed coupon budget and RFM state representation, our optimized policy improves customer lifetime value (LTV) by 19% over the estimated behavior policy and 8% over a myopic baseline. Although the demonstrated action space is binary, the proposed framework is action-agnostic, yielding a general-purpose decision module for targeting systems that manage multiple interventions.

items.title: Tight lower bounds for Lipschitz geodesically convex optimization on hyperbolic space
items.summary: We determine the dimension-independent first-order query complexity of minimizing a Lipschitz geodesically convex (g-convex) function on hyperbolic space. Given a ball of radius $r$ containing a global minimizer, we prove that $Ω(ζ_r/ε^2)$ queries are necessary to attain accuracy $εMr$, where $M$ is the Lipschitz constant and $ζ_r=r/\tanh r$ captures the effect of curvature. This matches the known $O(ζ_r/ε^2)$ upper bound for the Riemannian subgradient method (Zhang and Sra, 2016). This is the first query-complexity result for g-convex optimization that is tight simultaneously in curvature and target accuracy. The standard Euclidean recipe of constructing hard instances as maxima of affine functions does not transfer to hyperbolic space, so the lower bound requires a new mechanism. Our starting point is the worst-function construction of Criscitiello and Boumal (2023, Appendix A). It gives the same lower bound for a subclass of algorithms, including the subgradient method, whose queries remain in prescribed g-convex regions. We retain this geometric setup and carefully tune and augment their hard function to accommodate every deterministic first-order algorithm. The key new mechanism is an advance-or-stall scheme: when a query lies in these regions, the oracle reveals at most one new information direction (advance); when a query leaves them, we show that the oracle can answer without revealing any new hidden direction (stall). Unlike earlier curvature-dependent lower bounds, the proof uses no ball-packing argument.

items.title: Data Center Oscillation Isolation and Grid Support: Fundamental Limits and Source-Selective Control
items.summary: The grid integration of large data centers poses a growing power-system stability challenge. Rapidly varying computing demand can induce oscillations, while the facilities must provide a prescribed response to grid disturbances. Existing controls address load fluctuations and grid support but do not establish their jointly achievable performance. This paper derives fundamental limits and develops a source-selective controller for simultaneous oscillation isolation and grid support. A coupled closed-loop model gives a condition for distinguishing disturbance sources and reveals a direct isolation-support conflict under grid-import-power feedback alone; additional electrical measurements can remove this pointwise conflict but leave a conditional cross-frequency sensitivity limit. Guided by these limits, we design a local residual-feedback storage controller through convex frequency-domain optimization with stability, isolation, and grid-response constraints across operating points. Tests on a single-generator interconnection and a modified nine-bus network show stronger oscillation isolation than equal-order optimized comparators while meeting the prescribed grid response across operating points.

items.title: Matrix-Vector Complexity of Low-Rank Approximation
items.summary: We establish matching polynomial query bounds for low-rank approximation from exact matrix--vector products. Given an unknown matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, at each step a randomized algorithm chooses either $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and receives $Av$, or $u\in\mathbb{R}^m$ and receives $A^\top u$. The choice may depend measurably on all previous queries and replies and on the algorithm's private randomness; each vector product costs one query. The output is a rank-$k$ right projector with Schatten-$p$ residual at most $1+\varepsilon$ times optimal. Write $N=\min\{m,n\}$ and let $Q_p^*$ denote the worst-case query budget for success probability $2/3$ on every input. For every $1\le k<N$ and sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, our lower bounds, combined with existing Krylov upper bounds, give $Q_p^*=\widetildeΘ\!\left(\min\{N,k\min\{p^{1/6}\varepsilon^{-1/3},\varepsilon^{-1/2}\}\}\right)$ $(2\le p<\infty)$, $Q_\infty^*=\widetildeΘ\!\left(\min\{N,k\varepsilon^{-1/2}\}\right)$. These bounds have universal constants and allow $p$ to vary with the problem parameters, identifying the transition at $p\varepsilon\asymp1$. A complementary result for each fixed $1\le p<2$ gives $\widetildeΘ_p(\min\{N,k\varepsilon^{-1/3}\})$, with constants and an accuracy threshold that may depend on $p$. Together, the results recover this fixed-norm rate for every fixed finite $p$, supplying the multiplicative rank dependence missing from previous lower bounds. Tildes suppress logarithmic factors. The proof extends adaptive Wishart deferred decisions to a rectangular factor with a $k$-dimensional nullspace. Posterior overlap gives a short fixed-norm argument, while persistence of small compression eigenvalues controls growing $p$ and the spectral endpoint. Exact range recovery handles target costs of order $k$; the Wishart family covers the remaining regimes.

items.title: An Exotic Congruence for Irregular Weight Picard Modular Forms
items.summary: We construct a new type of congruence from irregular weight mod $p$ Picard modular forms (for $p$ inert) to ones of regular weight, analogous to the one obtained by Kansal--Levin--Savitt in the Hilbert setting. The congruence is obtained by using a geometric Jacquet--Langlands phenomenon, as first established by Vollaard, to transfer irregular weight mod $p$ Picard modular forms from the Picard modular surface to a Shimura set. We call this an exotic congruence, since it relates mod $p$ automorphic forms associated to different groups. This congruence will be used in upcoming work of the author proving mod $p$ local-global compatibility for irregular weight Picard modular forms (in the $p$ inert case).

items.title: Asymptotics of Constrained Quantization for Compactly Supported Measures
items.summary: We study constrained quantization of a compactly supported probability $P$ on $\mathbb{R}^D$ by codebooks in a nonempty closed set $S$. For $0<r\le\infty$, the constrained error $e_{n,r}$ is attained and satisfies $e_{n,r}\downarrow L_r=\|\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,S)\|_{L^r(P)}$. Set $Δ_{n,r}=e_{n,r}^r-L_r^r$ for finite $r$. A Borel nearest-point selector $T$ induces $μ=T_*P$. Writing $q_{n,s}$ for the classical $L^s$ quantization error, we obtain $e_{n,r}-L_r\le2q_{n,r}(μ)$ and $Δ_{n,r}\le C_rq_{n,1}(μ)$ for $1\le r<\infty$, with $C_r$ independent of $n$, and $Δ_{n,r}\le2^rq_{n,r}(μ)^r$ for $0<r<1$. Also, $e_{n,\infty}-L_\infty\le2c_n(E)$, where $E$ is the nearest-point image of $\operatorname{supp}P$ and $c_n(E)$ is its covering radius. For $1\le r<\infty$, a weighted power-growth condition with exponent $β>0$ on a fixed source set $F$ bounds $Δ_{n,r}$ below by the classical $β$-power quantization cost of $ν_F=T_*(wP|_F)$. If $dν_F=\widehat w\,dη$ for a compactly supported reference probability $η$ and $\widehat w\in A_p(η)$, $1<p<\infty$, then $Δ_{n,r}\geν_F(\mathbb{R}^D)[\widehat w]_{A_p(η)}^{-1}q_{n,β/p}(η)^β$. These comparisons yield bounds for the quantization dimensions defined by $e_{n,r}-L_r$ and $Δ_{n,r}^{1/r}$, with distinct behavior at positive and zero baselines. Convex and uniformly prox-regular constraints supply the growth weights through their projection inequalities. Circle and lifted Cantor distributions give matching quadratic-excess rates, while rectifiable weighted projections give lower Zador estimates.

items.title: Second-Order Stationarity with Common Random Losses: Matching Tolerance Bounds
items.summary: We establish tight polynomial tolerance bounds for stochastic second-order stationarity when each fresh oracle response is a derivative of one common random scalar loss. For a population objective $F$ with Lipschitz gradient and Hessian, the target is $\|\nabla F(x)\|\le ε$ and $λ_{\min}(\nabla^2 F(x))\ge -γ$, with independent tolerances $ε,γ>0$. Under bounded gradient variance and almost-surely bounded Hessian error, the minimax number of fresh gradient or Hessian-vector-product calls is $\widetildeΘ\!\left(ε^{-3}+γ^{-5}\right)$. The characterization fixes positive gap, smoothness, and noise parameters, suppresses logarithmic factors, and allows dimension to grow within an explicit polynomial envelope. The upper bound removes the mixed term $ε^{-2}γ^{-2}$ from the earlier fresh-HVP guarantee. Direct random-line Hessian estimates and a dyadic gradient tracker separate gradient drift from randomly signed curvature motion. The lower bound realizes the endpoint costs through globally defined smooth random losses: a smooth partition localizes scalar noise without a chain-length penalty, while exact cancellation limits the information in the entire response. Consequently, the same tolerance exponents hold even for joint value, gradient, and full-Hessian responses with bounded value variance. For a population Hessian with Hölder exponent $ν\in(0,1]$, fresh gradient/HVP complexity becomes $\widetildeΘ\!\left(ε^{-3}+γ^{-(3+2/ν)}\right)$ under the corresponding dimension envelope.

items.title: Directional Expansiveness for the chair tiling
items.summary: We study directional expansiveness of the chair tiling. We show that for every direction $V$ and every $r>0$, there exist distinct chair tilings that agree on $\mathbb{Z}^2\cap V^r$. Hence the chair tiling has no expansive direction.

items.title: A simplified proof of the FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
items.summary: We give a simplified, self-contained proof of OpenAI's FPRAS for counting perfect matchings in general graphs. As in the original proof, we use a restricted Poincaré inequality for two matchings to sample weighted perfect matchings and estimate their total weight. We simplify the proof of this inequality by isolating parts of alternating cycles directly on the original vertex set and controlling the resulting error terms. This avoids the auxiliary vertices and tree constructions used in the original proof. The argument preserves the required parameter bounds and yields the same FPRAS guarantee.

items.title: Pseudolocality and strong uniqueness for complete Ricci flows
items.summary: In this paper, we prove a uniform pseudolocality theorem for smooth complete Ricci flows whose initial metrics have Ricci curvature bounded below and uniformly positive injectivity radius. No a priori curvature bound is assumed on the flow. As a consequence, we obtain strong uniqueness for smooth complete Ricci flows from a complete metric with the above geometric bounds. We also prove that every smooth complete Ricci flow from a complete Ricci-flat metric with uniformly positive injectivity radius is stationary. The same conclusion holds for any complete flat initial metric. In particular, we give an affirmative answer to Chen's question on the strong uniqueness of Ricci flow from Euclidean space in every dimension.

items.title: Uniform convergence of canonical discrete uniformization on equilateral approximations
items.summary: We prove uniform convergence of the canonical discrete uniformization maps for every sequence of equilateral polygonal disks whose mesh tends to zero and whose marked Jordan boundaries converge uniformly. The limit is the normalized Riemann map, with convergence on the entire closed reference triangle. This proves Conjecture 7.3 of Luo, Sun and Wu for the original construction with Delaunay flips. The proof combines closed-domain compactness, marked lattice limits, a packing and resistance estimate for logarithmic cusp scales, and an envelope comparison principle, followed by a local affine energy argument.

items.title: Reeb orbits frequently intersecting a symplectic surface
items.summary: Consider a symplectic surface in a three-dimensional contact manifold with boundary on Reeb orbits (periodic orbits of the Reeb vector field). We assume that the rotation numbers of the boundary Reeb orbits satisfy a certain inequality, and we also make a technical assumption that the Reeb vector field has a particular ``nice'' form near the boundary of the surface. We then show that there exist Reeb orbits which intersect the interior of the surface, with a lower bound on the frequency of these intersections in terms of the symplectic area of the surface and the contact volume of the three-manifold. No genericity of the contact form is assumed. As a corollary of the main result, we obtain a generalization of various recent results relating the mean action of periodic orbits to the Calabi invariant for area-preserving surface diffeomorphisms.

items.title: Geometric Methods for Stochastic Dynamical Systems: A Concise Introduction
items.summary: Geometric methods are indispensable for analyzing, predicting, and mitigating the complex behaviors inherent in nonlinear systems. In this regime, the most probable transition path minimizes the Onsager-Machlup action functional, marking the likeliest route across an energy barrier. Lifting the analysis from individual sample paths to the infinite-dimensional space of probability densities, the book recasts these transitions as Schrödinger bridges - optimal paths between boundary distributions defined by minimizing relative entropy - and shows that the Onsager-Machlup path emerges as a special case when metastable states are idealized as Dirac masses. Generalizing further through α-divergences, which connect to entropies and the thermodynamic cost of nonequilibrium transitions, it introduces information geodesics as the resulting optimal density paths, offering a unified geometric account of how complex systems move between metastable regimes under uncertainty.

items.title: Dipole Formation in the Two-Component Plasma
items.summary: We consider the two-dimensional two-component plasma, or Coulomb gas, consisting of $N$ positive and $N$ negative charges with logarithmic interaction. We introduce a suitable regularization of the interaction by smearing the charges over a small length scale $λ$, which allows us to give meaning to the system in the continuum at any temperature. We provide an expansion of the free energy for each inverse temperature $β\ge2$, as $N \to \infty$ and $λ\to 0$. Doing so allows us to show that, for $β\geq 2$, the charges (for the most part) pair into neutral dipoles of very small size as $λ\to 0$. This complements the prior work of Leblé, Zeitouni, and the second author, which proved that this does not happen for $β< 2$, thereby implying a transition at $β= 2$ from free charges to dipole pairs. Moreover, we obtain an estimate on the size of linear statistics. The description in terms of dipoles is made via a decomposition into nearest-neighbor graphs of the point configurations, à la Gunson-Panta. This is combined with new energy estimates obtained via an electric reformulation of the interaction energy and a ball-growth method, which are expressed in terms of the nearest-neighbor graph distances only. In this way, the model is compared to a reduced nearest-neighbor interaction model, by showing the relative smallness of the dipole-dipole interactions.

items.title: Gaussian fluctuations for the stochastic wave equation with drift
items.summary: In this article, we study the spatial fluctuations of the solution to the stochastic wave equation with a nonlinear drift and multiplicative Gaussian noise in dimensions one and two. The noise is white in time, and its spatial covariance is either integrable or given by a Riesz kernel; space-time white noise in dimension one is also included. We establish spatial ergodicity, convergence of the rescaled covariance, and prove a quantitative central limit theorem for the spatial fluctuations. We also obtain the corresponding functional central limit theorem. Our approach exploits the compact support of the wave kernel to obtain an estimate for the spatially integrated second Malliavin derivative which is compatible with a bound for the total variation. Further arguments based on the Clark-Ocone formula are used to control the drift contributions.

items.title: Near-Optimal Higher-Order Oracle Complexity for Convex--Concave Minimax Optimization
