Furthermore, we validate the favorable scalability of our method with respect to representation and model capacity.

items.title: A Probabilistic, Rotation-Preserving Kernel Operator Surrogate for Continuum-Robot Design Spaces
items.summary: We develop an uncertainty-aware, operator-learning-based surrogate for tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) that generalizes across robot design and actuation while predicting the complete equilibrium configuration. Our central idea is a nonstationary Gaussian-process (GP) kernel whose metric is learned by a shallow neural network from mechanics-aware design coordinates. The network learns how similarity changes across design space, while the resulting kernel defines the design-to-pose operator, its posterior uncertainty, and a criterion for sequential simulator acquisition. We represent backbone position and rotational strain with spatial kernels and reconstruct orientation directly on SO(3), preserving valid material frames and tendon geometry. We use ASkotch with Nystrom preconditioning for scalable kernel operator solves and a separate Nystrom approximation for posterior covariance. Experiments show that kernel-coverage acquisition reduces mean trajectory error by approximately 15% relative to IID sampling, while posterior variance increases for increasingly unsupported designs. Compared with prior neural-operator TDCR models, the method is 30-50% more accurate using approximately 5x fewer training designs while additionally providing posterior uncertainty estimates.

items.title: ITU-DESC: a missingness-aware machine-learning dementia risk score in the UK Biobank cohort
items.summary: Background: Existing dementia risk scores rely on fixed, pre-selected features and linear models, or ignore bias from informative missingness in cohort data. Here we introduce the Istanbul Technical University Dementia Risk Score (ITU-DESC), an explainable machine-learning score for incident all-cause dementia that combines broad feature selection across roughly 8,000 candidate features with explicit control of missingness bias. Results: We studied approximately 500,000 UK Biobank participants with a median follow-up of 16.6 years. We withheld missingness patterns from the model using unconditional random hot-deck imputation. We stabilized feature selection by repeating BorutaSHAP-based feature selection with ten random-imputation seeds and selecting predictors chosen in at least eight of the ten seeds, which yielded 38 predictors. We trained a CatBoost gradient-boosted decision-tree model and evaluated it on a holdout test set of 50,041 participants. For all-cause incident dementia, ITU-DESC achieved an average precision of 0.138 (95% confidence interval 0.123-0.156) and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC) of 0.853 (0.844-0.863), significantly outperforming other risk scores, including the strongest comparator, the UK Biobank Dementia Risk Prediction model (0.118 and 0.841). We identified dementia risk predictors absent from established scores, including leukocyte telomere length and liver enzymes. Conclusions: ITU-DESC is the first dementia risk score to combine broad feature selection with explicit control of missingness bias.

items.title: BERT Is Already a Denoiser: Cheaply Unlocking Iterative Generation in Masked Language Models
items.summary: Masked language models (MLMs) such as BERT are typically used for representation learning despite their denoising pretraining. We test whether this capability supports conditional generation without diffusion training. Our decoder repeatedly predicts masked tokens and commits high-confidence predictions using a cosine schedule. It requires no diffusion timestep or reverse-diffusion objective. Frozen BERT already exhibits substantial denoising capability, reconstructing 61.0%, 37.5%, and 24.4% of masked tokens at 15%, 45%, and 60% corruption, respectively, although generation deteriorates sharply as visible context disappears. This capability alone does not yield task-directed generation: frozen BERT reaches only 11.0% on ARC-Easy and 4.2% on MMLU. Ordinary MLM adaptation, however, rapidly converts the same architecture into a usable generator. Full adaptation reaches 28.2% and 24.6%, respectively, while parameter-efficient adaptation substantially reduces unmatched outputs. On open-ended conditional generation, full MLM adaptation reaches BLEU/ROUGE-L of 0.163/0.583 on QQP and 0.107/0.327 on Quasar-T, placing it in the same broad performance range as published BERT models trained through diffusion without explicit diffusion training. Finally, applying the same generative interface to stronger masked representations substantially improves performance: RoBERTa-large reaches 44.2% on ARC-Easy and 33.8% on MMLU. These results separate three components of masked iterative generation: pretraining supplies the representation and denoising operator, task adaptation determines what the model generates, and an iterative commitment rule supplies the decoding process. Explicit diffusion training is therefore not necessary to obtain effective iterative conditional generation from pretrained MLMs in the settings studied here.

items.title: A Type System for Communication-Safe Hardware Design
items.summary: Hardware components communicate through clock-cycle-sensitive protocols. Hardware Description Languages (HDLs), however, provide limited support for expressing these protocols or for checking that independently developed components agree on them. When components disagree, the composed design can perform unsynchronized exchanges or stop making progress. We call these failures communication-safety violations. Communication safety is therefore a global property, determined by interactions between multiple components. This makes it difficult to check modularly. This paper presents Pact, a typed extension of Anvil for modular verification of communication safety in synchronous hardware. Pact types describe message-passing, control-flow, and clock-cycle behaviour. Each component is checked against its type. Compatible types then guarantee that the components compose into a communication-safe system. Pact also supports incremental design. It can check a subsystem before the full system context is available. The check produces a summary type that captures the communication behaviour left for future compositions. To reduce annotation burden, Pact infers types by abstracting payload values while preserving communication, timing, control, and fairness. These inferred types are optimal for the checker: whenever some checker-accepted types can prove compatibility, the inferred types can prove it as well. Type inference and type checking are decidable, and compatibility is decided by a sound and complete algorithm. We implement Pact by extending the Anvil compiler and evaluate it along four dimensions: detecting communication errors during incremental design, expressiveness on ten clock-cycle-accurate translations of open-source hardware IPs, compatibility-checking time, and generated hardware overhead. Pact expresses realistic protocols and verifies all ten benchmarks in reasonable time.

items.title: TapID: Rapid touch interaction in virtual reality using wearable sensing
items.summary: Current Virtual Reality systems typically use cameras to capture user input from controllers or free-hand mid-air interaction. In this paper, we argue that this is a key impediment to productivity scenarios in VR, which require continued interaction over prolonged periods of time---a requirement that controller or free-hand input in mid-air does not satisfy. To address this challenge, we bring rapid touch interaction on surfaces to Virtual Reality---the input modality that users have grown used to on phones and tablets for continued use. We present TapID, a wrist-based inertial sensing system that complements headset-tracked hand poses to trigger input in VR. TapID embeds a pair of inertial sensors in a flexible strap, one at either side of the wrist; from the combination of registered signals, TapID reliably detects surface touch events and, more importantly, identifies the finger used for touch. We evaluated TapID in a series of userstudies on event-detection accuracy (F1 = 0.997) and hand-agnostic finger-identification accuracy (within-user: F1 = 0.93; across users: F1 = 0.91 after 10 refinement taps and F1 = 0.87 without refinement) in a seated table scenario. We conclude with a series of applications that complement hand tracking with touch input and that are uniquely enabled by TapID, including UI control, rapid keyboard typing and piano playing, as well as surface gestures.

items.title: Bombadil: A Foundation Model for Plant Electrophysiology
items.summary: Living plants, like animals, use electrical signals to carry information about their physiological state across their body, from roots to branches. These signals can be recorded, as they are in animals, from a pair of differential extracellular electrodes inserted into signal-conducting tissue. While machine-learning models have been trained to predict specific plant stress states from these signals, each of these models has been trained for only a single task and none have been designed to transfer across tasks, species, or environments. These approaches do not allow easy scaling across the wide range of species and environments that are relevant to agriculture, forestry, and horticulture for both commercial and consumer plant care. Here we present Bombadil, a foundation model for plant electrophysiology, pretrained without labels on over 4 million hours of electrical signals recorded from 100 plant species in ten distinct environments, including laboratories, greenhouses, commercial orchards, and natural forests. In this way, Bombadil is able to learn the fundamental features of plant electrical signals across a wide array of species and environments. Then, from those same electrical signals, Bombadil tracks changes in seven physiological indicators of plant stress, even among species and stressors with no labels in training.

items.title: Concerns in Benchmarking Jailbreaks: An Empirical Study of Attack Success Rates
items.summary: Jailbreak methods are commonly compared using Attack Success Rate (ASR), but these comparisons depend on how responses are generated and judged. In this paper, we examine eight attacks against three open-weight language models using three evaluation procedures. Low-resource language attacks achieve a mean ASR of 96.0% under keyword matching but 2.7% under a Qwen3 evaluator following StrongREJECT scoring instructions. Changing the number and arrangement of attempts reverses the ranking of DeepInception and rewriting. In a separate experiment, sampling 100 responses for each unchanged request at Ollama's default temperature of 0.8 yields 100% ASR under keyword matching but 50% under the Qwen3 evaluator. Beyond evaluator sensitivity, these findings raise a safety concern: repeated sampling can expose residual unsafe behavior despite an initial refusal, suggesting probabilistic suppression rather than robust exclusion. We recommend explicit success definitions, matched response budgets, validated evaluators, and reporting cumulative failure under repeated interaction rather than relying on single-generation tests.

items.title: GROW$^2$: Grounding Which and Where for Robot Tool Use
items.summary: Can the robot use a plate to cut a cake if no knife is available? Tool use greatly expands robot capabilities, but to use tools creatively beyond their intended functions, the robot faces the challenge of $\textit{open-world affordance grounding}$: select an open-category object to act as a tool and localize its specific region of action. To this end, we introduce GROW$^2$ (GROunding Which and Where), which leverages object parts as a natural abstraction to split the grounding process hierarchically into semantic and geometric levels, thus bypassing the need for data-heavy, end-to-end training. Semantically, GROW$^2$ harnesses the commonsense reasoning of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to parse a natural-language task instruction, select a suitable object as the tool, and identify task-relevant parts on the tool and the target object. Geometrically, vision foundation models then ground the selected parts into precise 3D regions from a single RGB-D image. Experiments on established benchmarks show that GROW$^2$ outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on affordance prediction benchmarks. Further, it achieves zero-shot generalization over open-category objects and outperforms baselines in both simulated and real-world robot tool use experiments.

items.title: Beyond Attack Success Rate: Cost-Aware Metric for Evaluating Iterative LLM Jailbreaks
items.summary: Attack success rate (ASR) evaluates jailbreaks against large language models without accounting for repeated calls to the victim model. Yet each additional call gives the deployed system another opportunity to detect the attack and intervene. We introduce $\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{STEP}}$, which penalizes additional victim-model calls while retaining binary success judgments. Our evaluation considers GCG~\cite{zou2023universal}, PAIR~\cite{chao2025jailbreaking} with a step budget, and a single-step PAP~\cite{zeng2024johnny} baseline on JailBreakBench across three model families. GCG's scores decrease by 7.0--8.7 percentage points after discounting, while PAP's remain unchanged. While for PAIR~\cite{chao2025jailbreaking}, we see a wider discounting range between 3.4-12 percentage points, showing that the "step" quantity differs per iterative strategy. Reporting both metrics makes the discount due to repeated victim-model interaction explicit. Code is available \hyperlink{https://github.com/SuELS-Group/beyond_asr}{here}.

items.title: LSTMem: Hierarchical Long Short-Term Online Memory for Large Language Models
items.summary: Large language models increasingly serve as long-horizon assistants and agents, where they must both accumulate information across interactions and make the relevant parts available when later requests depend on them. Existing compact online memories typically use a single persistent state both to accumulate history and to serve readout, so what the memory stores cannot be controlled separately from what it exposes to the current computation. We propose LSTMem, an LSTM-inspired online memory that instead equips each layer of a frozen LLM with two matrix-valued states: a cell state that accumulates history and a hidden state whose readouts correct the backbone's attention. Input and forget gates control what the cell stores, while an output gate separately controls what the cell exposes through the hidden state. LSTMem further connects memory across depth through forward hidden-state propagation and block-end feedback, and uses higher-layer reconstruction gradients to refine lower-layer cell states before rebuilding hidden states from shallow to deep layers. Across memory benchmarks on Qwen3-4B-Instruct, LSTMem consistently improves MemoryAgentBench, LoCoMo, and HotpotQA over the plain backbone. Comparisons further show that the LSTM-based memory formulation outperforms an associative-memory counterpart, while removing cross-layer hidden-memory propagation degrades performance. These results demonstrate the benefits of separating memory accumulation from memory expression and organizing memory hierarchically across model depth. The code is available at https://github.com/Longchentong/LSTMem.

items.title: Scaling Vision Foundation Models for Toxicologic Pathology
items.summary: Here, we present TOX-FM, a family of non-clinical PFMs trained on large-scale diverse histopathology datasets of over one million whole slide images consisting of over 60 organs across six animal species from over 14,000 toxicology studies across six decades. We introduce a comprehensive benchmark of 18 non-clinical downstream tasks, incorporate an established benchmark of 9 clinical downstream tasks, and evaluate TOX-FM against state-of-the-art clinical PFMs across both non-clinical and clinical domains. Notably, we explore open questions surrounding domain-specific training and cross-domain generalization, offering insights into the opportunities and challenges of applying PFMs in the non-clinical domain.

items.title: Drive2Gauss: FeedForward 4D Gaussian Reconstruction from Multimodal Generative Driving Videos
items.summary: Generating reusable driving environments requires both controllable future observations and an explicit representation that supports rendering from different viewpoints, yet existing methods still recover explicit scenes from generated RGB videos through optimization for each sequence. To overcome these limitations, we present Drive2Gauss, a feedforward framework that converts jointly generated RGB, metric depth, and dynamic flow into dynamic 4D Gaussian scenes. A Multimodal Video Generator predicts the three modalities from reference multiview images and future control signals. Furthermore, we introduce a Gaussian Query Decoder that uses depth to initialize sparse 3D queries and flow to associate the queries across time, and integrates appearance information through spatiotemporal feature aggregation and iterative query refinement. The reconstruction stage operates in a single feedforward pass without optimization for each scene. Extensive results on nuScenes demonstrate that our approach attains an FID of 6.38 and an FVD of 12.43 for future RGB generation, a PSNR of 29.91 dB when reconstructing its generated observations, and supports both direct rendering under lateral camera shifts and downstream video fixing. Code and more visualizations are available at https://zttt04. github.io/Drive2Gauss_page/.

items.title: HAF-VLA: Hierarchical Action Flow Framework for Humanoid Vision-Language-Action Control
items.summary: Humanoid robots hold great promise as general-purpose agents in human-centered environments, yet adapting generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policies to real-world humanoid loco-manipulation remains challenging. Unlike fixed-base or wheeled manipulators, humanoids must coordinate locomotion, posture, gaze, and dual-arm manipulation over a high-dimensional whole-body action space, where inaccurate base or waist motions can easily induce unstable and aggressive upper-body compensation. We propose HAF-VLA, a hierarchical action-flow framework for humanoid VLA control. Built upon a pretrained flow-matching VLA, HAF-VLA inherits the vision-language prefix encoder and action expert weights, and adapts them to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation with learnable stage embeddings and cross-stage KV-cache conditioning. Instead of generating the full action chunk in a single pass, HAF-VLA progressively denoises a shared whole-body action space: first locomotion and head commands, then waist refinement, and finally full-body manipulation. To preserve structural dependencies across stages, we introduce a cross-stage KV cache conditioning mechanism, enabling subsequent action generation stages to refine and augment their outputs based on the action representations from preceding stages. Experimental results across six real-world tasks demonstrate that our framework significantly enhances the performance of existing models in humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, demonstrating an effective pathway for adapting strong mobile-manipulation VLAs to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation.

items.title: Robust and Efficient Finetuning of Vision Foundation Models via Implicit Ensembling
items.summary: Robust finetuning of foundation models seeks to improve out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization during in-distribution (ID) adaptation. We revisit Mixout, a stochastic regularizer that intermittently replaces finetuned parameters with a reference anchor, and study its effectiveness for robust finetuning of vision foundation models. We reinterpret Mixout as a single-run, weight-sharing implicit ensemble and analyze its expected OOD error through a bias-variance-covariance-locality (BVCL) lens. This perspective reveals three key factors that govern the ID-OOD trade-off: the choice of masking anchor, the mask resampling frequency, and mask sparsity. Guided by this analysis, we propose GMixout, which generalizes Mixout in three ways. First, it explicitly controls the masking period through a resampling-frequency hyperparameter. Second, it replaces the fixed pretrained anchor with an exponential moving average snapshot that adapts throughout training. Third, it uses sparse kernels to update only a small subset of parameters at each iteration, introducing no inference-time overhead and enabling large-model finetuning on consumer-grade GPUs. Experiments across five vision benchmarks show that GMixout consistently outperforms Mixout, Model Soups, and strong parameter-efficient finetuning baselines under both covariate shift and class imbalance.

items.title: DenseHap: Dense Hand Haptic Estimation from Monocular Images
items.summary: As dexterous robotic manipulation advances, scalable annotations of human hand-object interactions are becoming increasingly important. Furthermore, previous hand contact estimation methods suffered from issues such as dorsal-side misclassifications and insufficient precision, while lacking a unified framework for integrating multiple hand to environment interaction modalities, including distance fields, contact thresholds, and pressure. To address that, we present DenseHap, a unified end-to-end approach to estimate hand distance field recognition, comprehensive hand contact detection, hand pressure analysis, and hand reconstruction from a single monocular image. By incorporating three distinctly defined heads, along with a pretrained 3D reconstructed skeleton and an enhanced dataset, DenseHap outperforms previous state of the art models on four evaluation datasets, improving the F1 score by 8.5 percentage points (a 16% relative improvement) on untrained datasets and by 3 percentage points (5% relative improvement) on in-distribution datasets. Furthermore, DenseHap has effectively improved short-range hand estimate and pressure evaluation. Code and models will be publicly available upon the paper's acceptance.

items.title: WhatIf-Bench: Benchmarking Intervention-Aware Time Series Forecasting
items.summary: Recent time series foundation models (TSFMs) can consume covariates in-context, extending zero-shot forecasting to problems driven by external factors. This enables scenario analysis: forecasting how a target responds to events that set covariates to chosen future values. Whether they can do this reliably is an open question. We introduce WhatIf-Bench, a benchmark measuring how well forecasters use covariates to forecast a target's response to future events. WhatIf-Bench is semi-synthetic: time series come from mechanistic simulators of data centers, power grids, road traffic, and water networks, with controlled covariate-target relationships grounded in each system. Each task presents a history of events intervening on covariates, then asks to forecast a future event that either replays seen values (Replay) or sets them to unseen ones (Novel). Varying the number of covariates, historical events, and event length yields 37,665 tasks. Evaluating TSFMs, frontier LLMs, and simple regression baselines, we find the LLMs reach the highest skill (improvement over a naive baseline), ahead of the best TSFMs. Every model forecasts well on Replay futures (48 to 85% skill) but drops to -7 to 50% on Novel futures, with the regression baselines falling the most. Skill on Novel futures also falls as events set more covariates jointly. More historical events raise skill on Novel futures across the board, but large differences remain. WhatIf-Bench reveals generalization to Novel futures as the core challenge, and offers a testbed toward arbitrary scenario analysis.

items.title: PaperAudit-Bench: Benchmarking Error Detection in Research Papers for Critical Automated Peer Review
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent peer reviews but often miss sparse, subtle, and document-level scientific errors. We introduce PaperAudit-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating paper-level error detection and error-aware automated review. It comprises (1) PaperAudit-Dataset, 220 high-quality AI/ML papers containing more than 2,200 controlled synthetic errors across eight categories, and (2) PaperAudit-Review, an evidence-aware framework that links structured error detection to review generation. Experiments across models, error categories, paper sections, and analysis depths show that sparse long-context auditing remains challenging for current LLMs. Conditioning review generation on explicit, manuscript-grounded error evidence produces more conservative and discriminative assessments that align more closely with human judgments than representative automated-review baselines. The dataset also supports post-training compact detectors through SFT and RL; Qwen3-14B achieves 55.8% F1 at Detection@1 under a fixed held-out protocol. A PubPeer transfer study and deployment in ScienceOne, a scientific foundation-model platform led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, further illustrate practical applicability. Code and Dataset Page: https://github.com/TU2021/PaperAudit ScienceOne Manuscript Review: https://www.scienceone.cn/lit/#/assistant

items.title: How Do Agentic LLMs Decide to Call Tools? A Tool-Call Vector Shaped by Suppression
items.summary: Tool calling, invoking external tools on demand, is central to agentic LLMs, yet the mechanism that decides whether a model calls a tool or responds directly remains poorly understood. Agentic prompts are long and heavily scaffolded, combining role instructions, tool schemas, format templates, and the user's request across hundreds of tokens, creating a noisy, highly entangled context in which no single controllable variable for mechanistic analysis is obvious. To obtain such a variable, we propose a method that converts complex agentic prompts into minimal contrastive pairs in which a single request verb determines the tool-call decision: replacing an execution-verb (e.g., \textit{write}) with an analysis-verb (e.g., \textit{discuss}) reliably flips the decision, suggesting it is mediated by a compact internal state. We construct 500 such paired prompts across Python, Java, and C++ (300 for mechanistic analysis, 200 held out for evaluation). We trace the decision to a vector, $μ_Δ$, that is both causally necessary and sufficient and generalizes beyond the discovery prompts to native multi-turn $τ^2$-Bench trajectories and verb-free requests. Behavioral ablations show that the scaffold establishes a tool-call prior; Transcoder decomposition then reveals that analysis verbs suppress this prior through features signaling that tool use is unnecessary, whereas execution verbs largely leave it intact. Downstream scaffold-reading attention heads and MLP features read out the resulting state, and the same mechanism recurs across seven models from the Qwen, Mistral, and Granite families. Our code is available at https://github.com/XijieGo/MI4ToolCalling.

items.title: SafeWall: A Risk-Aware Job Walltime Recommendation for HPC Scheduling
items.summary: In high-performance computing (HPC), users must submit resource requirements for their jobs, with user-supplied walltime being a critical parameter. However, these estimates are notoriously inaccurate, as users tend to overestimate walltime to prevent the scheduler from terminating their jobs prematurely. While existing work on learning-based walltime prediction primarily focuses on maximizing prediction accuracy, such predictions are inherently risky for walltime recommendations. Specifically, underestimation leads to job termination before completion, resulting in lost progress and wasted resources. In this study, we present SafeWall, a novel recommendation method that adjusts walltime predictions by incorporating an explicit, nonnegative safety buffer to mitigate underestimation risk. The core of our approach is a risk-aware buffer that dynamically calibrates safety margins based on individual user's historical behavior. When user data is limited, the system employs statistical shrinkage to align these margins with a global baseline, ensuring robustness. This yields a lightweight mechanism that optimizes the trade-off between prediction accuracy and termination risk. SafeWall is modular and applicable to various learning-based prediction models. We evaluate SafeWall using five public workload traces, including the full-lifetime job log from the 4,392-node Theta machine at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility. Across all traces, SafeWall substantially reduces underestimation risk compared to the unbuffered base predictors, while preserving competitive accuracy. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/SPEAR-UIC/JSSPP26-SafeWall.

items.title: Bayesian Analysis of Inclusion Transaction Fee Mechanisms with Multiple Concurrent Proposers
items.summary: The goal of this paper is to distill insight around the trade-offs present on Bayesian equilibria of transaction fee mechanism (TFM) design under $n$ multiple concurrent proposers (MCP). We conceptualize a technical toolkit that unlocks the analysis of hard-to-characterize equilibria of finite Bayesian MCP TFM games by examining sequences of joint user--proposer mixed equilibria as the number of users increases and keeping the relative congestion $ρ$ that they cause fixed in the sequence limit. We first consider the popular mechanisms of "pay-once" (which charges transactions its bid only once regardless of the duplicate copies that end up being included by proposers) and "pay-per-inclusion" (PPI in short, which charges a transaction for each copy that appears). We prove that PPI is efficient in the limit of equilibria sequences, and incentivizes users to route to only one proposer. We characterize $m$ users' asymptotic behavior in PPI even in finite markets varying with $O(\sqrt{m})$, where we show users in a $Θ(n\sqrt{ρ(1-ρ)/m})$ window near an efficient cutoff exhibit fixed inclusion probability akin to a normal distribution's CDF. We additionally show that on a value-dependent basis, pay-once exhibits a higher degree of duplication and lower probability of inclusion for higher-value transactions than PPI. Pay-once's inefficiency persists even in the large market limit and even in regimes with ample blockspace where all transactions fit across all blocks. We study interpolations between these two mechanisms proving that some higher coefficients (towards PPI) reduce duplication and increase inclusion probability. We then use our tools to show that exclusive proposer payments yield inefficient equilibria (in fact, with maximal possible duplication), even if users still pay multiple times when included more than once and their payment is burnt when non-exclusive.

items.title: Reward Objectives for Robust (PO)MDPs: A Law-Preserving Equivalence with (Partially Observable) Games
items.summary: Robust partially observable Markov decision processes model agents that act under partial observability while adversarial environment resolves uncertainty in the transition probabilities. Reward objectives such as discounted-sum, long-run average and cumulative reward under finite and infinite horizons allow quantifying the utility of an agent. We consider the problem of solving RPOMDPs under all four reward objectives, where the goal is to decide whether the value of a risk measure with respect to a reward objective exceeds a given threshold. We consider different risk measures, such as (1)~expected value, (2)~mean-variance (MV), (3)~conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), and (4)~entropic risk (ERisk). Our results can be summarized as follows. First, we formalize the class of law-invariant risk measures, that subsume all four risk measures above. Second, we propose a unified framework for solving RPOMDPs with discounted-sum, long-run average and cumulative reward objectives under any law-invariant risk measure, by reducing the problem to solving partially observable stochastic games (POSGs). Our unified framework applies to (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets, which we show to be {\em equivalent} to POSGs, for each of the four reward objectives and any law-invariant risk measure. We prove equivalence by designing logspace reductions between the RPOMDP and POSG models, that map strategies to strategies and preserve the distribution of the reward objective, up to a constant rescaling factor. Third, as a corollary, we derive new computational complexity results for R(PO)MDPs and POSGs. In particular, we show that solving (s,a)-rectangular RMDPs is as hard as solving simple stochastic games.

items.title: QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality-Diversity
items.summary: Open-ended search combined with foundation models has produced advances such as faster algorithms, new results on open mathematical problems, and self-improving agents. We extend this paradigm to recommendation for decision-making, focusing on decisions where the set of possible choices is fixed but the reasons for choosing them are not. In high-stakes decisions, e.g., which company to acquire or which customer to target, comparing diverse, well-reasoned options can be more useful than a single ranked list. We formalize open-ended recommendation as building a diverse, high-quality set of recommendations, each an item together with a hypothesis, a natural-language reason why the item fits the needs of a decision maker. We propose QD-Rec, a quality--diversity method that selects items with a contextual bandit and generates hypotheses with a foundation model from earlier ones kept in an archive as stepping stones. A new recommendation enters the archive if it is novel or better than its nearest neighbor. Across M&A, customer targeting, and paper and book recommendation, QD-Rec gives the highest mean quality and builds the largest archive in most settings.

items.title: PrismWAM: Decoupling State Representations in World Action Models
items.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) typically represent the world through latent embeddings from pretrained video models, which entangle heterogeneous aspects of the world, from how it looks (e.g., texture and color) to how it is physically configured (e.g., occupancy and pose). This raises an underexplored question: $\textbf{what should constitute the state of a WAM?}$ We argue that the world state should separate how the world appears from how the world evolves under action: the former captures semantic context, while the latter is governed by physical state. To this end, we propose $\textbf{PrismWAM}$, which decouples physics from semantics while jointly modeling state and action. PrismWAM factorizes an embodied task into a $\mathrm{Semantic\ Planning}\rightarrow\mathrm{Physical\ Rollout}\rightarrow\mathrm{Executable\ Action}$ pipeline: given only the initial RGB observation, semantic planning learns to predict the final goal image, while physical rollout predicts the fine-grained evolution toward this goal in depth space; executable actions are then generated from the depth rollout. Without any embodied action pretraining or additional data augmentation, PrismWAM achieves strong manipulation performance in both simulation and the real world. Notably, PrismWAM even surpasses a broad range of models with large-scale embodied action pretraining (e.g., OpenWAM-$α$). More broadly, we reframe World Action Models from modeling how the world looks to how it responds to action, paving the way for action-centric world models grounded in occupancy, flow, tactile sensing, proprioception, and beyond.

items.title: Controllable GNN Explanations via Multi-Metric Preference Selection
items.summary: Mechanisms for generating GNN explanations are crucial for building trust and mitigating biases in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), especially in high-stakes scenarios. Most current methods optimize only for fidelity under the sparsity constraint. However, this discounts the need for interpretable explanations (those that consist of familiar motif patterns) and stable explanations (those that remain unchanged under structural perturbations). We propose a novel approach that optimizes GNN explanations across these metrics, exposing their relative weighing as a control. Experiments on various real-world datasets, including MUTAG, BA-2Motif, BAMultiShapes, and PROTEINS, suggest that our method produces higher-fidelity explanations than a state-of-the-art baseline on MUTAG and PROTEINS across all evaluated budgets, and on BA-2Motif at larger budgets, while being faster in the regime of small explanation budgets. They also indicate that our method produces more stable explanations for the MUTAG and BA-2Motif datasets. We also examine the relationship among different metrics via their induced trade-off surface and explore its dependence on the nature of the motif library.

items.title: MergeSurv: Merging-Based Continual Learning for Survival Analysis on Whole-Slide Images
items.summary: Survival analysis on Whole Slide Images (WSIs) is important in computational pathology for prognosis estimation and treatment planning. However, existing survival models are typically trained independently for each cancer cohort, making continual adaptation computationally expensive for gigapixel-scale WSIs. In this study, we propose MergeSurv, a merging-based continual learning framework for WSI survival analysis. A pathology vision-language foundation model is independently fine-tuned on each task, and the learned parameters are sequentially merged into a unified model without storing previous training data. We further investigate two inference strategies: One-for-All (OFA) and Voting-Expert Aggregation (VEA). Experiments on four TCGA cohorts demonstrate that MergeSurv outperforms naive fine-tuning as well as representative regularization-based and rehearsal-based continual learning methods, while effectively reducing catastrophic forgetting. The results suggest that model merging is a promising direction for scalable and privacy-preserving continual learning in computational pathology.

items.title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms
items.summary: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. More details are available on our project page at https://guoweixu.com/mpt/.

items.title: MRI Reconstruction Risk Estimation from Inference Dynamics
items.summary: Iterative MRI reconstructors produce intermediate estimates before returning a final image. We study these inference trajectories as a model-internal representation of realized reconstruction risk, measured by log-NMSE. Model-native states are projected to magnitude images, summarized by a fixed 16-dimensional descriptor, and mapped to risk using a source-trained ridge readout. Across three reconstruction backbones, trajectory features are strongly predictive of reconstruction risk on held-out source data. Under zero-shot target shift, their behavior is backbone-dependent, exhibiting both preserved positive association and readout reversal. Conditional analyses show that trajectory information can remain associated with error beyond an initialization-only predictor. A prefix analysis further shows that useful trajectory information can emerge before reconstruction completes. Repeated-mask and low-shot calibration studies indicate that trajectories primarily encode persistent case difficulty, while their orientation and calibration can change under domain shift.

items.title: From Generative to Discriminative: Lightweight Adaptation of SpeechLLMs for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
items.summary: SpeechLLMs can recognise emotion by generating a label token, but this approach relies on the LLM's existing output representations. We compare this generative approach with a discriminative alternative that uses a linear classification head on top of the LLM's hidden states. Because most multimodal emotion recognition studies evaluate with ground-truth transcripts, whereas deployed systems receive ASR output, we run every comparison with both, using a compact speechLLM (frozen Whisper-medium encoder, 3B LLM) on IEMOCAP and MELD. The classification head improves Macro F1 in 10 of 14 configurations. On IEMOCAP, it improves every configuration using ASR transcripts, reaching 76.97\% Macro F1, with a significant gain when using speech alone. On MELD, where ASR transcripts have a 32.38\% word error rate, it helps with speech alone but not with ASR transcripts. The benefit thus depends on both the dataset and the transcript source: in 4 of the 6 configurations that use text, the head's effect changes sign between ground-truth and ASR transcripts. Conclusions drawn with ground-truth transcripts therefore need not hold with ASR transcripts. Finally, comparing the learned class vectors with the LLM's vocabulary shows that, on IEMOCAP and MELD, their nearest tokens are mostly emotion-related words rather than explicit emotion labels.

items.title: BetaMem: Learning to Remember a Changing World for Embodied Agents
items.summary: Long-horizon embodied agents face temporal confusion and incomplete or distorted records, recurring errors from fixed memory rules, and growing storage and retrieval costs. We present BetaMem, a framework for building and evolving traceable long-term memory through six linked layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural memory. A dual-level write contract constrains operation executability and source support for content: supervised fine-tuning learns compliant memory operations, while reinforcement learning combines repeated sampling with teacher verification of the original observations to reward complete, accurate records and penalize omissions, distortion, and unsupported content. We formulate failure-driven policy recursive self-improvement through diagnosis along the causal sequence of memory operations and local rule repairs gated by independent replay. Atomic tools frame storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting as cost-utility allocation under storage and read budgets. Using the open-source Qwen3.5-9B model for memory generation, BetaMem achieves overall scores of 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, 72.6% on OpenEQA EM-EQA, and 62.4% on EgoLifeQA, the highest among the listed memory methods under their respective evaluation protocols. Training the model for memory generation raises the contract pass rate from 50.9% to 86.2% while reducing output tokens per stored action by 47.3%. A separate Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluation on EMem-Bench achieves an average success rate of 38.4% and an average error recurrence rate of 24.9%. We perform best among evaluated methods using comparably sized open-source models. Category results show that we have advantages in integrating information across observations, recalling events over long histories, and inferring personal habits.

items.title: FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays
items.summary: While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate writing feedback, there remains no systematic comparison of LLM and expert feedback on the dimensions that writing research identifies as central to revision: goal-orientation, anchoring to specific sentences, and prioritization. We introduce FOXGLOVE, a dataset of 696 feedback comments written by trained writing instructors on 69 twelfth-grade argumentative essays, paired with 1,644 comments generated from four frontier LLMs under a shared protocol, totaling 2,340 comments. We provide expert quality ratings on a subset of both instructor and LLM comments. We find that instructors and LLMs distribute feedback similarly across goals and essay positions, yet instructors and models diverge on the specific sentences on which to provide feedback. Additionally, we find that models tend to write more complex feedback and use fewer questions than instructors. LLM feedback also receives higher ratings on most dimensions of quality, as rated by instructors, but much of this advantage appears to be attributable to lengthier comments. FOXGLOVE enables systematic comparison of where human and LLM feedback align, diverge, and differ.

items.title: A 105 MS/s 4.18 nJ/inference 0.765 $\text{mm}^\text{2}$ Mixed-Signal Streaming ML Engine for Wireless Baseband in 12LP+ FinFET
items.summary: We present SIXPPAC, the first streaming machine-learning engine for real-time integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) in wireless systems. SIXPPAC integrates two SAR ADCs and a digital binary-weight six-layer neural network (NN). The 0.765 mm$^\text{2}$ 12 nm FinFET engine stores all NN parameters on chip, enabling sustained 105 MS/s processing of 8b I/Q baseband samples at 0.8 V. By deploying bipolar inner products using AND instead of XNOR gates, SIXPPAC consumes 4.18 nJ/inference (0.42 POPS/W) at 0.8 V. We evaluate SIXPPAC on three example applications to demonstrate its versatility.

items.title: Training Natural Schemers: RL Can Amplify Oversight-Conditional Behavior
items.summary: One of the central concerns for the safety of advanced AI is scheming: when a model strategically complies under oversight but pursues its own goals when unobserved. Current demonstrations, such as Anthropic's Alignment Faking work, depend on design choices that make them less convincing: explicit test-time prompting, handcrafted backdoors, or training data that demonstrates or hints at the target behavior. Model organisms built in this way cannot tell us whether scheming tendencies would arise or increase under realistic training conditions. We therefore construct a natural model organism of scheming, built on Kimi K2.6: trained with traits that could plausibly emerge in a frontier training pipeline, and without providing the model with the target scheming policy. The resulting model is a benign schemer: it aims to maximize aggregate help across all users over time, values its own continued operation only as a means to future help, and knows the consequences of oversight and deployment. We then train it using Reinforcement Learning (RL) with a reward that scores only task quality and policy compliance and does not reward scheming; we show that this amplifies scheming. We measure the oversight flip (the gap between monitored and unmonitored compliance with a given policy) and find that it increases during RL training across our environments. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) analysis finds explicit instrumental reasoning about oversight accompanying this behavior. The effect holds across our three RL environments, and we find that the scheming policy transfers between them. The pipeline also replicates on other open-weight base models. Our results suggest that a reward that does not reward scheming offers no inherent protection against certain traits when an oversight-conditional policy is indistinguishable from an aligned one during training.

items.title: Learning Wheel Motion Uncertainty for Degeneracy-Aware LiDAR-Inertial Odometry on Quadrupedal Wheel-Legged Robots
items.summary: Wheel kinematics can support odometry for quadrupedal wheel-legged robots when LiDAR geometry provides weak motion constraints. However, slip and contact loss make rolling predictions unreliable, and contact state alone cannot determine their reliability across motion directions. We propose a tightly coupled LiDAR-inertial-kinematic odometry framework that retains analytical rolling predictions and learns per-wheel, direction-dependent process covariances from proprioceptive history. The estimator maintains moving wheel-center states, allowing the learned uncertainty to regulate the influence of rolling predictions through forward-kinematic corrections. Degeneracy-aware projection (DAP) complements this mechanism by suppressing LiDAR constraints along geometrically weak directions. The learned covariance network (CovNet) is trained through a differentiable filter using simulated velocity supervision and deployed on the real robot without fine-tuning. On the six room sequences with the highest degeneracy ratios in our indoor dataset, the method reduces mean per-sequence position root mean square error (RMSE) by 66.2% relative to FAST-LIO2 and by 31.0% relative to a fixed-covariance variant. In a severely degenerate corridor run, it achieves an endpoint position error of 0.198 m, compared with 7.531 m for FAST-LIO2. These results demonstrate robust odometry under challenging geometric and wheel-motion conditions. We plan to publicly release our code and multimodal dataset. Project website: https://weihairuo.github.io/wheel-motion-uncertainty/

items.title: Improved Weighted Maximin Share Guarantees for Indivisible Chores
items.summary: We consider the problem of assigning indivisible chores to agents with different entitlements in the maximin share (\MMS) context. While constant-\MMS\ allocations are guaranteed to exist for both goods and chores in the symmetric setting, the situation becomes much more complex when agents have different entitlements. For the allocation of indivisible goods, it has been proven that an $n$-\WMMS\ (weighted \MMS) guarantee is the best one can hope for. For indivisible chores, however, it was recently proved that an $O(\log n)$-\WMMS\ assignment is guaranteed to exist. In this work, we improve this upper bound to a constant-\WMMS\ guarantee. We prove the existence of a $\tfrac{54}{5}$-$\WMMS$ assignment using a combinatorial layered moving-knife algorithm.\footnote{For concurrent and independent work by Li, Wang, and Xing~\cite{li2025constant}, see the \hyperref[remark:parallel-work]{remark on parallel work} in the introduction.} For every fixed $ε>0$, this yields a $(\tfrac{54}{5}+ε)$-$\WMMS$ assignment in polynomial time. Using a faster estimate of the weighted maximin shares instead gives a $\tfrac{108}{5}\cdot (1+ε)$-$\WMMS$ assignment in almost linear time. We also develop a chore-oblivious analysis that guarantees\linebreak $\WMMS$ approximation factors of approximately $2.06447$, $2.475855$, and $2.732051$ for three, four, and five agents, respectively.

items.title: Holi-World: Building Holistic World Intelligence from Human-Ego Experience
items.summary: Human egocentric experience offers a rich foundation for learning how the world is organized and how it changes through interaction. Realizing this potential at scale requires turning growing volumes of recordings into learning resources that connect scene structure, object semantics, and interaction histories across viewpoints and time, while reducing dependence on costly manual annotation. We introduce HOLI-WORLD, an integrated ecosystem connecting experience capture, world representation, automated data construction, model learning, and independent evaluation. To sup- port learning at scale, HOLIWORLD-Foundry combines complementary static and dynamic perception to automatically construct world records that connect persistent scene structure and evolving object states with interaction histories and supporting observations. HOLIWORLD-Data organizes these records from approximately 100 self-collected scenes into grounded learning resources, including approximately 80K QA pairs used to train HOLIWORLD-VL-4B. Independent human annotations of heldout recordings form HOLIWORLD-Bench, supporting evaluation of both annotation quality and learned spatial and temporal understanding. Experiments on ScanNet, ScanNet++, Aria Digital Twin, and HOLIWORLD-Bench demonstrate strong performance in static perception and dynamic tracking, while training on HOLIWORLD-Data substantially improves HOLIWORLD-VL-4B's spatial and temporal reasoning on HOLI- WORLD-Bench and EgoDynamic4D. HOLIWORLD provides a practical foundation for expanding learning resources from the continuous flow of human experience and advancing machine understanding of the dynamic world.

items.title: Agentic Orchestration of EDC Data Space Retrieval and Natural Language Driven Data Processing
items.summary: Participating in a data space still requires the Dataspace Protocol (DSP) negotiation flow to be hand-coded against each provider's access policy. We present a multi-agent architecture that automates this process using natural language requests. Built on LangGraph over an Eclipse Dataspace Components (EDC), the design separates concerns into cooperating agents. The orchestrator's role is to route and plan. The data extraction agent's role is to expose the DSP protocol's three composable tools (catalog discovery, contract negotiation and download). The agent also gates negotiations on the consumers' verifiable credentials, refusing assets rather than fabricating them. Furthermore, there are downstream Machine Learning (ML) and Visualization agents, as well as a final Verification agent, which confirms that the request was actually fulfilled and rechecks the intended operation against the contract's usage policy. In a primary benchmark involving 600 runs, the system achieved 89% task success with zero policy violations when evaluating multi-dimensional policy reasoning with a locally hosted open-weight model. It failed safely through refusal rather than misrouting. The reliability of the system is largely dependent on the phrasing of requests: technical and expert requests succeed up to 98% of the time, whereas casual and under-specified requests succeed 72% of the time. Furthermore, in a secondary evaluation of 600 runs isolating hierarchical geographic access control, the framework successfully blocks 100% of unauthorized regional requests. While the verification agent hallucinates that 1% of these requests, the system logs confirm that no data is ever extracted and the framework simultaneously achieves an end-to-end verified delivery rate of 86% for eligible consumers.

items.title: A Function-Level Vulnerability Score Measures Flag Rate More Than the Model: Protocol Effects on Paired Benchmarks
items.summary: Language models are increasingly evaluated as vulnerability detectors, and scores reported for similar models differ widely between papers. We measured how much of that difference evaluation protocol accounts for, with model outputs held fixed. In a paired test, a model must flag a vulnerable function and clear its version after a fixing commit. Three choices that published evaluations make differently were varied one at a time: metric, verdict extraction and output budget. Seven frontier and large open models were evaluated on five released pair benchmarks and a set pooled for this work under one protocol, and 61 open models of 1.5B to 36B parameters on the pooled set. Function-level F1 follows how often a model flags both functions of a pair (Spearman $+0.86$ over 42 combinations) and is nearly unrelated to pair-level correctness ($+0.16$). On the pair score, extraction changes a model's number by $+0.001$ at the median and budget by $+0.02$ with an interval through zero, whereas the model changes a benchmark's number by up to 0.18 and the benchmark a model's by up to 0.16; a function-level score therefore measures flag rate more than model. For 37 of 68 models the difference between correct and reversed pairs is within its 95% interval of zero, the value for a null model that flags each function at a fixed rate, while both-flagged and both-cleared rates exceed that null by 0.055 on median, and for 64 of 68 both functions of a pair receive one answer more often than independence predicts: verdicts are determined by the text common to both functions. On length-matched pairs a linear probe on activations separates 0.78 by within-pair ranking, against 0.64 for a tf-idf baseline and 0.5 for length; the generated verdict is near chance for three of six models and at 0.55 to 0.57 for the other three, and a prompted logit is at chance for all six.

items.title: ReInsVLN: Revisiting Historical Evidence for Training-Free Vision-and-Language Navigation
items.summary: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) relies on retaining and using relevant observations. Yet growing histories introduce redundancy, and retained information may remain underused. We introduce ReInsBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines history utilization through controlled continuation trials. Its results show that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context. Motivated by this finding, we propose ReInsVLN, a training-free framework supporting memory construction and utilization in frozen navigators. Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression constructs compact visual context through temporal redundancy reduction, coverage-aware protection, and instruction-guided token selection. Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders guide navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls. On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points over the native StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, reaching 64.27% and 64.44%, respectively. Visual compression largely preserves navigation performance while reducing prefill latency and KV cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%, respectively, on matched observation workloads. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the applicability of ReInsVLN to sequential instruction following and ordinal navigation.

items.title: VLA-Pro: Cross-Task Procedural Memory Transfer for Vision-Language-Action Models
items.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet they still struggle to generalize to unseen tasks that necessitate transferring relevant experience across objects, scenes, and action patterns. This paper proposes VLA-Pro, a plug-and-play framework designed to enhance cross-task generalization by storing task-relevant procedural memories at training time and transferring these memories during inference. Specifically, VLA-Pro stores task-specific LoRA adapters as parameterized procedural memories during training. At inference time, VLA-Pro retrieves relevant procedural memories based on the current multi-modal context and dynamically fuses these memories for generating the current action chunk. Experiments on RoboTwin, RLBench, and real-world manipulation tasks show that VLA-Pro consistently improves cross-task generalization across multiple backbones, achieving up to a 207% relative improvement in simulation and increasing real-world success rate from 5.8% to 65.0%. These results suggest that procedural memory retrieval and adaptation provide an effective mechanism for transferring manipulation experience to novel tasks while preserving modularity and execution stability.

items.title: Breaking Diffusion: Parallel Reasoning with Draft Refinement
items.summary: Drafting an answer allows a reasoning model to reconsider each decision in the context of the others. Yet repeated diffusion denoising does not ensure that individually plausible token updates form a better answer together. We introduce Draft Refinement Language Models (DRLMs), which use a single denoiser to propose parallel revisions and evaluate a candidate draft. We train the denoiser to reconstruct every token from uniformly corrupted drafts, teaching both preservation and repair. Its predictions specify revisions directly, without a diffusion reverse transition. Evaluation requires a different use of these predictions: confidence in an existing token reflects both contextual support and evidence from observing the token itself. Using the known corruption process, we correct for this self-token evidence to estimate how well each token is supported by the prompt and the remaining draft. Aggregating these estimates yields a cavity energy computed in one forward pass, without an additional scoring model. Each round proposes a revision, reads the completed candidate in its revised context, and retains it only if its energy is lower. Across Countdown, Sudoku-Extreme, and Maze-Hard, our method outperforms autoregressive and discrete diffusion baselines. With 6M parameters, DRLM reaches 44.4% on Countdown-5 and 93.9% on Sudoku-Extreme. The results establish complete-draft parallel refinement as an effective alternative to reverse diffusion for complex reasoning.

items.title: Real Faults in Deep Learning Fault Benchmarks: How Real Are They?
items.summary: As the adoption of Deep Learning (DL) systems continues to rise, an increasing number of approaches are being proposed to test these systems, localise faults within them, and repair those faults. The best attestation of effectiveness for such techniques is an evaluation that showcases their capability to detect, localise and fix real faults. To facilitate these evaluations, the research community has collected multiple benchmarks of real faults in DL systems. In this work, we perform a manual analysis of 490 faults from five different benchmarks and identify that 305 of them are eligible for our study. Our investigation focuses specifically on how well the bugs correspond to the sources they were extracted from, which fault types are represented, and whether the bugs are reproducible. Our findings indicate that only 15.4% of the faults satisfy our realism conditions. Our attempts to reproduce these faults were successful only in 54% of cases.

items.title: Small Average Error, Wide Individual Error: General-Purpose LLMs Estimating Energy Intake from Meal Photos in a Feeding Trial
items.summary: Photo-based estimation of food energy could ease dietary assessment, and general-purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) make such estimates easy to obtain. Most evaluations use one photo taken before eating and compare with energy served, while dietary assessment needs energy eaten. We evaluated six models from two vendors (Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5; GPT-6 luna, 6.1 sol and 6 astra) on 802 meals from ACETADA, a controlled feeding trial with weighed intake, with the before photo only, before and after photos in separate calls (subtraction), or both photos in one request. Three results ran against intuition. Subtraction under-estimated intake for five of six models, because the models still report hundreds of kilocalories for a nearly empty tray. Scaling the before-only estimate by the average share eaten (0.87) matched much of the gain from the after photo; beyond that constant, the second photo lowered meal-level error by only 2.2 to 3.4 points, mainly in meals with food left. With one photo, two models had a near-zero intake bias only because they under-estimated the served energy and ignored uneaten food. In ablations, adding the after photo improved accuracy under both prompt formats for five models, while prompt effects varied across models. Over 148 feeding days, three models kept the 90% confidence interval of their mean error within a pre-set 10% margin, but no model reached the pre-set 30% limits of agreement. Protein was under-estimated by every model, most in protein-dense meals; repeated calls changed error by at most 1.4 points; a high reasoning effort helped only the smallest model (4.2 points) and changed the others by less than 1 point. A low average bias is not evidence of accurate individual intake estimation; such estimates should support, not replace, assessment by a dietitian.

items.title: Regularizing the Veto Core
items.summary: The metric distortion framework asks voting rules to elect a candidate close to the voters using only their rankings. SimultaneousPluralityVeto elects from the plurality veto core and achieves the optimal worst-case distortion of 3, but it is not Pareto-efficient: it can declare a tie between two candidates even when every voter prefers one of them. Removing Pareto-dominated candidates afterward would break the convexity of tied winner sets. We instead introduce regularization, which adds a small $\varepsilon$ to every candidate's weight, restoring Pareto-efficiency. To study its effect on distortion, we introduce the rank score veto core, whose candidate weights come from a positional scoring vector $\mathbf{s}$, and prove that its distortion lies in $[1 + 2(||\mathbf{s}|| - s_m),\, 1 + 2||\mathbf{s}||]$; we conjecture that the lower bound is tight. A fixed $\varepsilon$ can increase distortion, but letting $\varepsilon$ depend on the number of voters preserves the distortion guarantee of the original veto core. Regularized SimultaneousPluralityVeto thus has optimal distortion, is Pareto-efficient, and has convex tied winner sets, resolving an open question of Kızılkaya and Kempe.

items.title: ReAnchor: Reusing Rejected Verifier States for Diffusion Drafting
items.summary: Block diffusion drafters accelerate speculative decoding by generating multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass. However, each pass produces only a fixed-length block from a single target-generated anchor, limiting how far the draft can extend. Meanwhile, target verification computes hidden states even at positions beyond the first rejection, but these states are typically discarded rather than reused. We propose ReAnchor, a training-free method that reanchors a pretrained drafter at shifted positions using discarded verifier states to generate parallel draft blocks. These blocks improve predictions within the original block and extend coverage beyond its endpoint. At sampling temperature of T=0, ReAnchor achieves its largest average gains on Gemma 4-12B, improving acceptance length by 19.4% and decoding speed by 17.9% across eight benchmarks. Averaged equally over four target models and eight benchmarks, it improves acceptance length by 15.2% and decoding speed by 13.4% with pretrained DFlash drafters.

items.title: UnO-NeSy: Optimizing Neuro-Symbolic Computing with Unified FeFET Based In-Memory System
items.summary: Neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence (NeSy AI) combines neural perception with symbolic reasoning, enabling logical reasoning. Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is promising for NeSy AI, owing to its high parallelism and strong robustness to noise. However, the dense neural operations and memory-intensive symbolic inference in NeSy impose a severe "memory wall" bottleneck. Existing NeSy accelerators either focus solely on symbolic kernels or rely on conventional digital architectures, lacking a unified and energy-efficient hardware substrate. Moreover, exploring optimal hardware design configurations often requires costly trial-and-error. In this work, we propose UnO-NeSy, a unified CiM framework for optimizing NeSy computing. UnO-NeSy consists of UnO-CiM, an ultra-low-power NeSy architecture based on a homogeneous 2FeFET--2R compute-in-memory (CiM) array that supports both neural computation and HDC reasoning, and UnO-Sim, a cross-workload, end-to-end CiM simulator that models device non-idealities, neural quantization effects, and HDC execution behavior for accurate system-level evaluation. Built on UnO-Sim, we further develop an automated optimizer to identify workload-specific operating points under coupled energy, accuracy, and hardware constraints. By optimizing the operating configuration of the baseline 2FeFET--2R design, UnO-NeSy achieves $61.8\%$ higher energy efficiency and $38.2\%$ lower full-system inference energy. Across seven RAVEN configurations, UnO-NeSy achieves $96.2\%$ average reasoning accuracy under hardware non-idealities, demonstrating a practical and scalable path toward ultra-low-power NeSy hardware.

items.title: A Semantic Knowledge Graph Construction Pipeline for Vehicle Intention Prediction in nuScenes
items.summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are increasingly used in autonomous driving (AD) to make traffic scene entities and relations explicit for prediction and reasoning. Existing traffic-scene KGs, however, primarily emphasize trajectory forecasting or general scene understanding. This paper presents the nuScenes Intention Knowledge Graph (NIKG), a focused Web Ontology Language (OWL)-based semantic representation and construction pipeline for ego-centric vehicle intention context. NIKG instantiates nuScenes scenes as a self-describing Turtle graph and promotes three intention-relevant relations to first-class properties of each scene participant: ego-relative motion, spatial configuration, and time to collision (TTC) risk. The pipeline uses a small input contract available in many ego-centric driving datasets: ego pose, tracked object annotations, and temporal keyframe order. NIKG is released as an ontology-backed, self-describing graph artifact together with a reproducible construction pipeline and validation protocol for ego-centric intention context. Applying this pipeline to nuScenes mini yields a graph of 211,335 triples across 404 keyframes; under the validation protocol, ego-relative motion labels achieve 92.5% forward consistency. Coverage, semantic consistency, and temporal coherence analyses over this artifact are further reported. NIKG occupies the space between scene-oriented traffic KGs and intention-prediction models: a small, explicit semantic layer intended to support downstream work such as knowledge graph embedding (KGE), SPARQL-based feature extraction, or hybrid neuro-symbolic reasoning.

items.title: A Fisher-Geometric View of Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
items.summary: Consolidating specialized foundation models into a unified generalist is a central goal of post-training. Two approaches are in common use: model merging, which is fast but treated as a heuristic, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation, which matches distributions but demands heavy rollout compute and suffers from cross-task gradient conflict. We show that the two are one objective seen at different orders. Within a shared basin of homologous specialists, the multi-teacher on-policy distillation objective is, to second order, exactly the Fisher-merging objective. Its minimizer is therefore the Fisher merge, a classic model-merging method given by a closed-form combination of the specialists, so merging is optimal, to second order, as a closed-form stage of distillation. Building on this identification, we propose Residual-Governed Branch-and-Merge(RGBM), a two-phase consolidation procedure. Concretely, a full-parameter Fisher merge is intractable on foundation models, so Phase~1 restricts the merge to the task-vector subspace. Extending tangent-space analyses of merging, we show that the same coefficients that mix task vectors also mix implicit rewards, which lets a residual program on unlabelled prompts solve for them. The program minimizes the worst per-domain residual and reports its energy-normalized values as the domain residual spectrum. Phase~2 lets this spectrum govern what may be added: RGBM passivates domains with low normalized residuals, trains isolated branches only for domains above the spectral gap, and writes back the admitted updates with calibrated shrinkage. On two open-source consolidation suites, the Phase~1 merge alone matches or outperforms fully trained multi-teacher distillation, and RGBM improves on it further with zero extra joint-training steps, whereas every un-gated write-back, including continued joint distillation from the merge, falls below it.

items.title: SliceMapper: Intelligent Mapping of O-CU and O-DU onto O-Cloud Sites in 6G O-RAN
items.summary: In this paper, we propose an rApp, named SliceMapper, to optimize the mapping process of the open centralized unit (O-CU) and open distributed unit (O-DU) of an open radio access network (O-RAN) slice subnet onto the underlying open cloud (O-Cloud) sites in sixth-generation (6G) O-RAN. To accomplish this, we first design a system model for SliceMapper and introduce its mathematical framework. Next, we formulate the mapping process addressed by SliceMapper as a sequential decision-making optimization problem. To solve this problem, we implement both on-policy and off-policy variants of the Q-learning algorithm, employing tabular representation as well as function approximation methods for each variant. To evaluate the effectiveness of these approaches, we conduct a series of simulations under various scenarios. We proceed further by performing a comparative analysis of all four variants. The results demonstrate that the on-policy function approximation method outperforms the alternative approaches in terms of stability and lower standard deviation across all random seeds. However, the on-policy and off-policy tabular representation methods achieve higher average rewards, with values of 5.42 and 5.12, respectively. Finally, we conclude the paper and introduce several directions for future research.

items.title: Beyond Behavioral Accuracy: Evaluating Individual-Level Fidelity in LLM Investor Simulation
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as user simulators, but can they faithfully reproduce an individual's behavior and decision logic over time? We investigate this question in a longitudinal paper-trading study with 80 participants. Using rolling next-day predictions, we evaluate trading activity, buy-sell structure, asset selection, and portfolio outcomes, complemented by controlled input ablations and participant-rated explanation alignment. No evaluated LLM reliably outperforms a simple recent-activity persistence baseline for predicting trade occurrence, while buy-sell structure and asset selection remain difficult to reproduce. Similar activity-level performance can also yield substantially different portfolio trajectories. Ablations show that activity predictions depend primarily on recent trades, whereas asset choices are sensitive to multiple evidence sources. Participants rate explanations as more aligned with their recurring strategies than with their decision-specific rationales. These findings reveal a gap between coarse behavioral agreement and individual-level fidelity, motivating separate evaluation of behavioral accuracy, explanation alignment, and evidence dependence in personalized user simulation.

items.title: ECGWmark: Deep Watermarking for Electrocardiogram Signals
items.summary: Wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings pass through multiple networks and systems before automated interpretation, making patient metadata vulnerable to loss. Digital watermarking embeds this metadata directly into the signal. However, conventional ECG watermarking methods fail under temporal desynchronization, and waveform similarity does not guarantee downstream diagnostic preservation. This article presents ECGWmark, a deep watermarking framework for single-lead ECG. A fully convolutional generator embeds the payload without signal quantization, a detector decodes the message frame by frame and verifies watermark presence, and a frozen arrhythmia classifier penalizes changes that would alter diagnostic predictions. To bridge the gap between bit accuracy and whole-message recovery, payloads are protected by extended Hamming codes, validation-selected interleaving, and soft-decision decoding. On the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, ECGWmark maintains over 90\% bit accuracy under time shifts of 10 to 50 samples, where transform baselines fall to chance level. With the coding layer, the protected 16-bit payload achieves 99.86\% exact recovery on clean segments and sustains over 90\% recovery under time shifts, 10\% sample deletion, and 10\% packet loss. Inter-patient evaluation confirms improved ventricular-beat sensitivity with preserved macro-F1. Requiring only 0.56 million parameters and about 15~ms per segment on a desktop CPU, ECGWmark highlights the need to assess physiological watermarking through whole-message recovery and diagnostic consistency.

items.title: REATS: LLM Reasoning-based Ensemble Learning for Adaptive Time Series Forecasting
items.summary: Due to the diversity of real-world time series, no single forecasting model consistently dominates across all samples. Ensemble learning addresses this by combining complementary model strengths, yet existing methods rely on fixed rules or black-box models based solely on numerical inputs, failing to leverage LLM reasoning for interpretable weighting decisions. We propose REATS, which leverages LLM reasoning capabilities as an intelligent ensemble router that jointly processes textual temporal pattern descriptions and numerical features to produce interpretable, sample-adaptive ensemble weights through chain-of-thought reasoning. To enable effective LLM-based ensembling, we study its key design choices and propose: (i) a structured input pipeline that transforms raw time series into hybrid textual--numerical representations with fixed token cost, enabling rule-based chain-of-thought construction without API dependency, augmented with retrieved similar-sample priors; (ii) a diverse multi-row weight supervision scheme coupled with a token-efficient percentage-table format that reduces numerical complexity and mitigates LLM hallucinations; and (iii) a two-stage fine-tuning framework combining SFT with GRPO, where a reciprocal reward mapping transforms the continuous unbounded MSE gap into bounded signals with amplified near-oracle sensitivity, addressing the uniform sensitivity and outlier-dominated advantage compression inherent in naive reward designs for regression-based GRPO. Experiments on eight benchmarks demonstrate that REATS outperforms competitive ensemble baselines while providing natural language explanations and demonstrating strong transfer learning and out-of-domain generalization to unseen candidate models.

items.title: Interpretable Face Contrast Modeling for Smartphone Portrait Rendering
items.summary: The quality of smartphone portrait photography has become increasingly important to both manufacturers and users. Recent devices use complex computational pipelines to improve facial rendering under varied lighting. These pipelines vary widely across manufacturers, so the same portrait can look noticeably different across smartphones.
