An attractive nature of fitting a joint model on this type of data is that we can dynamically predict the survival probability as additional longitudinal information becomes available. We propose a new similarity-based method for the dynamic prediction of joint models where we consider training the model on only a targeted subset of the data to obtain an improved outcome prediction. Through comprehensive simulation study and an application to intensive care unit data, we demonstrate that the predictive performance of the dynamic prediction of joint models can be improved with our proposed similarity-based approach.

items.title: Statistical Methods for Multiple Language Model Comparison on a Shared Evaluation
items.summary: A rigorous statistical treatment of two-model comparisons on the same evals can be achieved by paired t-tests, analyzing their standard errors and a clustering correction for correlated questions. Nevertheless, leaderboards, ablations studies, and hyperparameter sweeps, usually compare $K>2$ models simultaneously. In this paper, we present a single random-effects model for scores on shared evals. We leverage models as a fixed effects and questions (or question cluster) as random effects. We show that fitting it a classical ANOVA or a linear mixed model we can recover Miller's paired and clustered estimators for K=2, but we extend the results to any K and to unbalanced, clustered designs. We validate the described model in a simulation study and using a real-data application. We take six openly available language models scored on 1,497 shared MMLU-Pro questions across 14 subject clusters, and we show that pairwise ranking claims survive depending on properly accounting for both question-level pairing and multiple comparisons. By the end of the manuscript, we provide concrete recommendations for reporting multi-model eval results.

items.title: An RKHS Framework for Fixed Effects in Permanental Process Models
items.summary: This short work describes an extension of the permanental process model which includes fixed effects. By starting with a prior on the fixed effects coefficients we show that, in the diffuse prior limit, the intensity function of the permanental process can be found using the representer theorem and naturally decomposed into a fixed effects term and a function which is an element of a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). We show that the limiting equivalent kernel defines an RKHS whose squared norm is exactly the limiting penalty. This allows for straightforward scientific interpretation of permanental process models and the easy incorporation of domain knowledge into the estimation process.

items.title: A Distribution-Free Separation Between Learned and Fixed Features
items.summary: The success of neural networks is largely attributed to their ability to learn useful representations from training data. However, known results that prove a computational advantage of learned features over fixed ones are restricted to specific input distributions. We settle the COLT open question of Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026) by showing that this advantage can persist in the distribution-free setting. We construct a family of hypothesis classes that can be efficiently learned by a natural gradient-based algorithm on a two-layer ReLU network, but cannot be represented by linear predictors over any fixed feature map with polynomial dimension (and runtime). Specifically, for any sufficiently small error and any sufficiently large runtime budget R (depending on the error), there exists a hypothesis class that the neural network learns under any input distribution to the desired expected classification error in time at most R, while the dimension complexity (governing the dimension needed by linear predictors) is superpolynomial in R.

items.title: Ergodic Central limit theorem for subgeometric Markov chains
items.summary: We establish verifiable necessary conditions for central limit theorems (CLTs) of ergodic averages of Markov chains on general state spaces. Our criteria are based on discrete-time $\mathbf{L}$-drift conditions that can be verified through estimates for the one-step transition kernel of the original chain. They yield an integral criterion for failure of the CLT for a class of observables that includes unbounded functions and indicators of tail events. The main technical step transfers lower bounds for excursions of the original chain to regenerative excursions of its Nummelin split chain. The same drift conditions yield lower bounds on the tails of return times and modulated excursion functionals, on invariant tails, and on rates of convergence in $f$-variation and $L^p$-Wasserstein distance. These estimates apply without an explicit formula for the invariant distribution. Applications to unadjusted Langevin algorithms show preservation of polynomial target tail indices at every fixed step size. For Euler schemes with additive infinite-variance noise, we establish restrictions on invariant tails and transience under superlinear drifts. Schemes with linear drift, multiplicative noise and logarithmic innovation tails exhibit sharp polynomial convergence exponents and exact CLT thresholds, despite the absence of positive Euclidean moments.

items.title: Toward Automated Detection of Documentation Inconsistencies in Electronic Health Records
items.summary: Objective:To characterize the kinds of internal documentation inconsistencies a general-domain large language model (LLM) can surface from real-world discharge summaries, and to identify recurring failure modes that limit reliability at scale. Materials and Methods: We applied a two-stage LLM pipeline---open-ended candidate identification (Gemini 2.5 Pro) followed by context-grounded verification (Gemini 2.5 Flash)---to 3000 MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries drawn as three contiguous 1000-note batches from distinct positions in the corpus. Two clinicians independently reviewed a domain-stratified sample of 268 retained candidates; a third adjudicated disagreements. Results: Stage~1 proposed 11333 candidates; 3461 were retained after Stage~2 verification---machine-generated candidates---with at least one in 69.7% of admissions. Medication (43.2%) and diagnosis or clinical-finding (25.3%) candidates predominated. In the reviewed sample, reviewers agreed on 91.0\% of candidates, and 253 of 268 (94.4\%) were judged valid after adjudication. Representative examples from all seven domains carried direct implications for clinical reasoning or patient safety. Review also revealed recurring failure modes involving temporal reasoning, evolving diagnoses, and outpatient-prescribing conventions. Discussion: Detection is highly context-dependent: judging a flagged pair requires locating each statement and assessing whether the conflict reflects a true contradiction or missing context. We propose a graded ontology spanning strict contradiction, ambiguity, and gap, with a schema characterizing each flagged case by type, section, scope, domain, attribute, and inconsistency axis. Conclusion: This formative study establishes a methodological foundation and conceptual framework to guide subsequent validated, large-scale EHR-inconsistency analysis.

items.title: Variance Reduction for Stochastic Switching in Functionally Constrained Federated Optimization
items.summary: Federated learning (FL) is increasingly used in safety-critical and fairness-sensitive applications, where learning objectives must be optimized subject to functional constraints. This setting is challenging due to costly projection onto the resulting feasible set, stochastic constraint information, partial client participation, and limited communication at edge devices. We propose a federated stochastic switching framework based on primal-only updates, avoiding dual-variable tuning for functionally constrained federated optimization. For convex objectives, the framework further supports compression with error feedback to control compression-induced bias. We establish high-probability convergence and feasibility guarantees under stochastic gradients and partial client participation, and extend the analysis to weakly convex objectives through proximal-stationarity guarantees. Our bounds isolate the effects of stochastic gradients, constraint-evaluation noise, and partial participation, and show that direct switching can retain a nonvanishing constraint-estimation error even with exact local constraint evaluations. To overcome this limitation, we develop variance-reducing constraint estimators that yield vanishing feasibility and stationarity guarantees with fixed per-round client participation and constraint-evaluation batch sizes. Experiments on Neyman-Pearson classification, fairness-constrained learning on the ADULT dataset, and constrained deep reinforcement learning demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

items.title: State Space Modeling of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Process with Measurement Error: An Application to Microbiome Data
items.summary: Understanding the temporal dynamics of the human microbiome is critical for deciphering host-microbe interactions and identifying responses to environmental or physiological disruptions. In this study, we develop a likelihood-based framework grounded in Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) state-space modeling to analyze longitudinal microbiome data. By applying log-ratio transformations to genus-level relative abundances, we accommodate the compositional nature of microbiome profiles and enable biologically interpretable inference. We estimate the mean reversion rate of the OU process using maximum likelihood estimation and construct profile likelihood confidence intervals to assess temporal stability. Biologically, higher estimated mean-reversion rates correspond to stronger regulatory feedback and thus greater temporal stability of the gut microbiome, whereas lower rates reflect weaker stabilization and slower recovery from perturbations. In the datasets analyzed here, most estimated mean reversion rates were between 0.12 and 0.36, corresponding to a half-life in the range 2-6 days for the system to return to the equilibrium level. These mean-reversion rates are substantially lower than previous estimates obtained from OU models that did not account for measurement error. To capture structural shifts in microbial dynamics, we propose a statistical testing procedure that compares a single-parameter model to a split-parameter model across disrupted time periods. We also propose an OUSSM to jointly model multiple microbes, taking into account the special measurement error covariance structure for log-ratio transformed data.

items.title: Inverse Confounding Analysis: An Exact Method for Quantifying the Significance of Confounding
items.summary: The presence of unmeasured confounding factors during the collection of observational data may lead to biased estimates of the effect of an exposure on an outcome. Consequently, a central problem in causal inference based on observational data is sensitivity analysis with respect to unmeasured confounding. Existing sensitivity analyses generally focus on worst-case bounds. We propose an exact method for quantifying the significance of confounding, defined here in terms of the complete range of analytical estimates of the stratification-based Risk Ratio over the set of all joint distributions compatible with the observed characteristics. We refer to the proposed method as Inverse Confounding Analysis (ICA). The proposed ICA method extends the widely used E-value approach but, in contrast to it, does not restrict the analysis to a worst-case lower bound. Instead, it provides exact estimates over the entire set of admissible configurations. This requires several additional input parameters, namely the frequencies of the exposure, the confounder, and the outcome. The ICA method is based on an inverse problem: reconstructing the set of admissible joint distributions from specified frequencies and pairwise associations. We formulate this reconstruction problem as a system of nonlinear equations and obtain an analytical solution. Surprisingly, the complete solution set can be parameterized linearly by a single free parameter. The corresponding stratification-based Risk Ratio is then represented as a fractional-linear function of this parameter. This representation makes it possible to derive exact analytical measures of the significance of confounding over the entire set of admissible statistical configurations.

items.title: Federated Learning: From Theory to Practice
items.summary: This book offers a hands-on introduction to building and understanding federated learning (FL) systems. FL enables multiple devices -- such as smartphones, sensors, or local computers -- to collaboratively train machine learning (ML) models, while keeping their data private and local. It is a powerful solution when data cannot or should not be centralized due to privacy, regulatory, or technical reasons. The book is designed for students, engineers, and researchers who want to learn how to design scalable, privacy preserving FL systems. Our main focus is on personalization: enabling each device to train its own model while still benefiting from collaboration with relevant devices. This is achieved by leveraging similarities between (the learning tasks associated with) devices that are encoded by the weighted edges (or links) of a federated learning network (FL network). The key idea is to represent real-world FL systems as networks of devices, where nodes correspond to device and edges represent communication links and data similarities between them. The training of personalized models for these devices can be naturally framed as a distributed optimization problem. This optimization problem is referred to as generalized total variation minimization (GTVMin) and ensures that devices with similar learning tasks learn similar model parameters. Our approach is both mathematically principled and practically motivated. While we introduce some advanced ideas from optimization theory and graph-based learning, we aim to keep the book accessible. Readers are guided through the core ideas step by step, with intuitive explanations.

items.title: A Splitting Method for SDE Terminal-Law Estimation
items.summary: In many settings involving stochastic differential equations (SDEs), including diffusion based generative AI, our aim is to accurately generate samples from a distribution. Typically, this is done by generating i.i.d. samples of the SDE. Given a fixed simulation budget, a reasonable way to gain efficiency may be to instead generate a tree of paths through appropriately split partial paths. This suggests improved performance, but one worries about the injected dependence. In this paper, we study this issue comprehensively. We develop a general method to construct the splitting design and analyze its performance for a broad class of error measures, giving insight into the elegant underlying structure in the problem. For the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) distance and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), we identify the limiting errors of the associated empirical distributions as the simulation budget increases to infinity. We characterize a splitting strategy motivated by a corresponding asymptotic optimization problem. Overall, we observe a 12-26% improvement in mean KS over i.i.d. samples in many settings. On CIFAR-10 and FFHQ, splitting lowers the MMD by 17-26% relative to i.i.d. samples.

items.title: Estimating Causal Bounds from Observational Data With Neural Generative Models
items.summary: Identifying causal bounds from discrete observational data is a fundamental problem in causal inference. While exact analytical bounds exist for certain graphs, this is not generally the case. In this paper, we introduce a framework for estimating such bounds using neural generative models together with a new extrapolation procedure to estimate these bounds more accurately. Across multiple causal inference settings, it produces bounds that are consistently closer to the true bounds than those obtained with existing general neural approaches. We validate the framework on a range of benchmark problems for which exact bounds are available.

items.title: Recurrent Self-Attention Dynamics: An Energy-Agnostic Perspective from Jacobians
items.summary: The theoretical understanding of self-attention (SA) has been steadily progressing. A prominent line of work studies a class of SA layers that admit an energy function decreased by state updates. While it provides valuable insights into inherent biases in signal propagation, it often relies on idealized assumptions or additional constraints not necessarily present in standard SA. Thus, to broaden our understanding, this work aims to relax these energy constraints and provide an energy-agnostic characterization of inference dynamics by dynamical systems analysis. In more detail, we first consider relaxing the symmetry and single-head constraints traditionally required in energy-based formulations. Next, we show that analyzing the Jacobian matrix of the state is highly valuable when investigating more general SA architectures without necessarily admitting an energy function. It reveals that the normalization layer plays an essential role in suppressing the Lipschitzness of SA and the Jacobian's complex eigenvalues, which correspond to the oscillatory components of the dynamics. In addition, the Lyapunov exponents computed from the Jacobians demonstrate that the normalized dynamics lie close to a critical state, and this criticality serves as a strong indicator of high inference performance. Furthermore, the Jacobian perspective also enables us to develop regularization methods for training and a pseudo-energy for monitoring inference dynamics.

items.title: Vector Copula-Based Markov Models
items.summary: We propose the Vector Copula-based Markov Model (VCBMM) for describing multivariate time series with nonlinear dependence. To extend univariate copula-based Markov models to multivariate time series, we develop a hierarchical construction based on scalar aggregates and consider the Vector Sklar Theorem to obtain the joint density of the VCBMM. We further assume the Clayton copula for serial dependence and the multivariate Gaussian distribution for the marginals. The corresponding likelihood function and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) with the Inference Functions for Margins (IFM) method are provided. The performance of the proposed model is illustrated through simulation studies. In real data analysis, we apply the model to bivariate daily stock returns from the 2008 global financial crisis (2008 GFC) and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic (2020 COVID-19).

items.title: Decision-Target Reversal under Informative Label Missingness
items.summary: Informative label missingness can improve classification efficiency because the pattern of label availability may itself contain information about the discriminant structure. We show that this advantage need not persist across deployment objectives: with the data-generating model and statistical experiments held fixed, informative partial classification can be favourable under one loss and unfavourable under another. We call this phenomenon decision-target reversal. For binary Gaussian discrimination, we derive a local cost-sensitive excess-risk expansion and, in one dimension, obtain explicit critical cost ratios at which the first-order risk ordering reverses. We show that the required covariance geometry arises under finite uncertainty-dependent missingness mechanisms with a fixed marginal missing-label proportion. We then extend the analysis to multiclass finite-action problems through loss-specific active-boundary curvature, yielding a general decision-target frontier. Monte Carlo experiments illustrate the predicted reversals, and a descriptive gastrointestinal-lesion application with agreement-defined label availability illustrates sensitivity to deployment costs. The results show that favourable informative missingness is a property of the statistical experiment relative to the deployment decision, rather than of the experiment alone.

items.title: A Transport Geometry of Benign Overfitting
items.summary: Benign overfitting, the phenomenon that interpolating noisy data can be statistically harmless, is usually characterized through effective-rank conditions on the covariance spectrum. These conditions are fragile: a perturbation of vanishing relative operator and Frobenius norm can turn a benign covariance into one whose minimum-norm interpolator has non-vanishing excess risk. We argue that the natural geometry of benign overfitting is optimal transport of the log-eigenvalues, measured in units of the sample size $n$. In log-spectral coordinates, the deterministic equivalent of the risk becomes a functional of two measures smoothed by a logistic kernel centred at the interpolation threshold $\logκ$. We compute its exact first variation: the threshold moves by a sensitivity-weighted average of the log-eigenvalue displacements, and the influence of each eigenvalue decays exponentially with its log-distance to the threshold. We then derive global, dimension-free stability bounds. The variance functional is $8/(27n)$-Lipschitz in the 1-Wasserstein distance between log-spectra, with a sharp constant, and is controlled more generally by a threshold-localized transport discrepancy; an analogous bound controls the bias. Consequently, any rank-$k$ update of the covariance, of arbitrary norm, changes the variance functional by at most $3k/n$, and benign overfitting survives every perturbation whose localized transport cost is $o(n)$. The results extend to ridge regression and to infinite-dimensional trace-class covariances. Matching lower bounds show that the $n$-scaling is necessary and cannot be replaced by operator norms, Frobenius norms, or dimension-normalized spectral distances. Simulations, one-step feature learning in two-layer networks, and random features of real images support the theory and delineate its limits.

items.title: Dimension-free comparison inequalities between $f$-divergences for Gaussian location mixtures
items.summary: We establish dimension-free comparison inequalities between the Kullback-Leibler (KL) and $χ^2$-divergences and the squared Hellinger distance for Gaussian location mixtures with compactly supported mixing distributions. We show that both divergences are bounded by the squared Hellinger distance up to constants depending only on the radius of the support, independently of the ambient dimension and the number of mixture components. These results resolve an open question raised by \cite{jia2023entropic} and strengthen existing comparison inequalities. Our proof relies on a Gaussian interpolation argument that relates the derivatives of these divergences to differences between posterior means.

items.title: Enhancing Offline Model-Based RL via Active Model Selection: A Bayesian Optimization Perspective
items.summary: Offline model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) serves as a competitive framework that can learn well-performing policies solely from pre-collected data with the help of learned dynamics models. To fully unleash the power of offline MBRL, model selection plays a pivotal role in determining the dynamics model utilized for downstream policy learning. However, offline MBRL conventionally relies on validation or off-policy evaluation, which are rather inaccurate due to the inherent distribution shift in offline RL. To tackle this, we propose BOMS, an active model selection framework that enhances model selection in offline MBRL with only a small online interaction budget, through the lens of Bayesian optimization (BO). Specifically, we recast model selection as BO and enable probabilistic inference in BOMS by proposing a novel model-induced kernel, which is theoretically grounded and computationally efficient. Through extensive experiments, we show that BOMS improves over the baseline methods with a small amount of online interaction comparable to only $1\%$-$2.5\%$ of offline training data on various RL tasks.

items.title: SNACK: A Sequential Notation Framework for Probabilistic Graph Generation
items.summary: We introduce SNACK, a string representation for probabilistic graph generation that enables sequence models to generate and model graphs with discrete node and edge features. SNACK linearizes graphs by encoding the nonzero entries of the lower-triangular adjacency matrix, establishing a bijective correspondence between valid sequences and ordered adjacency matrices. This design enables invalid logit masking to enforce structural constraints--such as chemical valence and ordering rules--guaranteeing 100% valid generated sequences. SNACK also enables principled string-based GFlowNet training by explicitly accounting for node-ordering symmetries. Across standard graph-generation tasks and molecular distribution-learning benchmarks, SNACK achieves competitive sample quality, while substantially improving the throughput of GFlowNet training relative to graph-based generation. Probing analyses further show that models trained on SNACK encode meaningful local and global graph structure despite receiving only sequential supervision. These results position SNACK as a practical framework for probabilistic graph generation with deep sequence models.

items.title: Chopthin-Consensus Power Sampling: A Diversity-Preserving Approach to LLM Decoding
items.summary: Inference-time power sampling via Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) can substantially improve large language model (LLM) reasoning without requiring post-training. However, many existing SMC approaches rely on equal-weight resampling, which can aggressively prune low-weight trajectories, discarding potentially correct reasoning paths and degrading the genealogical diversity of the search space. To address this, we introduce Chopthin-Consensus Power Sampling (CCPS). Our method applies the Chopthin resampler to LLM decoding: rather than equalizing weights and forcing unnecessary particle duplication, it enforces an upper bound on the ratio between the largest and smallest weights and carries the unequal weights forward. This targeted intervention preserves a richer set of distinct reasoning paths, keeps the weighted SMC approximation unchanged in conditional expectation, and guarantees a lower bound on the post-resampling effective sample size (ESS). To fully exploit this enriched population, we employ a semantic-majority selection mechanism that merges token-identical final trajectories, clusters semantically equivalent answers, and returns the answer supported by the largest number of distinct trajectories. Evaluating across three open-weight models and five reasoning benchmarks, we show that Chopthin increases oracle coverage in 13 of 15 settings. Combined with semantic-majority selection, CCPS matches or exceeds the final-answer accuracy of the Power-SMC baseline in 14 of 15 settings, delivering absolute gains of up to 10.6 percentage points. These findings demonstrate that diversity-preserving resampling and diversity-aware selection are complementary mechanisms for training-free LLM reasoning. Code is available at github.com/MinooAhmadii/chopthin-consensus-power-sampling.

items.title: Certifying Whether to Adapt: Baseline-Relative PAC-Bayes-MMD Guarantees for Test-Time Adaptation
items.summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) needs a decision about an update, not only an absolute-risk estimate. We give PAC-Bayesian certificates for the target excess risk of a candidate relative to a pilot-fixed baseline. A radial certificate uses an MMD ambiguity radius; a direction-sensitive certificate retains the sign of the empirical RKHS shift and can therefore certify target improvement even when source risk increases. For finite binary state spaces we derive statewise marginal and signed conditional-shift refinements, with penalties localized to candidate--baseline disagreements. A source-worsening update with target excess risk $-0.576$ is accepted in all 1,000 repetitions by the directional certificate and never by the radial certificate; learned finite-state updates with excess risks $-0.800$ and $-0.401$ are likewise accepted in every repetition. On Covertype, the certificate safely rejects all updates and blocks geographic-shift adaptations whose unconditional deployment increases risk by up to $2.75$ percentage points in prespecified base libraries; an exploratory stress test reaches $5.66$ points. A feature-quantized CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C study is structurally vacuous and is reported only as a diagnostic limitation, not as a practical neural certificate.

items.title: "Game, Set, Match": Double Delight Watching a Grand Slam Tennis Match
items.summary: Probabilistic properties of tennis scoring systems are examined and compared with best-of-K systems. A model, where each player has his/her own probability of winning his/her service point and which remains invariant for the duration of the match, and where outcomes of points played are independent of each other, is assumed. Probabilities of winning a game tie-breaker, a game, a set tie-breaker, a set, and the match are obtained. Since tennis scoring systems are unique, probability calculations require decomposing big and complicated problems into smaller and simpler constituent problems, solving these sub-problems, then combining to obtain the solution to the big problem. The problems that arise from tennis scoring systems offer excellent pedagogical venues for teaching probability, in particular, the use of the Theorem of Total Probability and the Iterated Rules for Mean, Variance, and Covariance. There are also many interesting questions in tennis, foremost of which is whether a tennis match under this assumption will actually end with probability one; or whether when two players of `equal abilities' play a match, the first server possesses an advantage. These questions are addressed in this work. Tennis scoring systems are technically statistical decision systems to determine the better player. Since such a decision system is based on a finite number of points played, erroneous decisions could arise, such as the inferior player winning the match. We compare different systems in terms of the probability of the better player winning, as well as the duration of the match in terms of the number of points played.

items.title: Robust Direct Preference Optimization under Preference Label-Flip Attacks
items.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is widely used for offline Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. However, recent works have shown that DPO can be easily manipulated by adversarial preference label flip attacks, which are specifically designed to mislead the learner toward an attacker-chosen target policy. To address this issue, we design robust DPO methods that can defend against such attacks. Building on the property that lable flips induce parameter-independent gradient shifts in log-linear DPO, we propose Trim-$K$ Robust-DPO, which removes the $K$ highest-impact pairs, and Soft-Trim-$K$ Robust-DPO, which smoothly downweights them. We establish deterministic gradient perturbation bounds uniformly over all attack sets containing at most $K$ flips, explicitly separating defense-induced bias from surviving attack effects. Under bounded-region assumptions, these bounds yield time-uniform parameter and policy deviation guarantees. We further quantify how quadratic regularization improves curvature while introducing additional bias. Experiments on Stanford Human Preferences, HH-RLHF, and UltraFeedback-Binarized validate our analysis.

items.title: Approximation Theory of Laplacian-Based Neural Operators for Reaction-Diffusion System
items.summary: Neural operators provide a framework for learning solution operators of partial differential equations (PDEs), enabling efficient surrogate modeling for complex systems. While universal approximation results are now well understood, quantitative approximation analysis specific to nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems remains limited. In this paper, we study Laplacian-based neural operators applied to the solution mapping from initial conditions to time-dependent solutions of nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems. By exploiting the Laplacian spectral representation of the diffusion semigroup, we obtain polynomial complexity bounds on the network depth, width, and spectral rank, demonstrating that Laplacian eigenfunction-based neural operators can exploit the structure of the underlying PDE while avoiding the curse of parametric complexity encountered in generic operator learning. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and illustrate the benefit of Laplacian eigenfunction representations compared with Fourier-based spectral representations.

items.title: Tweedie's Formula and Score-Driven Updating
items.summary: Tweedie's formula expresses a conditional mean in terms of a score function, and this connects score-driven models with Bayesian updating. We show that the score-driven update is identical to a Bayesian update in some special cases. More generally, we show that score-driven updating is a local approximation to Bayesian updating, with an error of second order in the predictive variance. The second-order approximation error has two components, one from the curvature of the log likelihood and one from the asymmetry of the posterior distribution. Implicit score-driven (ISD) updating, which evaluates the score at the updated parameter, corrects for the former but not the latter. A simple correction for the second component leads to an improved third-order approximation, which we denote ISD*. Numerical experiments show substantial gains from ISD and ISD*.

items.title: Optimal Cox regression under federated differential privacy: coefficients and cumulative hazards
items.summary: We study two canonical problems in distributed survival analysis under federated differential privacy (FDP): estimation of cumulative hazard functions and Cox regression coefficients, allowing for heterogeneous per-server sample sizes and privacy budgets. To quantify the fundamental cost of privacy, we derive minimax lower and upper bounds that match up to poly-logarithmic factors, revealing server-level phase transitions between private and non-private regimes. Our algorithms are computationally-efficient and are based on adapting differentially private binary tree and gradient descent algorithms to handle estimating equations with dependent terms. We also study three related problems: estimation of the cumulative baseline hazard and survival functions in the Cox model under FDP, and estimation of regression coefficients under the federated label differential privacy, a relaxed privacy notion. For these problems, we develop efficient algorithms, establish theoretical guarantees and investigate minimax optimality. Numerical experiments, including a real-data application, support the theoretical findings. The proposed methods are implemented in the accompanying R package FDPCox.

items.title: Conformal prediction regions for dependent censored lifetimes
items.summary: Joint-life insurance often involves several lifetimes subject to censoring at known dates. We construct prediction regions by reducing the lifetime vector to a suitable scalar outcome. We first characterise the reduction maps for which arbitrary componentwise censoring becomes ordinary right censoring. These maps are minima of coordinatewise nondecreasing transformations, with upper orthants as prediction regions. Under a common censoring date, the admissible class also includes the first-death and last-survivor times. Applying univariate weighted split-conformal calibration to the reduced outcomes then gives finite-sample marginal coverage with known retention probabilities under conditionally independent censoring. With estimated probabilities, asymptotic validity follows from consistent weight or outcome-quantile estimation under the respective regularity conditions. We then quantify retention through the censoring copula, compare joint calibration with coordinatewise bounds and study path selection and estimation. Simulations examine several aspects of the proposed method. Finally, an application to a Canadian joint-life annuity portfolio illustrates one-sided lower prediction bounds for reported first- and second-death times. The five-year observation period puts a limit to the attainable lower bounds, with different limits for different paths; the bounds seem most informative for older annuitants.

items.title: Scalable Bayesian Clustering for Integrative Analysis of Multi-View Data
items.summary: In the era of Big Data, scalable and accurate clustering algorithms for high-dimensional data are essential. We present new Bayesian Distance Clustering (BDC) models and inference algorithms with improved scalability while maintaining the predictive accuracy of modern Bayesian nonparametric models. Unlike traditional methods, BDC models the distance between observations rather than the observations directly, offering a compromise between the scalability of distance-based methods and the enhanced predictive power and probabilistic interpretation of model-based methods. However, existing BDC models still rely on performing inference on the partition model to group observations into clusters. The support of this partition model grows exponentially with the dataset's size, complicating posterior space exploration and leading to many costly likelihood evaluations. Inspired by $k$-medoids, we propose using tessellations in discrete space to simplify inference by focusing the learning task on finding the best tessellation centers, or "medoids". Additionally, we extend our models to effectively handle multi-view data, such as data comprised of clusters that evolve across time, enhancing their applicability to complex datasets. The real data application in numismatics demonstrates the efficacy of our approach.

items.title: Statistical Inference and Learning for Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP)
items.summary: The SHAP (short for Shapley additive explanation) framework has become an essential tool for attributing importance to variables in predictive tasks. In model-agnostic settings, SHAP uses the concept of Shapley values from cooperative game theory to fairly allocate credit to the features in a vector $X$ based on their contribution to an outcome $Y$. While the explanations offered by SHAP are local by nature, learners often need global measures of feature importance in order to improve model explainability and perform feature selection. The most common approach for converting these local explanations into global ones is to compute either the mean absolute SHAP or mean squared SHAP. However, despite their ubiquity, there do not exist approaches for performing statistical inference on these quantities. In this paper, we take a semi-parametric approach for calibrating confidence in estimates of the $p$th powers of Shapley additive explanations. We show that, by treating the SHAP curve as a nuisance function that must be estimated from data, one can reliably construct asymptotically normal estimates of the $p$th powers of SHAP. When $p \geq 2$, we show a de-biased estimator that combines U-statistics with Neyman orthogonal scores for functionals of nested regressions is asymptotically normal. When $1 \leq p < 2$ (and the hence target parameter is not twice differentiable), we construct de-biased U-statistics for a smoothed alternative. In particular, we show how to carefully tune the temperature parameter of the smoothing function in order to obtain inference for the true, unsmoothed $p$th power. We complement these results by presenting a Neyman orthogonal loss that can be used to learn the SHAP curve via empirical risk minimization and discussing excess risk guarantees for commonly used function classes.

items.title: Scalable and Adaptive Distribution Regression via Random Features
items.summary: Distribution regression seeks to learn mappings from probability distributions to response variables and has emerged as a unifying framework for kernel methods, multi-instance learning, and set-valued learning. Despite its success, kernel-based distribution regression remains computationally expensive and sensitive to kernel choice, motivating scalable and adaptive representations. Building on random feature approximations, we develop a finite-sample analysis of Random Feature Distribution Regression (RaDR) under two-stage sampling. Our perturbation analysis separates the effects of distribution-level sampling, finite within-bag sampling, and random feature approximation. We establish sufficient feature-budget conditions under which RaDR preserves the order of our excess-risk upper bound for exact two-stage kernel distribution regression while maintaining computational efficiency. We further propose Adaptive Random Feature Distribution Regression (A-RaDR), a unified score-guided framework that adaptively allocates random features according to downstream learning objectives. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and 41 real-world datasets demonstrate that RaDR delivers substantial computational savings while maintaining competitive predictive performance, whereas A-RaDR further improves learning accuracy in distribution regression while retaining the computational speed up. Together, these results establish a practical and theoretically grounded framework for adaptive, scalable distribution learning

items.title: Logistic vegetation trajectories and their implications for land surface phenology
items.summary: Vegetation trajectories describe canopy development and underpin phenological metrics, including the start and end of the growing season. We derive a generalized logistic function (GLF) to represent canopy growth under explicit assumptions: exponential development combined with a Michaelis-Menten-type saturating response yields an ordinary logistic function, and a power transformation introduces asymmetry. Using the GLF as a common mathematical basis, we relate trajectory shape to phenological metrics and date uncertainty. We derive shape-dependent relative thresholds for derivative-defined transition points and recover the 9.18% onset threshold for an isolated ordinary logistic growth curve under the small-slope approximation. For a symmetric double-logistic seasonal trajectory, we derive the realized amplitude, full width at half maximum and a critical dimensionless temporal separation between growth and senescence components at which interior third-derivative extrema merge. Exact curvature-change transition points also depend on the metric assigned to the time and response axes. Local noise propagation and 4,800 nonlinear fits show how trajectory geometry affects date uncertainty: additional shape flexibility can reduce bias while increasing uncertainty in the seasonal tails. Together, these results explain how trajectory shape determines the location and existence of phenological transition points and uncertainty in their estimated dates. The framework supports phenology retrieval that preserves the underlying trajectory and interprets each metric through its mathematical definition and uncertainty.

items.title: Relaxation times of non-reversible Markov processes
items.summary: We develop a systematic approach to quantify $L^2$-relaxation times for non-reversible Markov processes based on the singular value gap of the generator introduced by Chatterjee. The inverse of the singular value gap is equivalent to the relaxation time of the time-averaged transition semigroup. We show that, moreover, the inverse singular value gap of the two-point motion is equivalent to the relaxation time of the non-averaged transition semigroup, and that it provides a lower bound on the usual spectral gap of the generator. We then introduce a method for deriving lower bounds on singular value gaps for Markov processes with degenerate noise that is based on the concept of a first- and second-order collapse of the generator. It follows ideas from hypocoercivity developed in a previous series of works but is simpler and more broadly applicable. In contrast to previous results, it includes settings with non-vanishing first-order collapse, and thus applies directly to Markov chains (in continuous time), but also to diffusion processes and piecewise-deterministic Markov processes. Our approach yields sharp upper and lower bounds for several classes of examples. First applications include the proof of a conjecture by Diaconis and Miclo on a square-root speed-up for lifted random walks on abelian groups, as well as bounds on relaxation times of switching flows perturbed by noise and of non-reversible diffusion processes.

items.title: Multi-Resolution Analysis of Variable Selection for Road Safety in St. Louis and Its Neighboring Area
items.summary: Generally, Lasso, Adaptive Lasso, and SCAD are standard approaches in variable selection in the presence of a large number of predictors. In recent years, during intensity function estimation for spatial point processes with a diverging number of predictors, many researchers have considered these penalized methods. But we have discussed a multi-resolution perspective for the variable selection method for spatial point process data. Its advantage is twofold: it not only efficiently selects the predictors but also provides the idea of which points are liable for selecting a predictor at a specific resolution. Actually, our research is motivated by the crime and accident occurrences in St. Louis and its neighborhoods. It is more relevant to select predictors at the local level, and thus we get the idea of which set of predictors is relevant for the occurrences of crime or accident in which parts of St. Louis. We describe the simulation results to justify the accuracy of local-level variable selection during intensity function estimation.

items.title: A Statistical Viewpoint on Adam, Shampoo and Muon
items.summary: We provide new statistical insights into designing stochastic optimization methods. By modeling the gradient via a normal distribution, we argue that the stochastic gradient should be whitened using its covariance. We give an online method for estimating the mean and variance of the gradients based on regularized likelihood or, equivalently, through a maximum a posteriori estimate. We then show how to use structured approximations to the covariance within this same framework, which includes diagonal and Kronecker-factored approximations. The diagonal approximation results in a method that is very closely related to Adam and performs as well in practice. The Kronecker approximation results in the new MN method, which is a variant of Shampoo and KL-Shampoo. We also recover Muon by applying this same statistical framework to the gradient direction rather than the full gradient. By combining this with a whitening step, we arrive at MN-Muon, a novel preconditioned version of Muon. Our experiments on GPT-2-type models at Chinchilla scale indicate that MND, the diagonal implementation of MN, outperforms both the Distributed Shampoo and the KL-Shampoo implementations in terms of stability, final validation loss and time taken. MND-Muon, the diagonal implementation of MN-Muon, improves on Muon in 21 of 24 paired GPT-small runs and achieves a lower best validation loss on GPT-medium, where it remains stable over the six tested learning rates. However, we found that NorMuon was comparable to MND-Muon and achieved a slightly lower validation loss on GPT-medium and at GPT-small batch 512 on FineWeb.

items.title: Calibrating hierarchical Bayesian domain inference for a proportion
items.summary: Small area estimation (SAE) improves estimates for local communities or groups, such as counties, neighborhoods, or demographic subgroups, when data are insufficient for each area. This is important for targeting local resources and policies, especially when national-level or large-area data mask variation at a more granular level. Researchers often fit hierarchical Bayesian models to stabilize SAE when data are sparse. Ideally, Bayesian procedures also exhibit good frequentist properties, as demonstrated by calibrated Bayes metrics. However, hierarchical Bayesian models tend to shrink domain estimates toward the overall mean and may produce credible intervals that do not maintain nominal coverage. Hoff et al. developed the Frequentist, but Assisted by Bayes (FAB) intervals for subgroup estimates with normally distributed outcomes. However, non-normally distributed data present new challenges, and multiple types of intervals have been proposed for estimating proportions. We examine domain inference with binary outcomes and extend FAB intervals to improve nominal coverage. We describe how to numerically compute FAB intervals for a proportion and evaluate their performance through repeated simulation studies. Leveraging multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP), we further refine SAE to correct for sample selection bias, construct the FAB intervals for MRP estimates and assess their repeated sampling properties. Finally, we apply the proposed inference methods to estimate COVID-19 infection rates across geographic and demographic subgroups. We find that the FAB intervals improve nominal coverage, at the cost of wider intervals.

items.title: Tilted Mondrian: Triage and Mitigation of Fine-grained Disparities in Conformal Prediction
items.summary: Fairness in conformal prediction is often pursued through Mondrian calibration, which provides finite-sample coverage guarantees separately across groups. These guarantees, however, are coarse: substantial disparities can remain within finer strata. This coarse-to-fine fairness issue raises two questions: how severe can such disparities be, and how can they be mitigated? Aggregate disparities can depend on how groups are distributed across strata. For severity assessment, we introduce propensity standardization to examine the effect of population composition, and show how group composition can induce disagreement between aggregate and finer-stratum comparisons. For mitigation, we develop Tilted Mondrian to improve fairness compared to group-Mondrian at a finer level without additional model training. Tilted Mondrian retains groupwise coverage guarantees and mitigates coverage and prediction set size disparities within finer strata. Finally, we derive a method-agnostic bound that quantifies how much reduction in finer-stratum coverage disparity can be achieved.

items.title: The Causal Description Gap: Information-Theoretic Separations Across Pearl's Hierarchy
items.summary: Pearl's causal hierarchy shows that observational, interventional, and counterfactual queries are qualitatively distinct. We ask a quantitative version of this question: how many additional bits are needed to specify higher-rung causal answers once lower-rung answers are known? We formalize this via query-class description length, the Kolmogorov complexity of the answers a structural causal model (SCM) gives to a class of queries, with system size given. Our main construction gives acyclic SCMs on $n$ binary variables whose common observational distribution has constant description length, while single-variable intervention answers can require $Θ(n^2)$ additional bits. For SCMs with independent noises, fixed finite gate-schema and noise libraries, and at most $d$ parents per variable, a degree-sensitive upper bound gives an observational-interventional gap of at most $O(nd\log(en/d)+n\log n)$. This makes the quadratic construction order-optimal in the dense regime and a rooted-tree construction order-optimal for bounded indegree. The quadratic separation persists under $\varepsilon$-accurate total-variation descriptions for every fixed $\varepsilon<1/4$. At the next rung, even knowing every hard-intervention distribution can leave a $Θ(n)$ counterfactual description gap; a masked-parity construction extends this to $Θ(n^2)$. These separation rates hold in the worst case and with high probability under uniform hidden parameters. A general ambiguity-to-bits theorem and Shannon analogue, together with explicit encodings, show that the gaps in our constructions equal the logarithm of residual higher-rung ambiguity up to lower-order terms.

items.title: Sequential generalized kernel equating: Providing comparable scores across multiple test forms with nonequivalent groups and differently measured covariates
items.summary: Test equating using covariates may be applied to provide comparable scores from multiple test forms when no anchor items are available. However, its performance may be compromised if some of the covariates themselves are measured using different test forms. In this work, we propose sequential generalized kernel equating to account for possible differences in the distribution of covariates used in the NEC design. We evaluate the proposed approach through a simulation study within the kernel equating framework. Results indicate that equating the covariate reduces bias in equated test scores, particularly when the covariate distributions differ and the correlation between the covariate and the test score is strong. A real data example from a national high school leaving examination further demonstrates the practical application.

items.title: Modeling Ordinal Survey Data with Unfolding Models
items.summary: Surveys that rely on ordinal polychotomous (Likert-like) items are widely employed to capture individual preferences because they allow respondents to express both the direction and strength of their preferences. Latent factor models traditionally used in this context implicitly assume that the response functions (the cumulative distribution of the ordinal outcome) are monotonic on the latent trait. This assumption can be too restrictive in several application areas, including in political science and marketing. In this work, we propose a novel ordinal probit unfolding model that can accommodate both monotonic and non-monotonic response functions. The advantages of the model are illustrated by analyzing an immigration attitude survey conducted in the United States.

items.title: Martingale Posterior Cox Processes
items.summary: Cox processes provide a principled Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling event-based data through an underlying intensity function. However, existing inference methods for estimating the intensity typically rely on computationally expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling or approximate inference techniques. In addition, to ensure tractability, these methods often define priors over indirect latent structures, making them challenging to interpret. In this paper, we introduce the Martingale Posterior Cox Process (MPCP), which recasts Bayesian intensity estimation as inference over unobserved events given the observed event history. This perspective avoids the need to define complex priors while retaining the flexibility of nonparametric modeling. We propose a scalable, GPU-friendly copula-based predictive update, and provide strong theoretical guarantees for the convergence of the predictive resampling algorithm. Empirically, we show that MPCP provides excellent performance in both simulations and real data at a fraction of the computational cost of competing Bayesian approaches.

items.title: Stochastic Optimization Under Power-Law Spectra: Tight Bounds and Shuffling Analysis
items.summary: Recent work has established that power-law spectral conditions on data enable tight convergence bounds for deterministic gradient descent, resolving the conflict between classical exponential bounds and observed power-law learning curves. In this work, we extend this result to the stochastic regime of high-dimensional machine learning. We provide two main contributions: (1) We generalize the power-law spectral theory to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), showing that the same spectral exponents govern stochastic dynamics; (2) For the fundamental case of isotropic Gaussian data, we provide a precise analysis of data shuffling, deriving exact constants that prove Single Shuffle is strictly superior to Flip-Flop and IID sampling. Our results bridge the gap between abstract spectral theory and practical stochastic training choices, offering a unified picture of how data geometry drives optimization speed.

items.title: Gaussian Process Bandits with Paired Auxiliary Observations
items.summary: Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used for expensive black-box optimization, yet observation noise makes each evaluation less informative and slows posterior learning. Standard BO learns from costly outcomes gathered during optimization. In many applications, however, low-cost auxiliary data are available beforehand. We introduce Auxiliary-Informed Gaussian Process Bandit (AI-GPB), a variance-reduction method that combines an offline estimate of the auxiliary mean with a correction coefficient learned from paired online observations. Notably, it exploits correlation between paired observation errors without requiring the auxiliary mean to approximate the objective. We establish finite-sample GP confidence bounds and regret guarantees, including explicit cumulative and simple regret rates for Matérn kernels. Numerical experiments across continuous BO benchmarks with varied landscapes and dimensions show consistent reductions in cumulative and simple regret relative to vanilla GP-UCB, even when within-pair correlation is moderate and the auxiliary mean is estimated from noisy offline data.

items.title: Exploiting sparse conditional dependence in remote sensing observing systems
items.summary: We develop a novel filtering algorithm for remote sensing inverse problems that exploits sparsity in the precision (inverse covariance) matrix arising from conditional independence structures in spatio-temporal satellite data. Motivated by NASA's Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 (OCO-2), Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation (EMIT), and upcoming Explorer for Artemis Geology Lunar and Earth (EAGLE) missions, we formulate a Bayesian inference framework for retrieving atmospheric and surface parameters from hyperspectral radiance measurements. Unlike traditional methods that operate on covariances and ignore spatio-temporal dependencies, our approach models the full spatio-temporal state using sparse Gaussian graphical models, which corresponds to a block-sparse precision matrix. We derive an information filter based on this structure, enabling scalable joint inference over large spatial grids with uncertainty propagation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the algorithm in two distinct remote sensing contexts. First, we apply the method to synthetic data configured to mimic the OCO-2 mission, focusing on retrievals of atmospheric CO$_2$, and observe a 50% reduction in CO$_2$ retrieval error compared to single-pixel methods. Then, we evaluate the algorithm using imaging spectroscopy data from the Surface Biology and Geology (SBG) High Frequency Time Series (SHIFT) campaign to retrieve surface reflectance, achieving a 20% reduction in retrieval error relative to baseline approaches.

items.title: Native Probability Outputs for Clinical Triage: An Evaluation of Calibration and Decision Accuracy
items.summary: Patient-facing triage requires an appropriate care recommendation and recognition of when information is insufficient. We evaluate whether Jev, a decision model that returns probabilities over predefined actions, supports both judgments. Using CARE-Bench, we compare Jev with four general-purpose language models and three input-independent baselines across 925 decision points from 439 public cases. On the public test subset, Jev ranks fourth of five models by macro-F1 (0.461) but has the lowest observed multiclass Brier score (0.610), an 18.7\% improvement over uniform prediction (case-bootstrap 95\% interval, 4.9--31.1\%). Noul has lower binary Brier than Choice (0.215 versus 0.276). A evaluation of 453 HealthBench conversations again gives Jev the lowest observed Brier score (0.299), but measures a distinct emergency-referral judgment. Jev combines lower probability error with missed clarification needs in the four-action task. Asking about information sufficiency separately increases recall but also produces frequent unnecessary clarification assignments.

items.title: Nesting or resolution? Facility proxies for variance estimation versus confounding adjustment in claims data without facility identifiers
items.summary: In claims databases, facility identifiers are often removed during de-identification, leaving only coarse attributes such as bed size. Yet facility information is needed for variance estimation, confounding adjustment and assessment of treatment availability. We examined whether accreditation-gated billing items can build strata standing for hospitals, and how to construct a facility proxy for each use. In 1,730,736 adults undergoing surgery (Medical Data Vision database, Japan, 2019-2023), we built marker-pattern strata from 66 accreditation-gated receipt codes (markers) and evaluated each grouping against a true facility identifier in an insurer-based database (DeSC Healthcare) and in simulation. The variance explained by the marker-pattern strata decreased with the extent to which a variable was patient- rather than hospital-determined ($R^2$ 0.921 for an accreditation item, 0.036 for sex). For variance estimation, the supplied-attribute cells, which can merge but never split hospitals, kept the type I error rate at 4.8% with a wild cluster bootstrap, against 5.4% for the true identifier and 39% when clustering was ignored; every finer marker-based grouping did worse. For adjustment, evaluated with real facility-level confounders and simulated null exposures, the marker pattern removed 51% of the confounding related to accreditation-linked facility characteristics, against 8% for the cells. The proportion of patients in groups mixing hospitals with and without the relevant accreditation was 49% for the marker pattern against 98% for the cells. No single facility proxy serves every purpose: nesting governs variance estimation, and resolution governs adjustment and treatment availability. Without a facility identifier, the supplied-attribute cells can carry the standard errors, and marker-pattern strata are worth considering for the other two uses.

items.title: Score-optimized copula coupling for multivariate ensemble post-processing
items.summary: Univariate post-processing techniques can provide calibrated marginal predictive distributions, however, their application may distort or remove dependencies between forecast dimensions. This paper introduces Score-Optimized Copula Coupling (SOCC), a two-stage multivariate post-processing method that estimates a dependence template by minimizing a weighted combination of the energy score (ES) and variogram score (VS). An extended variant additionally incorporates calibration penalties based on average rank and band depth. We evaluate SOCC using 2-m temperature and wind-speed ensemble forecasts and compare it with well-established empirical and parametric copula-based multivariate post-processing methods. In both case studies, all considered SOCC variants significantly outperform the best-performing reference method in terms of ES and VS. The regularized Dawid-Sebastiani score provides further evidence of improved dependence modelling, particularly for the Combined SOCC variants for wind speed. Multivariate rank diagnostics nevertheless reveal trade-offs between improvements in these scores and different aspects of multivariate calibration.

items.title: Conditional Weight of Evidence for Gradient-Boosted Credit Models: Estimation, Additivity and Its Relation to Adverse Action Reasons
items.summary: Traditional weight of evidence assigns a credit characteristic a value based on its association with default across a population. Credit analysis also requires an assessment of that characteristic in the context of an individual applicant's record. We study conditional weight of evidence for this purpose. It measures the change in default log odds from observing a characteristic after the remaining credit information is known. Its sign identifies whether the characteristic adds adverse or favorable information for that applicant, and its magnitude measures the strength of that information. The same characteristic value can therefore receive different assessments for applicants with different payment histories or other credit attributes. We develop estimators using gradient-boosted trees and evaluate their accuracy in a bureau-style simulation. Regressions of the full model's predicted probabilities recover conditional evidence more accurately than separate models fitted to default outcomes, provided the full model is accurate. They also recover a deliberately constructed file-age effect whose direction varies with utilization and is often missed by marginal weight of evidence. Local class-frequency estimates improve on marginal weight of evidence but remain inaccurate for some weak effects. An application to FICO HELOC data illustrates estimation when the population evidence is unknown. Conditional weight of evidence provides an applicant-specific interpretation of the information in a credit characteristic; its population summary, a conditional information value, splits the joint information in the record across blocks when averaged over orderings. Neither is an adverse action reason, which explains the fitted score difference between the applicant and chosen passing records.

items.title: The LR1 Lifetime Distribution: Properties, Nonmonotone Hazard, and Statistical Inference
items.summary: The LR1 distribution links an exponential lifetime and a four-stage gamma lifetime through a single positive parameter $λ$. Their rates, $2λ$ and $λ/2$, have a fixed ratio, whereas the exponential mixing probability $λ^2/(1+λ^2)$ changes with the parameter. This restriction produces a hazard that decreases near zero and eventually increases toward $λ/2$ for every $λ>0$. We establish this behavior analytically and obtain an explicit parameter threshold separating decreasing densities from densities with an interior local peak. Distributional calculations provide survival probabilities, moments, transforms, truncated moments, quantiles, order statistics, and reliability summaries. The density at zero establishes identifiability, and strict decrease of the mean ensures a unique moment estimate for every positive sample mean. Likelihood inference includes the score, observed information, a constrained expectation--maximization algorithm, and asymptotic confidence limits; spacing estimation and the likelihood under independent right censoring are also described. Eight Monte Carlo settings, comprising 4,000 generated datasets, quantify the error of likelihood and moment estimators and the coverage of log-scale intervals. The results apply in a fixed working time unit and concern mathematical properties and correctly specified simulation, rather than demonstrated superiority on observed data.

items.title: Mitigating Data Reconstruction Attacks in Federated Learning: Conditions, Bounds, and Theoretical Guarantees
items.summary: Privacy attacks, particularly data reconstruction attacks, pose significant challenges to federated learning despite its promise in privacy-preserving collaborative training. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical analysis of privacy leakage in federated learning through dual perspectives: linear algebra and optimization theory. By analyzing the client-update Jacobian, we identify conditions under which distinct data batches produce the same model update and derive a sufficient batch-size criterion for non-unique reconstruction. Through optimization theory, we establish a novel upper bound for privacy leakage that incorporates batch size, distortion extent, and other critical parameters. These theoretical insights elucidate the fundamental relationships between system parameters and privacy vulnerability, laying the groundwork for developing more robust privacy-preserving federated learning frameworks.

items.title: Correcting Bartlett factor-score error for latent covariates in partially linear double machine learning
items.summary: Substituting Bartlett factor scores for latent covariates leaves factor-score error that does not vanish as the sample grows and biases the adjusted structural coefficient. We propose Croon-DML, which subtracts the factor-score error covariance implied by the measurement model from the cross-fitted estimating equation of partially linear double/debiased machine learning (DML), and establish identification, Neyman orthogonality with respect to the conditional means, consistency, and asymptotic normality. Residual bias after correction comes from learning the conditional means of the factor scores: signal learning error, and noise fitting, in which the learner also fits the factor-score error. Signal learning error largely cancels when the three conditional means share a common penalty, and noise fitting by a linear smoother can be computed from its weights alone, so we also subtract it (Croon-DML-R). Across 12 Monte Carlo conditions, Croon-DML reduced the absolute bias of uncorrected DML by 66-95%, and the bias of Croon-DML-R with a common penalty differed from that of an oracle estimator using the true latent variables by at most 0.004. In an illustration with public longitudinal data, the correction was 15% of the latent-covariate adjustment; its size reflected the latent-covariate coefficients rather than the residualized reliabilities.

items.title: Solving Inverse Problems via Diffusion-Based Priors: An Approximation-Free Ensemble Sampling Approach
items.summary: Diffusion models (DMs) have proven to be effective in modeling high-dimensional distributions, leading to their widespread adoption for representing complex priors in Bayesian inverse problems (BIPs). However, current DM-based posterior sampling methods proposed for solving common BIPs rely on heuristic approximations to the generative process. To exploit the generative capability of DMs and avoid the usage of such approximations, we propose an ensemble-based algorithm that performs posterior sampling without the use of heuristic approximations. Our algorithm is motivated by existing work that combines DM-based methods with the sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) method. By examining how the prior evolves through the diffusion process encoded by the pre-trained score function, we derive a modified partial differential equation (PDE) governing the evolution of the corresponding posterior distribution. This PDE includes a modified diffusion term and a reweighting term, which can be simulated via stochastic weighted particle methods. Theoretically, we prove that the error between the true posterior and the empirical distribution of the generated samples can be bounded in terms of the training error of the pre-trained score function and the number of particles in the ensemble. Empirically, we validate our algorithm on several inverse problems in imaging to show that our method gives more accurate reconstructions compared to existing DM-based methods. Our code is available at the following Github repository~\url{https://github.com/HaoxuanSteveC00/AFDPS-TMLR}.

items.title: WUI-CAST: Real-Time Forecast Updating for Partially Observed Wildland-Urban Interface Fires
items.summary: Wildland-urban interface (WUI) fires couple landscape spread, structural fire development, and wind-driven ember transport. Forecasting building risk requires models that incorporate emerging observations and update predictions as fires evolve. This study presents WUI-CAST, a framework integrating established fire-propagation representations with sequential Bayesian state estimation to support real-time forecast updating under partial observation. A Dynamic Bayesian Network represents nonlocal ember-driven ignition and local structural propagation, while Bayesian filtering updates building-state probabilities using sparse reports. A retrospective Camp Fire application provides a proof-of-concept evaluation. Open-loop simulations captured key features of the wildfire-to-community transition. In two 30-minute forecasts evaluated against subsequently reported buildings before their assimilation, closed-loop updating increased Recall@10% from 29.03% to 83.87% and from 0.00% to 43.75%, with improved conditional spatial logarithmic scores in both windows. Regional and local diagnostics reveal how assimilation redistributes risk beyond directly observed buildings. Controlled experiments demonstrate gains across the tested observation conditions and filtering implementations. A forecast-update cycle averaged 42 s for a 5-min simulation interval. Together, these findings demonstrate improved spatial risk prioritization from sparse observations and a computationally feasible approach to real-time WUI forecast updating.

items.title: Accelerating Finite-Sum Bilevel Optimization with Fully First-Order Oracles
items.summary: We study nonconvex--strongly-convex bilevel optimization with finite-sum objectives and fully first-order oracles. We propose Sampled Implicit Corrections for Bilevel Optimization (SICBO), which combines a penalty approximation with variance-reduced corrections for the lower-level variables. Under componentwise lower strong convexity, SICBO finds a point $x$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}\|\nablaΦ(x)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$ within $\tilde{O}(N+\sqrt{N}κ^{7/2}\varepsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient calls, where $N$ is the total number of components and $κ$ is the normalized lower-level condition number. The bound achieves square-root finite-sum dependence using only gradients and preserves the best known deterministic fully first-order condition-number exponent for smooth problems. Our improvement follows from a curvature-dependent bound for nonlinear correction errors, which permits epochs of length $\tildeΘ(\sqrt{N/κ})$ with batches of size $\tildeΘ(\sqrt{Nκ})$. A single-level reduction shows that the dependence on $N$ and $\varepsilon$ is optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed $κ$.

items.title: Detecting acceleration in global mean temperature using supralinear trends
items.summary: Whether global mean surface temperature has accelerated has received opposite answers in quick succession, reported as undetectable on data to 2023 and as significant on data to 2024. This raises two questions: since when is acceleration detectable, and how far does the answer depend on the test used? We show that structural-break tests, often used for this purpose, cannot reliably date the onset of a continuously accelerating warming rate. We therefore test for curvature directly, under specifications whose null is exactly a constant warming rate and whose alternative is curvature rather than a break. One is a linearithmic trend, which grows faster than linear but more slowly than any polynomial of degree greater than one; the other estimates the curvature freely from the data. We report alongside them the quadratic trend used in the recent literature. Over 1970-2025, in a single full-sample test, the linearithmic and quadratic coefficients are positive and statistically significant in all five major temperature datasets once El Niño and solar variability are controlled for. The onset of acceleration is dated by re-estimating over expanding windows and correcting for multiple testing. Under the linearithmic specification, acceleration first becomes detectable in windows ending in mid-2023 for NOAA, late 2023 for GISTEMP and mid-2024 for ERA5, and not yet in HadCRUT or Berkeley. The free-curvature specification agrees on direction but rejects in fewer datasets, since estimating the shape costs precision. The linearithmic specification implies the least curvature of the three, with an acceleration that declines over time, and so the lowest warming of the three when extended to 2050.

items.title: Denoising Implicit Variational Inference
items.summary: Semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) expands the representational capacity of variational families, but optimizing the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) remains challenging because the marginal score of the semi-implicit distribution is generally intractable. Unbiased Implicit Variational Inference (UIVI) and related methods address this difficulty through reparameterized ELBO gradients, but existing approaches estimate the required score indirectly through reverse-conditional sampling or approximation, which can be computationally costly and unstable. We propose Denoising Implicit Variational Inference (DIVI), which learns the marginal score directly via denoising score matching. The learned score is used as a plug-in estimator in the pathwise ELBO gradient, replacing inner reverse-conditional sampling with a score-network evaluation. We analyze DIVI as inexact stochastic gradient ascent and show, under stated assumptions, that the averaged stationarity measure is controlled by the usual optimization term and the average score-matching error. Empirically, we evaluate DIVI on both synthetic distributions and a variety of real-data Bayesian inference tasks. The results show that DIVI improves over the current UIVI baselines while reducing the cost of ELBO-gradient estimation.

items.title: Muon Dynamics as a Spectral Wasserstein Flow
items.summary: Gradient normalization can stabilize deep-learning optimization, and spectral normalizations are especially natural for matrix-shaped parameter blocks; Muon is the motivating example. We study an idealized deterministic, continuous-time, vanishing-momentum version of this idea in the mean-field regime, where wide models are represented by probability measures on parameter space. Starting from normalized matrix flows, we introduce Spectral Wasserstein distances indexed by norms $γ$ on positive semidefinite matrices: the trace norm recovers the classical $W_2$ distance, the operator norm gives the Muon geometry, and Schatten norms interpolate between them. We develop a static Kantorovich formulation, a max--min robust-cost representation, and Gaussian reductions extending the Bures formula. For monotone norms, we prove equivalence with a Benamou--Brenier formulation and obtain a gradient-flow interpretation of normalized mean-field training dynamics. Numerical experiments illustrate the resulting flows for MMD objectives, Gaussian reductions, two-layer ReLU models, and shallow attention.

items.title: CLAPS: Aleatoric-Epistemic Scaling via Last-Layer Laplace for Conformal Regression
items.summary: Conformal regression provides finite-sample marginal coverage, but interval efficiency depends on how uncertainty is allocated across inputs. We propose \emph{Conformal Laplace-Aware Predictive Scaling} (CLAPS), which combines a learned heteroscedastic scale with last-layer Laplace uncertainty. The learned variance also weights the training features used to construct the posterior, yielding a noise-weighted support correction in the learned representation. The correction contracts as weighted feature information increases and becomes most influential under localized support imbalance. Experiments show near-nominal marginal coverage and modest efficiency improvements over the matched aleatoric baseline on real regression benchmarks.

items.title: Private Evaluation of High-Dimensional Functions
