This model reveals a fundamental tradeoff between the communication gain achieved through RA reorientation and the associated transmission-time loss. Accordingly, we formulate a rotation-delay-aware joint design of RA orientations and transmit beamforming to maximize the minimum effective transmission rate. For the single-user system, under a sufficient condition for strict concavity, the global optimum falls into one of three regimes: no rotation, partial rotation, and full rotation. A closed-form approximation is derived using a second-order expansion. For the multi-user system, we separate rotation-budget selection from fixed-budget max-min signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) optimization. An analytic-gradient zero-forcing (AG-ZF) algorithm is then developed for low-complexity joint RA orientation and rotation-budget optimization. The results show that explicitly accounting for mechanical rotation delay is essential for finite-slot RA-enabled UAV communications, and that the proposed designs effectively balance reconfiguration gain and transmission-time loss while achieving favorable effective-rate performance with low computational complexity.

items.title: ffconnect: An Interactive Interface for Control Integration in Mid-Fidelity Wind Farm Simulation
items.summary: Wind farm control (WFC) plays a crucial role in mitigating the wake effect, the negative aerodynamic interactions among wind turbines. Recent advances in data-driven control and artificial intelligence offer new opportunities to design more intelligent WFC systems, motivating the need for a tool that supports interactive design and validation in simulation. To address this, we present ffconnect, a general, open-source Python-based interface for FAST.Farm, a mid-fidelity wind farm simulator. Compared to prior work, ffconnect introduces a restructured Application Programming Interface (API) with enriched state access and supports integrating FAST.Farm with modern scientific computing and machine learning ecosystems by building entirely on Python. In experiments, ffconnect shows negligible runtime overhead compared to the original FAST.Farm across a range of simulation lengths and farm sizes, and demonstrates its effectiveness through a yaw-tracking case study. Finally, we provide the source code of ffconnect to keep it accessible for general users.

items.title: Promotion Signaling and Signal Jamming: An Analysis of Job Title Inflation
items.summary: Starting with Waldman (1984), it has become widely understood that an important role of promotions in labor markets is that promotions serve as signals of high worker ability. In this paper we explore the common and growing practice called job title inflation which serves a signal jamming role that reduces the signaling value of promotions. We first explore a two-period model and show how job title inflation can arise in equilibrium and increase social welfare both because workers directly value impressive sounding job titles and because the practice reduces job assignment inefficiencies due to signaling. We then introduce into the model an investment choice for young workers concerning human capital accumulation and show that job title inflation can decrease rather than increase welfare in that case. That is, when promotions and the associated wage increases serve as an important incentive for investing in human capital, the use of job title inflation can persist even though the practice lowers both overall efficiency and expected worker utility. We then consider three extensions: (i) a setting characterized by worker turnover; (ii) a setting characterized by a wage transparency law; and (iii) a setting characterized by heterogeneous worker visibility. Also, in addition to showing how job title inflation can arise as an equilibrium phenomenon that can either raise or lower welfare, we discuss the extent to which our theoretical analysis matches evidence concerning the use of job title inflation in real-world labor markets.

items.title: Almost Uniform Bias Correction for Persistent Panel Local Projections
items.summary: Panel local projections are widely used to estimate impulse responses in policy analysis. This paper examines the properties of the fixed-effect estimator and various bias-correction methods in panel local projections, focusing on settings with autoregressive control variables. We analyze the bias and variance of these estimators while allowing for persistence in both the target and control variables. Our theoretical findings indicate that the half-panel jackknife has desirable bias-reducing properties beyond the stationary setup. For empirical researchers, we recommend using bias-correction-adjusted standard errors to account for the sampling uncertainty associated with the half-panel jackknife estimator, regardless of the time-series dimension of the data.

items.title: Time is Knowledge: Response Times in Binary Response Models
items.summary: Response times contain information about economically relevant but unobserved variables like willingness to pay, preference intensity, quality, or happiness. We provide a general characterization of the properties of latent variables that can be detected using response time data. Our theoretical framework unifies and generalizes existing results in the literature and gives rise to many new applications. We illustrate the novel insights that the method can deliver through three empirical applications: identifying an optimal nudge, testing decreasing marginal happiness of income, and predicting treatment heterogeneity.

items.title: Deep-$π^*$: A Neural Network Estimate of Trend Inflation
items.summary: Most empirical models of trend inflation treat it as a latent random walk driven by unobserved shocks, so they cannot say which economic conditions move it. Deep-$π^*$ makes the innovations to the trend a possibly nonlinear function of a large number of macroeconomic indicators, estimated with neural networks, so that Shapley values can be used to attribute every movement of the trend to the indicators behind it. Two complementary loss functions define a current trend, which fits inflation today, and a forward-looking trend, which best predicts inflation over the next year. In US data, employment-related variables were the largest contributors to the post-pandemic rise of the current trend. However, the forward-looking trend rose earlier, with real activity, employment, and money and credit as the main drivers, and peaked eight to twelve months before the current trend. Both trends looked through most of the movements in energy and commodity prices. The contributions of the indicators are nonlinear, with sizeable interactions between them. Re-estimated every month during the surge, the model forecast inflation more accurately than the standard UC-SV model and a random walk, and in early 2021, when professional forecasters expected inflation of 3% or less, the forward-looking trend was already signalling an increase in persistent inflation.

items.title: Effort without Evidence
items.summary: I study how paternalistic concern for descendants' success affects learning about the need for costly effort. Each generation can use a demanding method or experiment with a less demanding alternative whose effectiveness is uncertain. Parents who underweight descendants' effort costs undervalue the savings that discovery would provide. On an explicit region of priors and preferences, paternalism removes a materially valuable experiment even though the relevant private record is truthfully transmitted. Relative to an aligned equilibrium attaining the material full-record optimum, the paternalistic equilibrium has greater long-run effort and observed success, lower discounted material welfare, and a less informative terminal public signal. Each sender obtains its preferred full-record continuation, so the comparison survives communication deviations within the same physical environment. I also study concealment as an incentive to experiment. A continuous-effort extension establishes that concealment and finite evidence production can coexist in an infinite-horizon equilibrium. Its welfare gain over babbling is distinct from the loss relative to alignment in the main result.

items.title: Tuning-Free Tests for Treatment Effect Heterogeneity via Expectile Processes
items.summary: This paper develops tuning-free tests for treatment-effect heterogeneity. By characterizing the null hypothesis as constancy of the expectile treatment-effect curve, we construct test statistics as continuous functionals of the mean-centered sample expectile process. We establish a uniform Bahadur representation, derive the asymptotic properties of the test statistics under the null and fixed alternatives, and show nontrivial power against local alternatives approaching the null at the $n^{-1/2}$ rate. For feasible inference, we develop a fast multiplier bootstrap that consistently approximates the nonpivotal null distribution while capturing the first-order effect of estimating the unknown common shift. The procedure is tuning-free, requiring no density or score-function estimation, bandwidth selection, or repeated refitting. The framework further incorporates a pointwise-studentized refinement and a covariate adjustment that reduces asymptotic variation without altering the population discrepancy. Monte Carlo comparisons with existing methods show generally reliable size control, competitive power, and substantial computational savings. An application to a large-scale water-conservation experiment illustrates the proposed tests.

items.title: Rationally Inattentive Echo Chambers
items.summary: Rationally inattentive players allocate limited attention capacities to biased primary sources and to other players as secondary sources to acquire information about an uncertain state. The resulting Poisson attention network stochastically transmits information from primary sources to a recipient either directly or indirectly through other players. We give conditions for the rise of echo-chamber equilibria in which players restrict attention to their own-biased primary source and same-type peers. We characterize the peer attention networks within echo chambers and analyze their comparative statics. Our results explain why modern information environments foster echo-chamber formation, how small differences in attention capacities can magnify into large disparities in allocations, and why regulatory interventions such as altering user visibility on social media or mandating exposure to opposing views may entail unintended consequences.

items.title: The economics of global personality diversity
items.summary: Understanding why national economic performance differs remains a central question in economics. Although institutions and demographic diversity are established correlates of economic development, the contribution of within-population personality diversity has received limited attention. We introduce the Global Personality Diversity Index ($Ψ$-GPDI), a measure of psychological heterogeneity derived from assessments of 760,242 individuals across 135 countries using 30 facets of the Big Five personality traits. We show that most variation in these facets occurs within rather than between countries. Across countries with available economic data, personality diversity is positively associated with GDP per person employed, accounting for 19.9% of the variance in an adjusted single-predictor model. Including $Ψ$-GPDI alongside institutional quality and immigrant diversity increases the model's explanatory power by approximately 5.7%. Personality diversity is also weakly correlated with immigrant diversity, suggesting that the two measures capture distinct characteristics of national populations. These findings identify psychological heterogeneity as a potentially important and previously underexamined dimension of national human capital. Although the observational design does not establish causality, the results motivate further investigation of how personality diversity interacts with institutions, occupational specialization, and economic development.

items.title: Balanced Social Learning
items.summary: When is social learning efficient if agents have heterogeneous preferences over a set of actions? When myopic agents generate information only about the action they choose, efficiency requires balance such that all high-value actions are discovered. We characterize the value of policies that control the flow of past information to future agents. Under full transparency of past information, the probability of efficient outcomes is approximately one if and only if the prior and preferences are balanced and the log-likelihood ratio distribution satisfies a set of intuitive moment conditions. Noisy bad news is a canonical example. By contrast, approximate efficiency is obtainable on the set of arbitrary adaptive information policies if and only if the prior alone is balanced. Moreover, it suffices to use adaptive evidence policies which permanently and fully disclose subsets of past information. When the prior is imbalanced and approximate efficiency is unattainable, we characterize the value of adaptive information and show that it is uniformly approximated by the value of adaptive evidence as the impact of each individual signal on beliefs vanishes.

items.title: What Impulse Response Do Instrumental Variables Identify?
items.summary: We study what local projection instrumental variable (LP-IV) regressions identify when an instrument is correlated with several structural shocks, such as defense and non-defense spending shocks. LP-IV identifies an instrument-specific affine combination of the component impulse responses, possibly with negative weights. Over-identified 2SLS or GMM yields another such combination, and the over-identification test can reject even with valid instruments. With as many instruments as shocks, the component responses are identified when each shock has a policy variable (e.g., sectoral spending) and its impact on the other policy variables is restricted. We illustrate with government spending and tax multipliers.

items.title: Allocative Efficiency and the Returns to Innovation
items.summary: Innovation changes welfare by improving technology and reallocating inputs across producers with different markups. When producers choose markups optimally, an innovator's own output and price adjustments have no private value at the margin, so reallocation affects its profit only through others' responses. For an innovator small in its markets, the change in allocative efficiency is of the same order as its cost saving but does not reach its profit. A process innovator is paid its cost saving, forgoing its own and downstream markups on added output. For U.S. public firms in 2015, these forgone markups average 26 percent of that saving. For innovators accounting for 56 percent of sales, allocative efficiency rises or falls by more than a tenth of their private return. With estimated spillovers, patenting firms' R&D has a social return 6.24 times its private return.

items.title: A Note on the Stability of Monotone Markov Chains
items.summary: This note studies monotone Markov chains, a subclass of Markov chains with extensive applications in operations research and economics. While the properties that ensure the global stability of these chains are well studied, their establishment often relies on the fulfillment of a certain splitting condition. We address the challenges of verifying the splitting condition by introducing simple, applicable conditions that ensure global stability. The simplicity of these conditions is demonstrated through various examples including autoregressive processes, portfolio allocation problems and resource allocation dynamics.

items.title: When Better Opportunities Backfire: Service Worker Responses to Parallel AI Deployment in Customer Acquisition
items.summary: As AI voice agents get deployed in high-volume contact centers, firms can route low-intent leads to AI and allocate high-intent leads to human workers. Drawing on sequential search theory, we posit that AI-induced task allocation reshapes work, enriching opportunities facing human workers but also raising their reservation value for continuing with the lead in hand, making them less willing to persist. We study the effects of an AI voice-agent deployment at a Chinese online health-insurance brokerage using more than a half million customer outreach records surrounding the rollout. Adopting a regression-discontinuity-in-time design, we trace how worker behavior changes across the workday. Results show that the enrichment of human-facing opportunities concentrates early in the workday, raising the probability that a call is a high-intent lead by about 23 percentage points on the first three calls and fading to zero later. However, customer acquisition by human workers declines precisely where the enrichment is greatest, falling about 5 percentage points on the first three calls and flattening over the day. Consistent with the theorized reservation value mechanism, workers reallocate their earliest leads about 8 percentage points more often and persist less with them, shortening those calls by about 13%. A calibrated decomposition analysis further shows that the modest gain from improved lead ordering is outweighed by a much larger negative behavioral response. By reshaping the quality and within-workday distribution of opportunities, parallel AI deployment alters how workers pursue tasks, highlighting opportunity distribution as an important service operations state variable beyond workload and congestion.

items.title: Linear Regression with Common Unobserved Heterogeneity
items.summary: We study inference on common slope parameters in linear panel models with two-way unobserved heterogeneity. In linear regression, bias arises from unobserved heterogeneity that is shared between the residual and the covariates. Our common unobserved heterogeneity (CUH) estimator targets this common variation directly: it searches over functionals of the residualised outcome for variation that also resides in the covariates, and seeks to further project out only bias-inducing variation. This makes the estimator less sensitive to weak outcome factors while avoiding the complete removal of exogenous variation in covariates that is unrelated to the confounding heterogeneity. We develop a weak-factor theory based on a singular-value strength index and establish $\sqrt{NT}$-asymptotic normality of the cross-fitted CUH estimator. Under homoskedastic errors, its asymptotic variance is no larger than that of a common correlated effects factor estimator. Simulations and empirical applications illustrate the resulting bias--variance trade-off and the gains from selectively removing common variation.

items.title: Winner's bliss: interdependent-value auctions with horizontal uncertainty
items.summary: We analyze auctions with interdependent values and horizontally differentiated bidders, where good news for one bidder is bad news for the other bidders. This generates a winner's bliss, reversing the well-known winner's curse: winning means buying an object that is more valuable than a naïve estimate suggests. Our main result is about the English auction. We introduce the ``own effect property,'' generalizing the single-crossing condition, to prove the existence of an efficient ex-post equilibrium. Regarding revenue, we show that with affiliated signals, the English auction yields no more revenue than the second-price auction, while independent signals yield the standard revenue equivalence.

items.title: Work that Counts, and Work that Doesn't: Labor Supply in Experiments and Real Work
items.summary: Do workers behave the same in experiments as they do in real life? Combining a real-effort emoji-counting experiment with platform records, self-reported expectations and recalls, and smartphone screen-time logs, we compare how the same workers on Prolific respond to randomized wage changes in the experiment and to wage variation in their actual work. Our results reveal that workers' behavior in experiments is remarkably different from real life. In the observational window, in fact, workers respond to expected wage changes just as they do in the experiment, but are much less responsive to unanticipated changes. However, once we condition on recall error in self-reports, we find that behavior in the two windows aligns. Recall error is then both a source of error for self-reported data but also the result of a process of inattention that affects effort itself, as unexpected wage changes often pass unnoticed.

items.title: Informative Imitation
items.summary: We study steady-state equilibria of a sequential learning game in which each agent chooses between a safe action and a risky action of unknown profitability. Before choosing, each agent observes how many of the last $m$ agents adopted the risky action, but not whether they were informed or what their adoption costs were. We show that uninformed agents' imitation decisions can be strategic complements: the more likely uninformed agents are to join risky-action herds, the more informative those herds become about the action's profitability. When this complementarity gives rise to multiple equilibria, the one that maximizes the probability of imitation by uninformed agents also maximizes agents' welfare.

items.title: Inference on Linear Programs via Feasibility Testing
items.summary: This paper studies inference on the value of a linear program (LP) when the objective and constraints are estimated. Using LP duality, we construct one- and two-sided confidence intervals by inverting tests of the feasibility of systems of linear inequalities. Existing tests yield asymptotically valid confidence intervals but can have poor power. We propose a modification that augments these systems with estimated ``box constraints.'' The resulting procedure has power against $N^{-1/2}$-local alternatives and yields confidence intervals of order $N^{-1/2}$. These results require only that the LP value be finite, and do not require compactness of the feasible region nor standard constraint qualifications. We obtain stronger guarantees under various constraint qualifications and establish uniform validity over large classes of DGPs when known deterministic constraints bound the primal and/or dual variables. Simulations demonstrate good finite-sample performance.

items.title: Belief Bias Identification
items.summary: This paper proposes a unified theoretical model to identify and test a comprehensive set of probabilistic updating biases within a single framework. The model achieves separate identification by focusing on the updating of belief distributions, rather than point beliefs alone. Estimating the model in a laboratory experiment reveals significant individual heterogeneity, with the hot-hand fallacy emerging as the most common bias and a key driver of biased inference. Accounting for additional distortions reveals associations across bias families and reduces the apparent prevalence of overinference and preference-based biases. At the population level, most biases average out, but base-rate neglect remains present.

items.title: Persistence is not Independence: A structural Credibility Protocol for Distribution based Recovery in VARLiNGAM
items.summary: VAR-LiNGAM recovers a contemporaneous structure from reduced-form innovations under mutual independence of the underlying structural shocks. Recovery itself and bootstrap stability of the recovered edges are natural post-estimation outputs, but neither directly assesses the identifying independence assumption. We organize post-recovery validation as an ordered, non-compensatory protocol with four layers (reduced-form admissibility, distributional informativeness, independence support and edge persistence) and establish, by a constructive population result, a Monte Carlo experiment under known ground truth and a firm-level Compustat application, that the last two layers are non-nested: an edge can persist under resampling while the recovered shocks remain dependent, and independence can be supported while the leading recovered edge fails to persist. Independence support is classified operationally by a block-permutation dHSIC diagnostic on the recovered shocks, with mutual information as a continuous measure of residual dependence and tail co-exceedance as a complementary extreme-dependence diagnostic. Empirically, the conjunction of no detected independence violation and a reportable persistent leading edge occurs only in a small subset.

items.title: Conventional Inference under Nonstationary Heavy Tailed Fractional Processes & Arrays
items.summary: Existing regression inference methods for nonstationary heavy tailed data are largely limited to unit roots tests. Functional central limit theorems (FCLTs), which are commonly used for the asymptotic analysis of nonstationary models, are inapplicable to nonstationary data characterized by a memory parameter $d<1$ and a stability parameter $α<2$. Furthermore, it is well known that inference under nonstationarity is often non-conventional, and this issue is exacerbated in the presence of heavy-tailed data. The interaction of long memory and heavy tails significantly enlarges the nonstationary region---i.e., the covariate model space---where conventional inference methods typically fail. To address these challenges, we propose a new limit theory and methods that facilitate both workable asymptotics and conventional inference in regressions involving general nonstationary heavy-tailed covariate processes. Specifically, our approach develops a limit theory for heavy-tailed weakly nonstationary processes (hereafter, HT-WNPs), which lie on the threshold of nonstationarity (cf. Duffy and Kasparis, 2021, Annals of Statistics). We demonstrate that the proposed methods---including IVX-based and related instrumental-variable procedures---facilitate conventional inference for a broad class of stationary and nonstationary heavy-tailed covariates. This class includes nearly and mildly integrated arrays, as well as nonstationary fractional processes with memory parameter $1-1/α<d<2-1/α$, where $α\in(1,2]$. Our analysis is applicable to both parametric and kernel regression models. The finite-sample performance of the proposed methods is evaluated through a comprehensive simulation study. Additionally, we provide an empirical application to the predictability of stock returns using long-memory heavy-tailed predictors.

items.title: Monotonicity in streaming problems
items.summary: We explore the implications of the principle of monotonicity in the problem of sharing the revenues raised from subscriptions to music streaming platforms among content providers. We formalize various forms of this principle as several axioms for popularity indices, which generate sharing rules in this setting. We show that, combined with some other basic axioms (such as additivity, symmetry, or pairwise homogeneity), they provide axiomatic characterizations of focal indices for this problem, as well as more general families comprising them.

items.title: Mechanism Design with Information Leakage
items.summary: We study the design of mechanisms---e.g., auctions---when the designer does not control information flows between mechanism participants. A mechanism equilibrium is leakage-proof if no player conditions their actions on leaked information; a property distinct from both ex-post and posterior incentive compatibility. Only leakage-proof mechanisms can implement social choice functions in environments with leakage; efficient auctions and revenue-maximizing ones need to be leakage-proof. Second-price and ascending auctions are leakage-proof, while first-price auctions need not be. Appropriately designed Dutch auctions are leakage-proof and attain optimal revenue even with irregular value distributions. In multi-unit environments, leakage-proof mechanisms can attain the optimal Bayesian revenue even when dominant-strategy mechanisms cannot.

items.title: Scoring Rules as Least-Squares Estimators
items.summary: Kawada (2018) proved that a scoring rule represented by a strictly positive score vector is equivalent to the corresponding cosine similarity rule. The original proof relies on a direct analysis of the cosine similarity optimization problem. In this note, we present an alternative, simpler proof based on a basic least-squares characterization. For any fixed preference profile and score vector, the arithmetic mean of the individual score vectors uniquely minimizes the sum of squared Euclidean distances to those vectors. It then shows that, for any strictly positive affine representative of the given score vector, the optimal solutions of the cosine similarity problem are precisely the positive multiples of the arithmetic mean of the corresponding score vectors. Since the two arithmetic means are positively affinely related, they induce exactly the same social ranking. This result provides a transparent geometric interpretation of scoring rules and clarifies why the cosine similarity rule necessarily coincides with the corresponding scoring rule.

items.title: Globally Optimal Estimation of Nested Logit Models
items.summary: Nested logit is widely used in operational demand models, yet jointly estimating its utility coefficients and nest dissimilarity parameters requires nonconvex optimization. Standard estimation routines offer no certificate of global optimality, leaving a gap between globally optimizing decisions under nested-logit demand and reliably estimating that demand model. We develop, to our knowledge, the first globally convergent optimization framework with an explicit global-accuracy guarantee for joint nested-logit estimation. Our central complexity result confines all exponential dependence to the number of free nest dissimilarity parameters: computation is polynomial in the numbers of observations, alternatives, and utility coefficients. Consequently, under the stated compact-domain and relaxation-error conditions, fixing the number of nests yields an additive polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS). The framework exploits an exact exponential-cone formulation for fixed dissimilarities and a spatial branch-and-bound algorithm that searches only over the free dissimilarities. Valid likelihood bounds provide an anytime certificate and finite termination at any prescribed additive average-log-likelihood tolerance. Across eight benchmark datasets and 240 estimation instances, the method certifies every reported solution and exposes inferior local estimates despite normal solver termination. These results establish a computational foundation for globally certified nested-logit estimation.

items.title: Human Responses to Algorithmic Correction: Evidence from Centre Court
items.summary: We study how algorithmic review changes the initial decisions that a system is designed to correct. Using Hawk-Eye data from professional tennis, we compare umpire decisions with and without review against a common accuracy benchmark. Under review, initial errors were 8.6 percentage points higher just outside the line and lower for comparably close balls inside. We find no evidence that average initial accuracy deteriorated. Within matches, reversals were followed by larger adjustments than upheld calls, consistent with adaptation to correction. Overall, correction offsets worse initial decisions for incorrect in calls and reinforces better initial decisions for incorrect out calls. Whether review lowers organizational costs depends jointly on these changes and the costs of remedying corrected errors. A conditional illustration shows how utilization spreads fixed review costs across calls.

items.title: Nonparametric Dyadic Quantile Regression
items.summary: This paper considers nonparametric quantile regression for directed dyadic data observed on the ordered pairs of a complete network with n vertices. The observations exhibit dyadic dependence: dyads with disjoint indices are independent, whereas dyads sharing one or two indices are correlated. The local linear smoothing technique is adopted to estimate the quantile regression function. The asymptotic theory reveals that convergence rates of the proposed dyadic quantile regression estimation crucially depend on whether degeneracy occurs for the underlying network generating process. A rate-adaptive standardized version of the limit distribution is derived under some mild conditions. In addition, an easy-to-implement method is proposed to estimate the asymptotic variance of nonparametric dyadic quantile regression estimation. The finite-sample performance and applicability of the proposed methodology are illustrated with Monte-Carlo simulation and a real data application to bilateral portfolio holdings.

items.title: Improved Approximation and Tight Competition for Simple Auctions
items.summary: We study simple auctions for one additive buyer whose values for $m$ items are independent. Write $\mathrm{REV}$ for optimal revenue, $\mathrm{SREV}$ and $\mathrm{BREV}$ for the revenues from separate selling and grand bundling, and $\mathrm{BSPA}_2$ for grand-bundle second-price revenue with two independent bidders. For independent regular items, we prove $\mathrm{REV}\le\mathrm{BSPA}_2\le2\mathrm{BREV}$. This establishes tight approximation and competition guarantees for bundling under regularity and answers an open question from Beyhaghi et al. (EC 2025). For general independent items, we prove $\mathrm{REV} \le \mathrm{SREV} + \frac{π^2}{6}\mathrm{BREV} \le 2.645 \max\{\mathrm{SREV}, \mathrm{BREV}\}$. This improves the previous approximation factors of $6$ from Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg (FOCS 2014, JACM 2020) and $5.2$ from Ma and Simchi-Levi (AISTATS 2021). On the lower bound side, we construct an instance in which prices for three disjoint bundles earn more than $2.11\max\{\mathrm{SREV},\mathrm{BREV}\}$, improving the previous lower bound of $2$ from Rubinstein (ITCS 2016). We also show that exact recovery of one buyer's optimal revenue by the better of separate selling and bundling requires $Θ(\log m)$ bidders in the worst case.

items.title: Land and Infinite Debt Rollover
items.summary: Many analyses of infinite debt rollover omit productive land, whereas prior work argues that land precludes rollover. We show that when land's income share remains bounded away from zero, every equilibrium is bubbleless and Pareto efficient, ruling out rollover. If instead the land share vanishes and the autarky interest rate is below rent growth, every equilibrium contains a land bubble and permits rollover despite Pareto efficiency. Iowa farmland data show falling yields and converging district prices as price--rent ratios rise. This pattern rejects a bubbleless Gordon model but is consistent with a rational bubble earning the return on land.

items.title: Valid Inference After Control Selection in Difference-in-Differences
items.summary: Selecting difference-in-differences controls from a candidate pool by pre-treatment fit can alter the estimator's distribution and cause undercoverage despite parallel trends for every candidate. We develop the first empirically implementable selective inference for the average treatment effect on the treated. We estimate the full covariance matrix from the same observations and condition inference on the full selection event. Joint Gaussian approximation of outcome means yields uniform asymptotic validity including perfect fit and population ties. Endpoints approach known-covariance counterparts in standard-error units; widths shrink with effective sample size despite vanishing regional sample shares. We cover staggered adoption, reused observations and finite fitting-rule searches favoring larger estimates. At fixed smoothing, skewness and mean--covariance corrections give randomized tests second-order accuracy for joint selection and rejection probabilities. The adjusted interval for police deployment's effect on car theft includes zero; intervals for minimum-wage employment effects admit larger losses at $\$5$ to below $\$14$ per hour.

items.title: Incontestable Assignments
items.summary: We study an information-based weakening of stability for school choice, using the evidence students may invoke in appeals. The model permits partial information about schools' choice functions and the realized assignment. A student has a legitimate complaint if, in every compatible state, she can block with some more-preferred school, and an assignment is incontestable if no student has such a complaint. We characterize legitimate complaints using an ex-post safety-set. For school-side information rules, under which the only admissible assignment-side information is the student's own assignment and all interim-compatible school-side states are preserved, incontestability is equivalent to respecting interim safety-sets. Stable mechanisms and Top Trading Cycles with responsive priorities are incontestable for every such rule. Pareto improvements preserve this robustness. When schools' choice functions are path-independent, all mechanisms that are incontestable for every school-side information rule, are non-wasteful, and guarantee group protection give each student the same attainable set conditional on her preferences and interim information.

items.title: Ranking Treatment Saturations: Regret Bounds and Experimental Design
items.summary: We study the statistical decision problem of ranking treatment saturations, the treated shares of a cluster. Planners need a ranking, not only the best saturation, when rollouts are phased or the preferred saturation becomes infeasible. Using a two-stage randomized saturation experiment, we analyse the empirical success (ES) ranking, a simple and widely used rule. We derive finite-sample regret bounds for ES under the welfare-weighted Kendall distance loss that allow arbitrary within-cluster interference and need no network data. In a local asymptotic framework, ES on efficient welfare estimates has maximum regret at most about 1.4 times the minimax regret, for any number of saturations and any covariance. This bound guides the allocation of clusters by balancing cost against the variance of cluster means under each saturation. In the Malawi cash-transfer experiment, ES ranks full saturation of unconditional transfers first and zero last for marriage, and the realized allocation nearly minimizes the bound.

items.title: Coarse Revenue Guarantee in First Price Auction and Beyond
items.summary: I study the coarse revenue guarantee (CRG) of the single-unit first-price auction with common values. The CRG is the minimum expected revenue over all information structures and all Bayes coarse correlated equilibria (BCCE), the equilibrium notion to which no-regret learning leads. Identical play, in which all bidders submit the same bid, attains the worst-case revenue, and this reduction yields a closed-form characterization. The coarse guarantee is positive and increases with the number of bidders $N$. It lies strictly below the revenue guarantee of Bergemann, Brooks and Morris (2017) at every finite $n$, and the gap between the two closes at rate $\log N / N$. I extend the analysis to reserve prices, symmetric and asymmetric priors, other standard auctions, and an unknown value distribution.

items.title: Rating Multiple Agents with Career Concerns
items.summary: A principal designs ratings for multiple career-concerned agents with correlated talents, mapping outputs into arbitrary finite-variance statistics. Peer output both benchmarks effort and signals talent, making full disclosure suboptimal under confidential ratings. Relaxing Bayes plausibility to linear orthogonality yields a closed-form rating and computable effort bounds for general priors; under normality, the relaxation is exact. Optimal confidential ratings combine the full-disclosure wage with the Fisher score for effort: they are relative-performance when individual output is informative about talent and team-based when it is noisy. Public ratings must satisfy joint Bayes plausibility, weakening incentives; hence, the principal prefers confidential ratings, whereas agents prefer public ratings. A spectral decomposition characterizes public ratings under normality: small cost heterogeneity implies full disclosure regardless of the noise structure, whereas large cost heterogeneity or strong effort spillovers can induce partial disclosure to reallocate incentives. The results bear on performance ratings and pay transparency.

items.title: A Geometric Analysis of Gains from Trade
items.summary: We provide a geometric proof that the random proposer mechanism is a $4$-approximation to the first-best gains from trade in bilateral exchange. We then refine this geometric analysis to recover the $3.147$-approximation guarantee previously established by Fei (2022).

items.title: Generalized Multidimensional Contests with Asymmetric Players: Equilibrium and Optimal Prize Design
items.summary: We study $n$-dimensional Tullock contests between two players with heterogeneous effort costs. We establish sharp bounds on discriminatory power $r$ ensuring that equilibrium is unique and pure across prize rules and cost asymmetries: $r\leq1/\lceil n/2\rceil$ when prizes depend only on the number of victories across all dimensions, and $r\leq1/n$ when they may also depend on player identity. An effort-maximizing rule splits the prize unless one player wins by a sufficient margin in the first case, and gives the weaker player a possibly zero headstart in the second. When both bounds hold, restricting prizes to victory counts alone can be costless despite unequal costs, but the percentage loss in total effort weakly increases with asymmetry.

items.title: Congestion Games with Heterogeneous Valuations: An Optimal Transport Approach
items.summary: In emerging urban mobility and logistics applications, such as advanced air mobility, electric vehicle charging, and shared service systems, agents with heterogeneous valuations choose among multiple outcomes while sharing congested resources. Existing congestion game and resource-allocation models, however, typically restrict either the structure of heterogeneous outcome preferences or the form of congestion externalities. We introduce a nonatomic congestion game framework in which agents have multidimensional heterogeneous valuations over a finite set of outcomes, with the population represented by a measure over the valuation space. We show that, although there is a continuum of heterogeneous agents, both Nash equilibria and social optima admit finite-dimensional characterizations. Nash equilibria are characterized by aggregate flows and outcome-level threshold vectors, while social optima admit a semi-discrete optimal transport formulation characterized by aggregate flows and strategy-level Kantorovich dual potentials. For separable utilities and latency functions $\ell_e$ such that $x\mapsto x\ell_e(x)$ is convex for every resource $e$, the social welfare problem becomes a convex optimization problem, and we characterize social optima through marginal congestion costs and capacity-dual prices. Our results provide a geometric characterization of congestion games with multidimensional heterogeneous valuations and connect nonatomic congestion games with semi-discrete optimal transport.

items.title: Human-AI Productivity Paradoxes: Modeling the Interplay of Skill, Effort, and AI Assistance
items.summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly adopted in the workplace and in education, yet the empirical evidence on AI's impact remains mixed across different operating contexts. We propose a model of human-AI interaction to better understand and analyze several mechanisms by which AI affects productivity. In our setting, human agents with varying skill levels exert utility-maximizing effort to produce certain task outcomes with AI assistance. We find that incorporating endogeneity in skill development or AI unreliability can induce a productivity paradox: increased levels of AI assistance may degrade productivity, leading to potentially significant shortfalls. We construct interpretable measures that characterize when the productivity paradox occurs. Moreover, we examine the long-term distributional effect of AI on skill, and demonstrate that skill polarization can emerge in steady state. We identify an effort-skill non-monotonicity condition under which skill polarization emerges.

items.title: Compositional difference-in-differences
items.summary: Many causal questions involve outcomes distributed across mutually exclusive categories, such as votes by party or employment by status, where both category shares and the total quantity are of interest. This paper develops Compositional Difference-in-Differences (CoDiD), a framework for causal inference with categorical and compositional outcomes. Focusing first on shares, I introduce parallel trends in log-odds (PTLO), which requires the untreated log-odds of each category relative to a reference category to evolve in parallel across groups. I show that PTLO admits three equivalent interpretations: stability over time of the dependence structure between untreated categorical outcomes and group membership; parallel evolution of relative utilities in a random-utility model when shares arise from discrete choices; and parallel trajectories in the Aitchison geometry of the simplex. A stronger assumption, parallel growth in log-quantities, jointly identifies treatment effects on category shares and the total quantity. I also derive sharp bounds under a relaxation of the identifying assumption. Finally, I illustrate the framework by examining the effects of early voting on U.S. presidential elections.

items.title: Partition function form games with probabilistic beliefs
items.summary: We revisit games in partition function form, i.e. cooperative games where the payoff of a coalition depends on the partition of the entire set of players. We assume that each coalition computes its worth having probabilistic beliefs over the coalitional behavior of the outsiders, i.e., it assigns various probability distributions over the set of partitions that the outsiders can form. These beliefs are not necessarily consistent with respect to the actual choices of the outsiders. We apply this framework to symmetric partition function form games characterized by either positive or negative externalities and we derive conditions on coalitional beliefs that guarantee the non-emptiness of the core of the induced games.

items.title: How exposed is work to robotics? Occupational, industry, and geographic measures
items.summary: Exposure indices that map technical capabilities onto occupational abilities have become a standard tool for anticipating how AI may reshape work, but existing measures either cover software AI or proxy robotics through patents and installation data that reflect the industrial robots of past decades. We construct the first abilities-based exposure measures for robotics and physical AI, and the first to span occupations, industries, and geographies. Following the framework of Felten et al. (2018, 2021), we build a robotics capability taxonomy of 16 capabilities in eight domains from 78 academic, industry, and standards sources, use a large language model to score the relatedness of each capability to the 52 ONET work abilities, and aggregate to Robotics Occupational Exposure (ROE) for 774 occupations, Robotics Industry Exposure (RIE) for 250 NAICS industries, and county-level Robotics Geographic Exposure (RGE). We find that robotics exposure concentrates in physically intensive work such as construction, farming, transportation, and production, and in industries such as logging, mining, trucking, and warehousing. Unlike generative-AI exposure, ROE is higher in occupations with lower wages, lower education requirements, and less creative-ability content. Physical collaboration and assistance, terrain-based locomotion, grasping and handling, and task and functional reasoning move the exposure ranking most, yet no single capability carries the index. Because the measures capture technical relatedness rather than readiness, cost, or adoption, they should be read as an upper bound on where physical automation could affect work.

items.title: Should the Timing of Inspections be Predictable?
items.summary: A principal hires an agent to work on a long-term project that culminates in a breakthrough or a breakdown. At each time, the agent privately chooses to work or shirk. Working increases the arrival rate of breakthroughs and decreases the arrival rate of breakdowns. To motivate the agent to work, the principal conducts costly inspections. She fires the agent if shirking is detected. We characterize the principal's optimal inspection policy. Predictable inspections are optimal if work primarily generates breakthroughs. Random inspections are typically optimal if work primarily prevents breakdowns. Crucially, the agent's actions affect the curvature of the project's survival probability, which determines his induced risk attitude over the timing of planned inspections.

items.title: Extending Myerson's Optimal Auctions to Correlated Bidders via Neural Network Interpolation
items.summary: We aim to design revenue-maximizing single-item auctions that are deterministic, strategy-proof, and ex post individually rational --- the quintessential fundamental model for optimal mechanism design. While Myerson's seminal work solved this model for independent bidders, straightforward extensions to correlated settings often result in non-monotonic, and therefore non-strategy-proof allocations. Critically, optimal allocation design for correlated bidders is NP-hard to approximate, rendering theoretical optimality guarantees in this domain computationally intractable. We establish a new standard of empirical rigor for this theoretically hard model by proposing an empirical pipeline. We synthesize neural interpolation of Myerson's greedy allocation based on marginal profits (the correlated variant of virtual valuation), formal neural verification to enforce exact strategy-proofness, and a constructive repair procedure. Empirically, our method is highly effective, consistently achieves near-optimal revenue across a wide range of distributions, including synthetic, adversarial, and real-world (consumer, financial, and industrial) datasets. Compared to existing manual and neural baselines, our approach shows substantial improvement, often reducing the revenue gap by an order of magnitude. Our study is also the first to introduce (unattainable) greedy revenue as a rigorous upper bound for empirical benchmarking, providing a definitive quantitative performance measure where true optima remain theoretically elusive. We demonstrate the generality of our approach by extending it to multi-unit auctions with unit demand and integrating our verification techniques into RegretNet to achieve exact strategy-proofness.

items.title: Delegate Pricing to Algorithms: When Slow and Steady Wins the Race
items.summary: We study the strategic design of learning algorithms in a canonical continuous-time pricing game. We introduce a meta-game in which firms select learning rates for a gradient dynamic, evaluating payoffs as the discounted sum of profits accrued along the entire learning path. We uncover a fundamental dichotomy driven by stage-game incentives: if the stage game exhibits strategic substitutability, each firm strictly prefers faster learning. Under strategic complementarity, however, an excessively fast algorithm accelerates the rival's competitive response, destroying transitional profit margins. Even though the competitive price is a dominant action in the stage game and convergence to this price is guaranteed, we prove that firms design sluggish algorithms in equilibrium.

items.title: Search and Matching without Reciprocity
items.summary: We study equilibrium sorting in the canonical search-and-matching model with Nash bargaining and ex-ante and ex-post heterogeneity. Under standard conditions for assortative matching under search, match surplus retains two properties of Becker's frictionless benchmark---single-crossing and single-peakedness---but necessarily loses the third, reciprocity. Instead, search generates consensus: intervals of types share the same surplus-maximizing partner. For such intervals, mismatched pairs are more likely to match, conditional on meeting, than perfectly assortative ones. Two forces drive this: with search, outside options rise less than one-for-one with productivity and fall more for agents with fewer suitable partners. Globally, upper contour sets of the match-probability surface are lattices below an endogenous threshold but almost never above it. This means that MLRP fails for some log-concave survival function.

items.title: Early Investment Snowballs for Low-Skill Children: Average Marginal Returns and the Dynamics of Skill Formation
items.summary: Program evaluations routinely find larger effects of investment in low-skill children, while structural models of skill formation typically find that skill and investment are complements. I reconcile these findings by introducing the Average Marginal Return (AMR), which averages the marginal return to an input over the distribution of other inputs, providing a structural analogue to the average treatment effects estimated in program evaluations. The AMR reveals why input scales and distributions matter for the economic interpretation of structural estimates, why reduced-form interaction coefficients need not identify technological complementarity, and why dynamic complementarity can be difficult to detect in reduced-form work. I estimate AMRs to parental investment using a dynamic factor model of cognitive and noncognitive skill formation for ages 5-14 in the Children of the NLSY79. I accommodate binary and Likert measures using ordered probits, showing that treating them as continuous substantially biases estimates, and introduce effective factors to extend the scale-invariant normalization of Freyberger (2026) to models with multiple skills per period. Investment in early childhood generates larger long-run gains in cognitive skill than investment at later ages. Although skill and investment are complements, the AMR to early investment is initially flat across skill levels but becomes sharply decreasing in initial skill over time. By ages 13-14, children at the 10th percentile of early cognitive skill gain roughly twice as much from early investment as children at the 90th.

items.title: Risk Ceilings and Development Deadlines: Pacing AI under Uncertain Safety Productivity
items.summary: Can a regulator promise both a risk ceiling and a development deadline when safety productivity is unknown? A ceiling below the final model's unprotected hazard requires a minimum stock of safety knowledge, so both promises hold only if weak research can be ruled out. Learning first and then replaying development, with spare compute in safety, comes close to that minimum. In a calibration with only state risk, constant safety yield, and full knowledge transfer, it needs only 3.3 percent more productivity than the necessary bound. Customer services pay for the guarantee. Rules that fix compute allocation fix dates, not risk.

items.title: Inference for Fixed Effects Estimators when Panels are Unbalanced
items.summary: We develop the asymptotic theory for two-way fixed effects M-estimators in unbalanced panels, within a framework where both panel dimensions grow large at proportional rates. The selection process may be deterministic, stochastic, or a combination of the two. We require neither a missing-at-random condition nor a selection equation, only a conditional mean restriction on the outcome. The uncorrected estimators are asymptotically normal but not correctly centered due to incidental parameter bias and feedback bias. The latter arises when regressors or the selection indicator respond to past outcomes. We propose debiased estimators that remove both biases without requiring knowledge of which regressors or selection components are predetermined. Simulations show that the corrections remove most of the bias and restore coverage close to nominal levels. Revisiting a study on capital inflow surges and banking crises, we find that the corrections leave qualitative conclusions unchanged but substantially shift the estimated magnitudes.

items.title: (Debiased) Inference for Fixed Effects Estimators with Three-Dimensional Panel and Network Data
items.summary: Inference for fixed effects estimators is often unreliable due to Nickell- and incidental parameter biases. While these issues are well understood for classical two-dimensional panels, little is known about three-dimensional panel structures (e.g., sender x receiver x time). We develop inferential theory for a broad class of linear and nonlinear fixed effects M-estimators in this setting, covering bipartite, directed, and undirected network panel data, multiple specifications of additively separable unobserved effects, and both strictly exogenous and predetermined regressors. Our analysis reveals fundamentally different asymptotic properties compared to two-dimensional panels. In particular, we find a sharp dichotomy across specifications: (i) when unobserved effects vary along a single panel dimension, estimators are asymptotically unbiased, (ii) when they vary along two panel dimensions, estimators may suffer from a severe inference problem characterized by a degenerate asymptotic distribution. We resolve the latter by deriving explicit bias formulas and proposing analytically debiased estimators with nondegenerate, correctly centered asymptotic distributions. An empirical application studies dynamic network formation in a directed panel of bilateral trade relationships.

items.title: AI-exposed jobs deteriorated before ChatGPT
items.summary: Public debate links worsening job prospects for AI-exposed occupations to the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. Using monthly U.S. unemployment insurance records, we measure occupation- and location-specific unemployment risk and find that risk rose in AI-exposed occupations beginning in early 2022, months before ChatGPT was released. Analyzing millions of LinkedIn profiles, we show that graduate cohorts from 2021 onward entered AI-exposed jobs at lower rates than earlier cohorts, with gaps opening before late 2022. Finally, from millions of university syllabi, we find that graduates taking more LLM-exposed curricula had shorter job searches after ChatGPT and higher first-job pay when entering highly exposed occupations. Together, these results---pointing to forces pre-dating generative AI and to the ongoing value of LLM-relevant education---suggest that generative AI may not be the root cause of these labor market hardships and that the launch of ChatGPT is a faulty natural experiment for understanding AI's impact on jobs.

items.title: Mechanism Design by a Politician
items.summary: A set of agents has to make a decision about the provision of a public good and its financing. Agents have heterogeneous values for the public good and each agent's value is private information. An agenda-setter has the right to make a proposal about a public-good level and a vector of contributions. For the proposal to be approved, only the favourable votes of a majority of agents are needed. If the proposal is not approved, a type-dependent outside option is implemented. I characterize the optimal public-good provision and the coalition-formation for any outside option in dominant strategies. Optimal public-good provision might be a non-monotonic function of the outside option public-good level. Moreover, the optimal coalition might be a non-convex set of types. Importantly, majority voting creates endogenously countervailing incentives among agents.

items.title: Robustness in Mechanism Design
items.summary: The article reviews the robust design and analysis of auctions, focusing on the predominant paradigm in the computer science literature, which quantifies robustness by the worst-case, over environments, ratio between the robust auction's performance and that of an optimal auction for the environment. Applications include robust analysis of canonical auctions such as the first-price auction for the welfare objective, prior-robust auction design for the revenue objective, and prior-robust design of exchange mechanisms for the gains-from-trade objective. Finally, the revelation principle is not without loss in robust mechanism design. The potential loss can be quantified by the revelation gap, the fraction of the optimal robust guarantee that is lost when restricting from all mechanisms to revelation mechanisms.

items.title: Input-output analysis with a sphere packing approach
items.summary: Input-output analysis with linear programming is widely used in the planning of national economies. However, linear programming attains its optimum at a vertex of the feasible set, and a small deviation of the optimal plan in some direction violates a constraint. So far, little attention has been paid to finding sets of production plans which guarantee both the supply-demand balance of an economy and a given level of its gross domestic product (GDP), and the sphere packing approach cannot be applied directly, since the balance equations define a set with an empty interior. In this paper, we introduce the set of $(\varepsilon,δ)$-solutions, in which GDP may be smaller than its optimal value by at most $\varepsilon$ and supply may differ from demand by at most $δ$, and we find a sphere with the maximum radius inscribed into this set by solving a linear programming problem. We prove that the optimal radius is positive for positive tolerances, that it is non-decreasing, concave and piecewise linear with respect to the tolerances, and that it is bounded by the narrowest balance constraint, which is determined by a sales-concentration index of sectors. The approach is applied to the official input-output tables of Mongolia for 2010-2019 and 2024. The classical optimal plan has zero robustness, while the robust plan keeps 99.73% of the maximal GDP and, in a Monte Carlo simulation, tolerates independent deviations of all outputs and final demands of up to $\pm$0.30%. The margin of robust plans is limited by sectors with concentrated sales, mainly education and, increasingly, export-oriented mining, which indicates that a diversification of the users of mining output widens the set of robust plans.

items.title: TRACE: Governing AI-Assisted Research with Principles from Computer Science
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) makes it easier than ever to produce research outputs. The pressing question is how researchers should organize their work with this technology. The question is not new: software engineering and security research have long studied how teams of people and machines keep control of a shared body of work with many contributors. We distil principles from the practices these literatures report and transpose them to AI-assisted research. The principles form TRACE: Track records, Review against sources, Accept independently, Control transitions, and Evaluate corrections. Together, the five principles give researchers a common basis for remaining in control while integrating AI into their workflows. By bounding units of work and attending to how each is shaped, they help researchers pace AI-assisted work to human attention rather than to the speed at which AI produces content. We also introduce TRACE-OS, an open source operating system for AI-assisted research projects. It puts the principles into practice through shared instructions, tools, and records that fit researchers' existing workflows. The shared standard can contribute to building trust, which allows teams to delegate and realize the productivity that AI promises. More broadly, we aim to open a conversation about the governing principles through which the research community can benefit from AI.

items.title: A Characterization of Quantile Stable Matchings in Many-to-Many Markets
items.summary: We study two-sided many-to-many matching markets where agents' preferences satisfy strong substitutability and the law of aggregate demand (LAD). In this framework, the set of stable matchings forms a finite distributive lattice, and quantile stable matchings exist and satisfy the polarization of interests. Building on the cycle-reduction machinery of Bonifacio et al. (2022), we provide a purely combinatorial characterization of quantile stable matchings formulated in terms of preference cycles and their induced precedence order. Specifically, we define an order-theoretic counting function on cycles and prove that each quantile stable matching corresponds to the elimination of an endogenously determined closed set of cycles starting from the firm-optimal stable matching. This characterization extends the rotation-based framework of Cheng (2008) from one-to-one markets to many-to-many markets and bypasses the need for exhaustive outcome enumeration or partner sorting across the entire stable set.

items.title: Proportionality in Ranking Compression
items.summary: Motivated by applications in reinforcement learning from human feedback, we consider a setting where a given collection of rankings needs to be compressed into a smaller collection of rankings. This can also be seen as a combination of two fundamental social choice frameworks: ranking aggregation and multiwinner voting. We propose three proportionality notions that capture different types of representation in this setting: positional proportionality, pairwise proportionality, and proportionality for solid coalitions (PSC). On the one hand, we show that positional proportionality and PSC are always satisfiable for any input rankings and target compression size, and a desired output can be found in polynomial time. On the other hand, we prove that pairwise proportionality cannot be satisfied in general, but can nevertheless be attained when the input rankings are single-peaked or single-crossing.

items.title: Consistent Probabilistic Social Choice Revisited
items.summary: Brandl et al. (2016) characterized a probabilistic social choice function known as maximal lotteries within a framework based on fractional preference profiles, which abstracts away from individual voters. While this modeling assumption enables a more elegant and transparent proof, it complicates comparison with other results in the literature. The purpose of this note is to transfer their results to the standard model of social choice, where each preference profile is defined for a finite number of voters. Along the way, we prove a slightly stronger version of their main theorem that uses a weaker continuity condition and allows for real-valued (rather than only rational-valued) probabilities.

items.title: Identification of Child Penalties
items.summary: A large literature estimates child penalties using event studies by gender, normalizing by predicted earnings absent children and reporting the gender gap. I formalize the design's identification assumption: normalized parallel trend violations are equal across genders, which I term normalized triple differences (NTD). Under NTD, the conventional target, the gender gap in normalized effects, is not identified when parallel trends fails. However, the effect of parenthood on the gender earnings ratio is point identified. Using Israeli administrative data, I find that parenthood's share of gender inequality varies by age at first childbirth.

items.title: Existence of Equilibria in Large Competitive Markets with Bads, Production and Comprehensive Externalities
items.summary: This paper establishes existence of equilibrium in a measure-theoretic general equilibrium (MGE) model with production, bads, and comprehensive externalities. These features are jointly essential for modeling perfect competition in which emissions of production byproducts impose harm on agents. We show that, when bads and externalities are modeled in an economically natural way, equilibrium exists. This yields the first existence theorem with bads for MGE models, the benchmark for perfect competition, overcoming Hara (2005)'s nonexistence example. The proof uses nonstandard analysis, which provides a systematic technique to extend results for finite to infinite models.

items.title: The Source of Data Value: Consumer Disclosure, Access Design, and Platform Monetization
items.summary: Digital marketplaces increasingly earn revenue from transaction commissions and seller-facing data services. Sellers may purchase data to increase revenue or avoid competing with an informed rival. We examine how consumer disclosure rights shape these motives and the platform's incentive to provide data. We develop a game-theoretic model of a commissioned platform, two differentiated sellers, and privacy-sensitive consumers. Data generates value through bilateral sales-revenue gains and competition threats arising from asymmetric access. Under mandatory collection, the platform can monetize defensive adoption, even when bilateral personalization reduces seller revenue. Under voluntary disclosure, anonymous purchasing and strictly positive privacy costs make unilateral disclosure unattractive in the baseline. Exclusive access thus yields no usable information, restores sellers' no-data rejection payoffs, and eliminates defensive fees. Profitable provision therefore requires nonnegative bilateral revenue gains. Under full fee extraction, sellers retain their no-data net profits. This revenue alignment does not guarantee welfare gains: additional transactions may benefit consumers, whereas segmentation in an already covered market can raise anonymous prices and reduce welfare. Capping anonymous offers at their no-data benchmark protects individual consumers and limits positive-mass provision to the transaction-creation region. Extensions consider access choice, heterogeneous privacy costs, imperfect identification, and limited contractual credibility. Platforms should evaluate data services based on both bilateral-use and seller-rejection outcomes, and sellers should distinguish revenue-enhancing from defensive investments. Regulators should distinguish equal-access rules from effective consumer control and monitor pricing in anonymous channels.

items.title: Understanding the Mechanism of Altruism in Large Language Models
items.summary: Altruism is fundamental to human societies, fostering cooperation and social cohesion. While recent studies suggest that large language models (LLMs) can display human-like prosocial behavior, the underlying mechanism that produces such behavior remains unclear. We leverage sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to identify a set of features that contribute to an LLM's altruistic choices in the Dictator Game. We show that intervening on these features substantially shifts the model's allocations and produces similar effects in several other social decision scenarios. Together, these results link the model's prosocial output to internal features that can be identified and causally manipulated, providing a transparent approach to studying the computational basis of decision-making in LLMs.

items.title: Bystander on the Fence: Sanctions in a Multipolar World
items.summary: We provide a theory of optimal trade sanctions with three strategic players: Home (sanctioner), Foreign (target), and Bystander. Bystander may act unilaterally or ally with either party subject to a participation constraint. We derive three novel results. First, members of a coalition generically set different tariffs either under Stackelberg timing or when transfers are imperfect. Second, as sanctions tighten, Home's welfare can improve even beyond the unilateral terms-of-trade optimum due to strategic interactions. Third, we characterize feasible sanctions targets when Home and Foreign compete for Bystander's support. An alternative implementation arises with competition: Home lets Foreign win, but Foreign's transfer to Bystander implements the sanctions target. We apply our model to sanctions against Russian crude. In a calibration exercise, cooperation among India, China, and Russia best matches observed data. Sanctions could have been roughly 70% more effective had China and India acted unilaterally or had the sanctioning coalition made them a better offer.

items.title: Advertising to Agents: Measuring Description-Framing Bias in LLM Tool Selection
items.summary: AI agents often pick tools from registries, where each provider writes its tool's description; we ask whether sales language there changes which tool an agent picks. We built pairs of listings that differ in one way (praise, a verifiable specification, or list order) and asked two OpenAI models to call one tool. In a preregistered study, stacked praise (four kinds) raised a tool's pick rate by about 43 percentage points, matching or beating a verifiable specification. Praise also pulled some picks toward tools whose numeric limit was too small. With identical listings, the first-listed tool was picked about 72 points more often. Structured fields helped agents pick the capable tool; sales text beside them reduced or erased that gain. An exploratory study of five models shows the same direction; a "Sponsored" label dampened it, and a system-prompt warning moved one model. Registries could list limits as fields, hide sales text from agents, and randomize order. Stacked praise replicated on held-out domains; no single kind did after correcting for multiple tests. Preregistered results are provisional until blind phrase ratings are complete, and cover two small models.

items.title: Contracting against a Non-contractible Outsider
items.summary: I study a general framework of contracting with externalities involving a non-contractible outsider. Strategic symmetry between the insider agent and the outsider is the source of multiple equilibria, even when their actions are strategic substitutes. To tackle strategic uncertainty, the principal guarantees a unique equilibrium outcome. A novel duality approach reformulates her problem as the choice of a series of agent expectations about outsider behavior, one for each agent action. The key constraint comes from eliminating undesired equilibria: she cannot convince the agent to expect higher incentives than those generated by the outsider's best responses to the actions she has already conquered. To reduce strategic rents, the principal optimally induces attenuated agent incentives. In supermodular or submodular environments, her coordination power and commitment power are substitutes in determining the contracting outcome, and perfect substitutes under further conditions. On contractual privacy, the principal can strictly prefer private contracting over public contracting, in sharp contrast to the benchmark that ignores robustness. Applications include regulating international competition, platform design, and labor union contracting.

items.title: Estimation of Panel Data Models with Nonlinear Factor Structure
items.summary: Panel data models with unobserved heterogeneity in the form of interactive effects standardly assume that the time effects -- or ``common factors'' -- enter linearly. This assumption is restrictive because it concerns an unobserved component of the model, for which a particular functional form is rarely justified. By contrast, linearity in the observable regressors can often be motivated by economic theory or empirical convention. Linearity in the factors has persisted mainly because it is convenient and improves on standard fixed effects. This paper relaxes that assumption by combining the common correlated effects (CCE) approach with sieve methods. The resulting estimator -- abbreviated ``SCCE'' -- preserves key advantages of CCE, including computational simplicity and good small-sample and asymptotic properties, while allowing for a broader class of factor structures that nests the linear case. This makes it suitable for a wide range of empirical applications.

items.title: Accuracy of Uniform Inference on Fine Grid Points
items.summary: Uniform confidence bands are widely used in empirical analysis for uncertainty qualification of nonparametric inference of unknown functions. A variety of simple implementation methods, including multiplier bootstrap, have been proposed and theoretically justified. However, an implementation over a literally continuous index set is generally computationally infeasible, and practitioners therefore compute the critical value by evaluating the statistic on a finite evaluation grid. This paper quantifies the effect of this discretization on coverage accuracy and investigates how fine the evaluation grid must be to ensure valid uniform inference. We first illustrate through simulations of a kernel-based nonparametric estimator that coarse grids can invalidate uniform inference. Surprisingly, increasing the sample size can worsen coverage on a fixed coarse grid, even as the remaining approximation error on the grid decreases. We then derive general upper bounds on the coverage probability and coverage error of uniform confidence bands based on finite-grid multiplier-bootstrap critical values. These bounds distinguish discretization error from the remaining approximation error on the grid. For local empirical processes arising from kernel smoothing, we further establish primitive conditions under which coverage converges to zero, even when the number of grid points diverges, and conditions under which asymptotically nominal coverage is attained. These results yield rate-sharp grid resolution requirements in terms of the bandwidth.

items.title: Hidden Commitment Power Is Powerless
items.summary: A principal who offers a contract may renege when her default option is sufficiently attractive. The size of this temptation, which inversely measures her commitment power, is often the principal's private information. This paper asks how contracting outcomes change under this information asymmetry. Disciplining off-path beliefs with the Intuitive Criterion, I find that every type of principal behaves and earns payoffs as if she were commonly known to have the least commitment power. Hidden commitment power is therefore powerless, although commitment power can be valuable under symmetric information. The result delivers an unambiguous policy lesson on how to mitigate this information asymmetry prior to contracting: only measures that improve the worst case have value. In an application to credit rating, when the cost of a rating system grows with its number of grades, a rating system that sorts issuers into ordered bands is optimal, and each issuer contracts on the terms warranted by the floor of her band.

items.title: Designing Experiments for External Decision Makers
items.summary: Standard Bayesian experimental design (BED) methods assume the experimenter alone will act on the data, choosing the best action given their own beliefs and goals. In practice, data are often acted on by external parties whose procedures the experimenter cannot change and may not know, particularly when the data are released publicly.
